inventory_refs.area_of_law: Attorney's fees — EAJA fee awards for administrative deportation proceedings as APA §554 adjudications
inventory_refs.caption: Ardestani v. INS

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's opinion joined by Stone, White, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter; six of eight participants.
metadata.Controlling explanation: EAJA did not refer generally to formal or trial-type agency hearings; it chose adjudications “under section 554.” *Marcello* establishes that the INA's deportation procedure supersedes the APA hearing provisions and supplies the exclusive statutory source for this proceeding. Functional similarity and agency regulations cannot enlarge Congress's fee authorization. EAJA's remedial purpose supports extending protection through enacted language, but it cannot erase the selected cross-reference. *Sullivan v. Hudson* involved administrative work integral to a qualifying court action and supplies no such predicate for this standalone administrative request. Because coverage fails, the Court does not review whether the agency's position was substantially justified under *Pierce*. The asylum award, judicial EAJA claims with their own predicate, and any separately presented constitutional claim remain open.
metadata.Dates and route: Argued October 8 and decided December 10, 1991, on certiorari to the Eleventh Circuit, 904 F.2d 1505.
metadata.Dependencies: *MCorp* reinforces attention to a specific administrative statutory structure but does not decide EAJA. *Hafer* does not govern federal fee liability. The same-day *Simon & Schuster* decision is uncoordinated and uses the common start-of-day baseline.
metadata.Dissent: Blackmun, joined by Stevens, reads the cross-reference functionally to cover a statutorily required, on-the-record adversary hearing where the United States is represented.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: An administrative deportation hearing governed by the INA's exclusive procedure rather than by 5 U.S.C. §554 is not an adjudication “under section 554” and therefore is outside EAJA §504's administrative fee authorization, even if the hearing resembles a formal APA adjudication.
metadata.Judgment: Eleventh Circuit affirmed, 6-2. Stone, White, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter support affirmance; Blackmun and Stevens dissent.
metadata.Law after decision: Effective December 10, INA deportation hearings outside §554 governance do not qualify for administrative EAJA §504 awards.
metadata.Natural key: *Ardestani v. INS*, 502 U.S. 129 (1991), No. 90-1141; merits decision; December 10, 1991; OT1991.
metadata.Opinion: O'Connor writes for the Court, joined by Stone, White, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter. Stone assigns O'Connor as Chief Justice in the majority.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Marcello* is applied; *Sullivan v. Hudson* is distinguished; *Shaw* and *Pierce* remain unchanged.
metadata.Published noncontrolling position: Blackmun and Stevens would treat “under section 554” as a functional category encompassing statutorily required on-the-record adversary adjudications with government counsel. Noncontrolling dissent.
metadata.Question and relief: Whether an administrative deportation hearing is an adjudication under 5 U.S.C. §554 for EAJA §504. Ardestani seeks restoration of a $1,071.85 administrative fee award.
metadata.Remedy: No administrative fee award under §504. Ardestani's asylum grant remains undisturbed.
metadata.Stage: Plenary merits review; affirmance closes the Supreme Court and administrative fee matter while leaving asylum intact.

metadata.Issue-specific snapshot: 4 U.S.C. §111; relevant Kansas income-tax and pension provisions; Davis, 489 U.S. 803; Phillips Chemical, 361 U.S. 376; Tyler, 105 U.S. 244; McCarty, 453 U.S. 210; 10 U.S.C. §1408(c)(1); 26 U.S.C. §219(f)(1). Davis requires a significant difference directly related to and justifying unequal tax treatment. Current Romein (March 9) concerns retroactive economic obligations, not tax-refund entitlement. McKesson and the supported propositions in Beam remain relevant if preserved retrospective-remedy questions arise on remand; neither is resolved here. Kraft occurs later in the inventory, and no later Harper rule enters.
metadata.Material record and requested relief: Military retirees and, where applicable, their spouses challenged taxes paid for tax years 1984–1989 in two class actions. Kansas exempted state and local pensions and certain federal retirement benefits while taxing military retired pay. The State relied chiefly on retained service status, discipline, employment restrictions and recall to characterize military pay as current compensation for reduced current services. Benefits were calculated by rank and completed years of service. The Kansas courts upheld the tax and therefore did not decide remaining retrospective-relief questions. The requested relief includes declaratory and injunctive relief and refunds, but the record does not establish a present individual refund amount.

inventory_refs.caption: Barnhill v. Johnson

metadata.Component application: Each numbered holding below operates on this snapshot; its identified authorities supply the applicable triggers, burdens, presumptions, exceptions and scope. Jurisdiction and remedies remain separate from the merits. No other current-term rule materially changes the stated issue. Refreshed later-date snapshots distinguish the intervening decisions rather than importing unrelated holdings. The provisional and reconciled positions remain valid under those refreshes.
metadata.Effective state: March 24 completed-law baseline (ledger entries 1–51); Suter remains stopped. No March 25 event supplies law to another March 25 event. Holmes remains unadjudicated; no RICO/SIPA law is assumed. Wyoming’s January 22 injunction and retained implementation jurisdiction remain, without a new filing.
metadata.Issue-specific statutory, constitutional: Section 547(b) requires a transfer of the debtor’s property and its other preference elements; §101(54) defines transfer broadly. Under McKenzie, 323 U.S. 365, transfer timing is federal law, while state law identifies the property interest. New Mexico commercial law does not assign the bank funds upon delivery of an ordinary check. Section 547(e)(2)(A) does not make a transfer take effect before an interest passes. Wolas (December 11) leaves §547(c)(2) available for long-term debt if each ordinary-course element is proved and supplies no timing rule. Dewsnup and Germain concern other bankruptcy questions. No operative opening Standards entry exists.
metadata.Material record and posture: The ordinary check was delivered November 18, dated November 19, and honored November 20. The parties’ chronology places honor on the ninetieth day before the bankruptcy petition. Delivery preceded the preference window. Before payment, the drawer retained control of the account and could stop payment. The state-law rules distinguish the payee’s instrument and claim against the drawer from any interest in bank funds.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Banking and bankruptcy — jurisdiction to enjoin Federal Reserve enforcement proceedings; Leedom v. Kyne review
inventory_refs.caption: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System v. MCorp Financial, Inc.

metadata.Application and remedy: The injunction against the source-of-strength proceeding is removed; the refusal to enjoin the §23A proceeding stands. Both may continue.
metadata.Authority: Stevens's opinion for the Court, joined by Stone, White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter; unanimous participating Court.
metadata.Case: *Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System v. MCorp Financial, Inc.*, 502 U.S. 32 (1991); Nos. 90-913 and 90-914; OT1991.
metadata.Chronology: First event in the uncoordinated December 3 group; it and *Griffin* use the same start-of-day baseline.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Section 1818(i)(1) expressly withdraws jurisdiction to affect the issuance or enforcement of Board notices or orders except as the statute provides. Congress separately authorized prompt challenges to temporary orders, appellate review of final orders, and Board enforcement actions; this adversary action fits none. Bankruptcy Code §362(b)(4) supplies an exception allowing governmental police and regulatory proceedings to continue. Sections 362(a)(3) and (a)(6) do not stop these ongoing, nonfinal proceedings, which have not seized estate property or recovered a prepetition claim. Section 1334 does not alter the result because the Board is not another “court,” and continuation before a final order does not displace bankruptcy-court control of estate property. *Leedom v. Kyne* supplied exceptional review when a specific statutory right otherwise would be lost. Here §1818(h)(2) preserves meaningful judicial review of the regulation's authority and application after a final order, while §1818(i)(1) directly manifests preclusion now. The Court reserves the regulation's validity and any actual conflict at enforcement.
metadata.Event: Merits decision December 3, 1991, after argument October 7, on certiorari to the Fifth Circuit, 900 F.2d 852.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Section 1818(i)(1) bars a district court from enjoining an ongoing Board notice-or-order proceeding except through channels that §1818 itself authorizes. Neither general bankruptcy jurisdiction nor *Leedom v. Kyne* supplies an alternative intervention channel where the proceeding falls within the governmental regulatory exception and meaningful review of a final order remains available.
metadata.Law after decision: The statutory-channel rule enters simulated law December 3, 1991. No agency-deference rule changes.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Kyne* is confined to absence of meaningful later review; *Boire*'s narrow understanding is applied.
metadata.Question / relief: Whether bankruptcy jurisdiction or *Leedom v. Kyne* permitted an injunction against two ongoing Board proceedings despite 12 U.S.C. §1818(i)(1).
metadata.Stage: Merits pending before; both regulatory proceedings may continue through statutory channels after the judgment.
metadata.Validation: Complete; shared same-day baseline, participation, 8-0 component arithmetic, judgment/remedy, joins, and reservations checked. True blindness was unavailable. Durable location is this file; committed September 14, 2026.

metadata.Action and judgment: Affirmed and remanded with modified instructions; ad valorem authority 8-1, sales-excise prohibition 9-0.
metadata.Ad valorem holding and operative rule: The General Allotment Act's established fee-land rule and the Burke Act proviso authorize state ad valorem taxation of reservation land validly patented in fee under that Act, including qualifying land later held by the Nation. The tax follows the land, but patent source and any independently applicable federal protection must be determined parcel by parcel.
metadata.Authority: Scalia's opinion joined by eight Justices.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Blackfeet* requires unmistakably clear congressional authorization, and here the County relies on more than alienability or policy inference. *Goudy* construed the General Allotment Act to permit taxation following an ordinary fee patent, while the Burke Act proviso expressly addresses removal of restrictions on sale, encumbrance, and taxation. The Indian Reorganization Act halted future allotments and preserved trust periods but also created a distinct mechanism for restoring land to trust; it does not automatically return every existing fee parcel to tax-protected status. *Mancari* requires compatible enactments to operate together. *Moe* rejects general personal taxing jurisdiction over reservation Indians, but a specific tax on qualifying land does not revive that discarded jurisdiction. *Brendale*'s fractured analysis of tribal regulation of nonmember land supplies no governmental-impact test for this statutory tax question. Remand is necessary because the stipulated record does not establish every parcel's patent source.
metadata.Issues not reached: Constitutional, as-applied, merits, damages, enforcement, or other collateral questions expressly reserved in the public action were not decided.
metadata.Law after decision: Qualifying GAA fee land is subject to ad valorem taxation; sales of that land by Indian owners remain outside the identified authorization.
metadata.Law-entering snapshot: The October 7 opening baseline plus all effective records through the preceding date. Earlier same-term decisions were checked and none displaced the issue-specific pre-divergence authorities identified below. The question and remedy were confined to the supplied record and posture.
metadata.Natural key: *County of Yakima v. Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakima Indian Nation*, 502 U.S. 251 (1992), Nos. 90-408 and 90-577; merits decision; January 14, 1992; OT1991.
metadata.Opinions and assignment: Scalia writes for Stone, White, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and himself; Blackmun concurs on excise and dissents on ad valorem authority. Stone, as Chief Justice in the judgment coalition, made the assignment where an authored Court opinion issued.
metadata.Participation: All nine Justices participated. Quorum was present; a majority of participating Justices controlled.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Goudy* is reaffirmed for qualifying GAA fee land; *Blackfeet*, *Mancari*, and *Moe* are applied and preserved; *Brendale* is distinguished.
metadata.Route and question: Argued November 5, 1991 on certiorari to the Ninth Circuit; whether ad valorem and sales-excise taxes may reach reservation fee land.
metadata.Sales-excise holding and operative rule: Congressional permission to tax qualifying fee land ad valorem does not unmistakably authorize a tax imposed on an Indian owner's sale of that land; securing the transactional tax with a lien does not change its legal incidence.
metadata.Stage before and after: Supreme Court merits or original-writ disposition; after the action, Supreme Court proceedings close and any stated remand returns to the identified lower court.

inventory_refs.caption: Estelle v. McGuire

metadata.Approved source: Section II version 1, expressly approved by the user for this Run. Its status line is superseded by that direct approval.
metadata.Argument and decision: Stone, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter participated. Thomas did not participate because argument preceded his October 23 oath.
metadata.Authority: White's opinion, joined on this proposition by all eight participating Justices.
metadata.Channel: Federal habeas review under then-current 28 U.S.C. §2254.
metadata.Chronology dependency: The December 3 *Griffin* rule concerns a factually unsupported lawful object in a general verdict. It does not govern whether this instruction relieved the State of elemental proof. The December 4 group shares a start-of-day baseline.
metadata.Dates: Argued October 9, 1991; decided December 4, 1991. The decision date is the manifest's historical ordering date and is confirmed by the reporter and docket.
metadata.Discretion envelope: Only nonmaterial wording and compatible joins were used; no substantive narrowing or additional ground was supplied.
metadata.Entering law: *Lewis v. Jeffers* and *Pulley v. Harris* exclude mere state-law error; *Lisenba* and *Dowling* reserve habeas relief for evidentiary use producing fundamental unfairness. *Winship* requires proof of every element. *Cupp* requires whole-charge review; *Francis* and *Sandstrom* forbid relieving the State of elemental persuasion; *County Court v. Allen* separately governs permissive inferences. *Boyde* supplies reasonable-likelihood analysis of ambiguous instructions. *Teague* restricts new collateral-review rules. If constitutional instructional error exists, *Rose* permits harmless-error review and *Chapman* places on the State the burden to prove harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt. No later AEDPA or *Brecht* rule is used.
metadata.Final position: Stone votes to vacate and remand. He joins the evidence-admissibility proposition of the Court's opinion and joins O'Connor's separate opinion on the instruction and remedy.
metadata.Fixed core: Vacate and remand for harmless-error review. Reject evidence-alone and state-law grounds; hold that evidence of repeated nonaccidental injuries can establish intentional harm without identifying the abuser, but that this charge created a reasonable likelihood that jurors attributed unidentified injuries to McGuire and inferred the charged killing without independently finding the required facts. Apply established *Winship*, *Francis*, *Sandstrom*, *Boyde*, *Rose*, and *Chapman* rules; reserve a general propensity-evidence rule.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: On federal habeas review, evidence of a child's prior nonaccidental injuries may be relevant to prove that the charged death was intentional even when the identity of the person who caused the earlier injuries is unknown. Admission for that nonidentity purpose does not itself violate due process, and a defendant's choice not to contest accident does not remove the State's burden to prove intentional killing.
metadata.Issues reached: Federal constitutional effect of the evidence and charge. State-law admissibility alone is not reviewed.
metadata.Judgment: 5-3. White, Blackmun, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter reverse the Ninth Circuit. Stone, Stevens, and O'Connor would vacate and remand for harmless-error review.
metadata.Natural key: *Estelle v. McGuire*, 502 U.S. 62 (1991), No. 90-1074; merits decision; December 4, 1991; October Term 1991.
metadata.Opinion of the Court: White, assigned by White as the senior Justice in the judgment majority, writes for the Court. Blackmun, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter join throughout. Stone, Stevens, and O'Connor join the evidence proposition but not the instruction or final-disposition portions.
metadata.Quorum and threshold: Eight qualified participants; six constitute a quorum; five votes control the judgment.
metadata.Relief sought: The warden requests reversal; McGuire requests habeas relief from his conviction.
metadata.Remedy: The federal habeas writ remains denied; no acquittal, retrial, or release is ordered.
metadata.Review and question: On certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 902 F.2d 749, which reversed the denial of federal habeas relief. The Court considers whether evidence of prior injuries, or the instructions governing its use, made the trial fundamentally unfair or relieved California of proving McGuire's identity as the killer.
metadata.Separate writing: O'Connor, joined by Stone and Stevens, concurs in the evidence ruling and dissents from the instruction holding and judgment. They would vacate and remand for the Ninth Circuit to decide harmlessness beyond a reasonable doubt on the full record.
metadata.Stage: Plenary merits review before decision. After decision, the Ninth Circuit judgment is reversed and the federal habeas proceeding ends without relief.

National Solid Wastes Management: Exactly five Justices support only the limited negative holding that §18 does not automatically displace supplementary occupational-safety rules merely because a federal standard overlaps and no state plan is approved. Souter's broader impossibility-only approach has four votes and is noncontrolling. Stone-Zsela's separate reservation for demonstrated conflict or clear exclusivity is not a new Court-wide test. Existing conflict authority remains, and provisions return for an actual basis of displacement. This statutory §18 holding does not decide the constitutional allocation of who must administer a program, negate Congress's enumerated commerce authority, authorize a court-created federal fallback, or hold all regulation with dual purposes immune from displacement.
metadata.Georgia v. McCollum: The five-Justice Court attributes a defendant's use of state peremptory authority to government for that jury-selection act, permits the State's supported assertion of jurors' rights, and applies ordinary Batson burdens. metadata.Kraft General Foods v. Iowa Department o: Domestic/foreign dividend discrimination is invalid on the specified comparison; partial incorporation of federal tax definitions is not congressional permission to discriminate, and administrative convenience does not overcome reasonable neutral alternatives. The rule preserves the distinction between actual congressional authorization and an inference from partial federal conformity. No general foreign-commerce or state-sovereignty rule decides an unpresented question.
metadata.Nordlinger v. Hahn: The Court retains ordinary rational-basis review, independently supports acquisition-value taxation on neighborhood continuity and existing-owner reliance, sustains the specified exceptions, and rejects assertion of absent travelers' rights without the necessary relationship and obstacle. Allegheny Pittsburgh is retained. Its personal-injury/third-party distinction remains relevant to identifying whose rights are at issue; it establishes no rule governing speech-license costs or federal direction of state governments.

Jurisdiction and remedies remain separate from the merits. No other current-term rule materially changes the stated issue. Refreshed later-date snapshots distinguish the intervening decisions rather than importing unrelated holdings. The provisional and reconciled positions remain valid under those refreshes.
metadata.Effective state: Completed March 25 decisions: Felix, Barnhill, Amtrak and Robertson, added to ledger entries 1–51. Suter and same-day Montana remain stopped; no law is inferred from either. Holmes remains unadjudicated; no RICO/SIPA law is assumed. Wyoming’s January 22 injunction and retained implementation jurisdiction remain, without a new filing.
metadata.Issue-specific statutory, constitutional: Brown I, 347 U.S. 483, and Brown II, 349 U.S. 294, require repair of state-imposed school segregation. Green, 391 U.S. 430, imposes an affirmative duty to eliminate its vestiges and identifies nonexclusive operational areas. Swann, 402 U.S. 1, ties equitable power to the violation and places responsibility on the district to explain remaining imbalance. Spangler, 427 U.S. 424, limits perpetual balancing for independently caused changes after compliance. Dowell, 498 U.S. 237, requires good-faith compliance and practicable elimination of vestiges. Milliken II, 433 U.S. 267, preserves local control consistent with an effective remedy. Rufo (January 15), Stone with White, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter, requires significant changed circumstances making continued enforcement inequitable and a suitably tailored modification; it preserves decree purposes and consent obligations beyond federal minima and expressly does not substitute for the school-decree termination inquiry. Its consent-modification threshold is not an additional prerequisite to finding that an obligation has been fulfilled. Suter and Montana remain uncommitted; neither supplies entering law. No operative opening Standards entry exists.
metadata.Material record and posture: A 1969 decree required dismantling DeKalb County’s dual school system. On the district’s 1986 dismissal request, the trial court found compliance in student assignment, transportation, facilities and extracurricular activities, but retained supervision over faculty and administrative assignments and educational resources and quality. It attributed the challenged student imbalance to demographic change and praised the district’s progress. The Eleventh Circuit required simultaneous compliance across all Green factors for several years. The factual findings, the legal completeness of the causal inquiry, and whether control in one area remains useful to cure another are distinct questions. Neither the Court’s judgment nor praise for progress establishes final systemwide compliance.

metadata.Application and remedy: The sufficiently supported IRS object sustains the conviction against this general-verdict challenge; no retrial or acquittal is ordered.
metadata.Authority: Scalia's opinion for the Court, joined at this proposition by Stone, White, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Souter; seven of eight participating Justices. Blackmun concurred only in the judgment.
metadata.Case: *Griffin v. United States*, 502 U.S. 46 (1991); No. 90-6352; OT1991.
metadata.Chronology: Second event in the uncoordinated December 3 group; start-of-day entering law shared with *MCorp*.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Stromberg v. California* and *Yates v. United States* supply the rule that a general verdict cannot stand when the jury may have selected a legally forbidden basis, because jurors cannot be expected to identify and disregard an invalid legal theory. *Turner v. United States* supplies the different rule for evidentiary inadequacy: jurors are ordinarily equipped to reject a lawful theory that the proof does not support. Both alleged objects here were legally capable of constituting a §371 conspiracy. The Government conceded that evidence did not connect Griffin to the DEA object, but the record contained sufficient proof on the IRS object under *Jackson v. Virginia*, which preserves the rational-factfinder inquiry, and *Winship*, which preserves proof beyond reasonable doubt. The trial court should ordinarily withdraw an unsupported route when timely asked, but preferable trial administration is not an independent constitutional reversal rule. The Court leaves legal invalidity, failure on all routes, element-diluting instructions, and an independently preserved unanimity issue open.
metadata.Event: Merits decision December 3, 1991, after argument October 7, on certiorari to the Seventh Circuit, 913 F.2d 337.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A general guilty verdict on a federal multiple-object conspiracy need not be set aside merely because the evidence is inadequate for one legally valid object when another object is supported sufficiently under the unchanged beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard. This rule does not govern a legally invalid object, failure of proof on every route, an element-diluting instruction, or a properly presented independent unanimity defect.
metadata.Law after decision: The factual-versus-legal inadequacy distinction enters simulated law December 3, 1991.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Turner* is applied; *Yates* and *Stromberg* are distinguished and preserved for legal invalidity; *Winship* and *Jackson* remain unchanged.
metadata.Question / relief: Whether a general multiple-object conspiracy verdict must be reversed when one lawful object lacks evidentiary support and another is sufficiently proved. Griffin sought reversal.
metadata.Stage: Merits pending before; conviction affirmed and Supreme Court proceedings concluded.

inventory_refs.caption: Hafer v. Melo

metadata.Application and remedy: The individual-capacity claims may proceed; no damages or reinstatement are awarded now.
metadata.Authority: O'Connor's opinion for the Court, joined by Stone, White, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter; unanimous participating Court.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Section 1983 reaches a “person” who, under color of state law, causes a federal-rights deprivation. *Kentucky v. Graham* supplies the capacity distinction: an official-capacity claim represents the government, while an individual-capacity claim seeks liability from the officer. *Will v. Michigan Department of State Police* excluded States and official-capacity damages defendants; its reference to officials acting officially described the capacity in which they were sued, not every act performed with state authority. *Scheuer v. Rhodes* confirms that executive officers may face personal liability, and *Monroe v. Pape* supplies the principle that misuse of official power remains action under color of law. Here the Court of Appeals construed the damages claims as personal claims against Hafer. Her authority to discharge employees provides the state-law nexus; it does not convert her into Pennsylvania for every remedy. Concerns about lawful administration are addressed through personal immunity doctrine, not categorical personhood. The Court leaves the alleged constitutional violations, qualified immunity, damages, and entitlement to reinstatement unresolved.
metadata.Event: Merits decision November 5, 1991, after argument October 15, 1991, on certiorari to the Third Circuit, 912 F.2d 628.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A state officer sued in an individual capacity is a “person” under 42 U.S.C. §1983 even when the challenged act was undertaken through official authority, and state sovereign immunity does not independently bar a judgment payable by that officer personally. The plaintiff must still prove the officer's own violation under color of law, and the officer retains applicable personal immunities.
metadata.Law after decision: The holding enters simulated §1983 law effective November 5, 1991. No immunity standard changes.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Will* is clarified and preserved for States and official-capacity damages; *Graham*, *Scheuer*, and *Monroe* are applied. *Ex parte Young*'s prospective-relief channel remains unchanged.
metadata.Question / relief: Whether a state officer sued individually is a §1983 person for official conduct. Hafer sought dismissal; respondents sought continued litigation.
metadata.Stage: Merits pending before; judgment affirmed and ordinary proceedings below follow.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Federal Employers' Liability Act — state-owned railroad liability in state court and sovereign immunity
inventory_refs.caption: Hilton v. South Carolina Public Railways Commission

metadata.Action and judgment: Reversed and remanded, 6-2; Stone, White, Blackmun, Stevens, Kennedy, and Souter support reversal; O'Connor and Scalia dissent.
metadata.Authority: Kennedy's opinion joined by five of eight participants supplies the controlling rationale; Blackmun supplies the sixth judgment vote.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Parden* separately interpreted FELA's coverage of “every” interstate common carrier and treated operation of a railroad as waiver of federal-court immunity. *Welch* displaced the constructive-waiver rationale but expressly reserved statutory coverage. The remaining construction has governed the specialized railroad relationship for decades, Congress retained the relevant language, and States and employees arranged compensation against that background—including South Carolina's exclusion of FELA-covered employees from workers' compensation. *Will* construed a different statutory term and does not silently overrule the specific FELA holding. Statutory stare decisis thus requires retaining the independently grounded coverage rule unless the Court squarely abandons it. Under *Howlett*, a competent state court may not use state immunity to defeat a defendant's liability under valid federal law. The Court does not reopen Hilton's dismissed federal suit, decide negligence, or announce that entering commerce generally waives immunity.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: FELA's established inclusion of state-owned interstate railroads remains enforceable in a competent state court. This rule does not revive constructive waiver of Eleventh Amendment immunity in federal court or establish a general rule for every Article I damages action against a State.
metadata.Issues not reached: Constitutional, as-applied, merits, damages, enforcement, or other collateral questions expressly reserved in the public action were not decided.
metadata.Law after decision: State-owned interstate railroads remain FELA defendants in competent state courts under the specific retained precedent.
metadata.Law-entering snapshot: The October 7 opening baseline plus all effective records through the preceding date. Earlier same-term decisions were checked and none displaced the issue-specific pre-divergence authorities identified below. The question and remedy were confined to the supplied record and posture.
metadata.Natural key: *Hilton v. South Carolina Public Railways Commission*, 502 U.S. 197 (1991), No. 90-848; merits decision; December 16, 1991; OT1991.
metadata.Opinions and assignment: Kennedy writes for Stone, White, Stevens, Souter, and himself; Blackmun concurs in judgment; O'Connor dissents joined by Scalia. Stone, as Chief Justice in the judgment coalition, made the assignment where an authored Court opinion issued.

Germain (March 9; Thomas, Stone, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter) preserves overlapping statutes with their own conditions; its four judgment-only writers adopt no contrary participation-to-liability rule. Molzof (January 14; Thomas for all nine) permits established legal language to carry its traditional meaning without inventing a functional screen. There is no applicable register title, Present operation effective entry or Current wording authority to invent. Current-term records supplement that baseline by effective date.
metadata.Questions and lawful channel: Under 28 U.S.C. §1254(1), review concerns SIPC's right to sue under §1964(c) when its nonpurchasing customers could not maintain the implied securities action. Proximate cause is fairly included in that right-to-sue question under then-effective Rule 14.1(a), and was briefed despite SIPC's scope objection. The separate question about responsibility for coconspirators' acts was not granted and is assumed without decision. SIPC's asserted §78eee(d) basis for recovering its own advances is separately resolved. No new certiorari event or poll is created.
metadata.RICO issue snapshot: Sections 1961, 1962(c) and (d), and 1964(c), as effective in 1992, supply the predicate, violation, business/property injury and causal requirements. Sedima rejects a special racketeering injury and prior-conviction requirement. Associated General Contractors construes analogous Clayton Act language using common-law causal limits; Agency Holding identifies the close statutory relationship but decides limitations, not this case's causation issue. Blue Chip Stamps governs the implied §10(b)/Rule 10b-5 action; extending its purchaser-seller rule to RICO remained open. Celotex and Rule 56 distinguish an essential legal defect from genuine factual disputes. No new evidentiary burden, damages measure, limitation period or conspiracy-liability rule enters this decision.
metadata.Record, lower judgment and relief: SIPC obtained protective decrees for First State Securities Corporation and Joseph Sebag, Inc. in July 1981. SIPC and their liquidation trustees sued in 1983 over an alleged conspiracy to manipulate six companies' stock. Alleged false statements and trading created artificial prices; losses on the brokers' proprietary holdings allegedly caused insolvency and customer shortfalls. SIPC advanced nearly $13 million to satisfy customer claims and separately funded liquidation administration. The amounts, causation and fraud remain allegations, not liability findings. The district court found genuine issues concerning conspiracy participation and actual causation but entered a Rule 54(b) judgment for Holmes, applying a purchaser-seller restriction and isolating Holmes's conduct in its proximity analysis. The Ninth Circuit reversed, rejecting that restriction for RICO and treating the alleged conspiracy as a whole. Holmes seeks relief from SIPC's permitted recovery; SIPC asserts customer subrogation and its own statutory claim. Trustees' standing was not challenged in this Court. A separate securities judgment concerning unauthorized use of customer assets was not appealed.
metadata.SIPA issue snapshot: Section 78eee(d) grants participation, hearing and intervention rights; §78fff-3(b)(2) imposes administration-advance duties when the estate is insufficient. Customer subrogation in §78fff-3(a) is distinct; the absence of equivalent express text in (b) is not a ruling that every other-law subrogation right is impossible. Barbour's 1975 denial of a customer action to compel SIPC predates the 1978 addition of (d) and does not decide SIPC's own third-party claim. Each statutory route requires separate analysis.
metadata.Stage: Before: plenary merits review of the certified partial judgment. After: this Supreme Court review ends; the Ninth Circuit must give effect to judgment for Holmes on the two SIPC claims and conduct further proceedings consistent with the preserved claims. No retained Supreme Court proceeding or later mandate-issuance date is invented.

metadata.Action and judgment: Vacated and remanded, 6-2 on the controlling disposition; no directed immunity. The separate warrant ruling remains intact.
metadata.Authority: Stone's opinion joined by Stone, Blackmun, O'Connor, Kennedy, and Souter; five of eight participants and therefore controlling.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Harlow*, *Anderson v. Creighton*, and *Malley* protect reasonable mistakes and require early judicial resolution where supported facts permit it. Rule 56 nevertheless requires the court to identify genuine disputes about historical predicates and draw supported inferences for the nonmovant. The agents could consider the assassination references, reported gesture, oral statements, confusing interview, and refusal to elaborate. They also had the letter itself, which repeatedly attributed the supposed plot to an outside group; that feature matters to whether Bryant communicated a serious threat prohibited by §871 or reported an imagined danger. *Watts* supplies the contextual distinction between a true threat and protected expression. The Ninth Circuit erred by asking which interpretation was more reasonable and by suggesting the legal immunity issue belonged generally to a jury. But the opposite error would treat presidential-security concern as dispositive without connecting the accepted facts to the offense. The remand court must decide immunity promptly after specifying any supported material dispute; the Court finds neither guilt, innocence, bad faith, nor a constitutional violation.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Qualified immunity from a claim of arrest without probable cause is a legal question for the judge under ordinary summary-judgment constraints. A court must evaluate whether a reasonable officer could believe the arrest lawful on the supported nonmovant version of the complete contemporaneous record; choosing the “more reasonable” interpretation is not the test, but a generalized security concern alone does not establish reasonable belief that the elements of the offense were satisfied.

metadata.Law after decision: Qualified immunity remains judge-decided and protects reasonable probable-cause mistakes, subject to Rule 56's supported-fact constraints and offense-specific analysis.

metadata.Authority: Stevens's unanimous opinion for all nine Justices.

metadata.Controlling explanation: Section 242(a) authorizes release on conditions prescribed by the Attorney General; it does not restrict every condition to securing physical appearance. The regulation's heading, exception, contemporaneous explanation, and operating instructions establish that its target is unauthorized employment. *Witkovich* requires delegated immigration authority to remain connected to the statutory scheme, and Congress's labor-market protections supply that connection. *American Hospital Association* permits general rules to structure delegated discretion so long as legally required individual determinations remain. Here officials must determine existing work authorization, address colorable citizenship or status claims, and consider the regulation's avenue for discretionary relief. The narrower construction therefore defeats the proposition that every application exceeds statutory authority. The Court does not approve interference with lawful employment, presume disputed deportability, decide the complaint's constitutional claims, or foreclose an as-applied challenge where the represented procedures are unavailable or misused.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: INA §242(a) permits a generally applicable release condition forbidding unauthorized employment when the regulation is construed not to reach authorized workers and retains individual status determinations and discretionary relief. That facial statutory ruling does not resolve constitutional objections or particular misapplications.

metadata.Issue-specific statutory, constitutional: Sorrells, 287 U.S. 435, Sherman, 356 U.S. 369, and Russell, 411 U.S. 423, preserve subjective entrapment while permitting undercover opportunities. When induced criminal conduct and the defense are at issue, the prosecution must establish predisposition independently existing before official cultivation beyond reasonable doubt. Jackson, 443 U.S. 307, requires prosecution-favorable review of reasonable inferences without lowering that burden. Burks, 437 U.S. 1, bars retrial after evidentiary insufficiency. Mathews, 485 U.S. 58, preserves the evidentiary basis needed for an entrapment instruction. Griffin and the now-completed Felix decision supply no entrapment rule. No operative opening Standards entry exists; no later criminal-law changes are used.
metadata.Material record and posture: Jacobson legally bought material in 1984 before the federal amendment. Beginning in January 1985, government agents used fictitious organizations, surveys, a pen pal and appeals against censorship over twenty-six months. He eventually ordered illegal material twice; the first order was unfilled, and a controlled delivery followed the second. The prosecution relies on prompt orders, requests for more, expressed interests and precautions about detection. The search found the lawful earlier magazines and government-supplied material, with no independent illicit collection. His testimony about the expected contents of the earlier purchase and the meaning of later correspondence must be assessed within the whole record. Inducement is not disputed for the question before the Court; the contested issue is independent predisposition.

inventory_refs.caption: King v. St. Vincent's Hospital

metadata.Action and judgment: Reversed and remanded, 8-0; implied and per se duration limits rejected.
metadata.Authority: Souter's opinion for all eight participating Justices.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Section 2024(d) ties protected leave to the period required to perform covered duty, and the Army required the three-year tour associated with King's position. The statutory scheme expressly imposes duration limits on neighboring service categories but omits one here. *Morash* requires provisions to be read as part of the whole enactment; that comparison makes the omission meaningful rather than accidental. *Fishgold* supports protective construction of reemployment rights, although the text and structure—not solicitude alone—control the result. The Hospital's concern about disruption from a lengthy voluntary absence is substantial, but the words “leave,” “employee,” and “return” do not provide an administrable judicial measure for writing a missing cap. The Court rejects both a per se three-year exclusion and a free-ranging reasonableness balance. It does not excuse failure to meet enacted requirements, decide damages, or determine obligations arising after a failure properly to return.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Section 2024(d) contains no implicit reasonableness limit on the duration of otherwise covered military service. An employee must still satisfy the provision's actual coverage, notice, service, and return conditions.
metadata.Issues not reached: Constitutional, as-applied, merits, damages, enforcement, or other collateral questions expressly reserved in the public action were not decided.
metadata.Law after decision: Effective December 16, otherwise covered §2024(d) leave has no judicially implied duration limit.

metadata.Material record and disputed premises: Organizers sought to reach employees at a retail shopping plaza. The ALJ found reasonable alternatives but ordered access under Fairmont's balancing; the Board instead applied Jean Country and found no reasonably effective alternative.

inventory_refs.caption: Molzof v. United States

metadata.Action and judgment: Reversed and remanded, 9-0; no additional damages are directed.
metadata.Authority: Thomas's unanimous opinion for all nine Justices.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The FTCA generally makes the United States liable like a private person under the law of the place while withholding “punitive damages.” Congress used an established tort term associated with punishment for culpable misconduct. *Morissette* supports reading borrowed legal language against that settled background, and *Massachusetts Bonding* confirms the distinction between punitive recovery and compensation in explaining the Act's special wrongful-death provision. The Government's proposed “punitive effect” test would authorize federal courts to revise state compensation rules whenever an award seems excessive or imperfectly tied to perceived loss, without statutory criteria. Its concession that compensation may be reasonably approximate underscores the absence of a workable boundary. These claims arise from admitted simple negligence and seek categories labeled compensatory under state law; alleged duplication or unconsciousness does not alone change their legal nature. Wisconsin law must still determine whether future care, lost enjoyment, survival, and offsets permit any recovery. The Court neither authorizes punitive payment nor directs an award.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Section 2674 bars damages whose legal nature is punishment for culpable wrongdoing, not every compensatory award alleged to be excessive, duplicative, or difficult for the injured person to perceive. Rejecting the federal bar does not establish entitlement under the governing state law or determine an amount.

inventory_refs.caption: National Railroad Passenger Corp. v. Boston & Maine Corp.

metadata.Component application: Each numbered holding below operates on this snapshot; its identified authorities supply the applicable triggers, burdens, presumptions, exceptions and scope. Jurisdiction and remedies remain separate from the merits. No other current-term rule materially changes the stated issue. Refreshed later-date snapshots distinguish the intervening decisions rather than importing unrelated holdings. The provisional and reconciled positions remain valid under those refreshes.
metadata.Effective state: March 24 completed-law baseline (ledger entries 1–51); Suter remains stopped. No March 25 event supplies law to another March 25 event. Holmes remains unadjudicated; no RICO/SIPA law is assumed. Wyoming’s January 22 injunction and retained implementation jurisdiction remain, without a new filing.
metadata.Issue-specific statutory, constitutional: 45 U.S.C. §562(d) requires inability to agree on sale terms and property required for passenger service; need is presumed unless both significant impairment of the railroad’s common-carrier duties and an adequate available alternative are shown. The 1990 reconveyance amendment applies. Chevron, 467 U.S. 837, K mart, 486 U.S. 281, and Everhart, 494 U.S. 83, require attention to text and structure before accepting a permissible agency construction. Chenery, 318 U.S. 80, and State Farm, 463 U.S. 29, prohibit replacement of agency grounds by appellate rationalization. Midkiff, 467 U.S. 229, and Berman, 348 U.S. 26, govern public use despite private reconveyance. Lechmere (January 27) preserves binding judicial statutory constructions; none fixes §562(d) here. Arkansas (February 26) preserves reasoned agency review and substantial-evidence requirements. Neither changes this statute. No operative opening Standards entry exists.
metadata.Material record and posture: The Montrealer used B&M’s 48.8-mile segment. After maintenance problems and service suspension, Amtrak arranged acquisition and immediate reconveyance to Central Vermont, with rehabilitation, twenty-year passenger rights and continued freight access for B&M. Amtrak made a take-it-or-leave-it purchase offer. B&M proposed discussing upgrades while declining the sale proposal. The ICC found inability to agree, allowed Amtrak to elect the acquisition remedy, applied the statutory need presumption, and ordered conveyance with $2,373,286 compensation. The circuit rejected the transaction; Judge Ginsburg would instead remand for adequate findings. A 1990 amendment expressly authorizes service-promoting reconveyance and applies to pending cases. Its applicability here is undisputed. Maintenance allegations are not converted into independent judicial findings. Valuation, competition and other issues left unresolved by the circuit remain open.

metadata.Gade v. National Solid Wastes Management: Exactly five Justices support only the limited negative holding that §18 does not automatically displace supplementary occupational-safety rules merely because a federal standard overlaps and no state plan is approved. Souter's broader impossibility-only approach has four votes and is noncontrolling. Stone-Zsela's separate reservation for demonstrated conflict or clear exclusivity is not a new Court-wide test. Existing conflict authority remains, and provisions return for an actual basis of displacement. This statutory §18 holding does not decide the constitutional allocation of who must administer a program, negate Congress's enumerated commerce authority, authorize a court-created federal fallback, or hold all regulation with dual purposes immune from displacement.
metadata.Georgia v. McCollum: The five-Justice Court attributes a defendant's use of state peremptory authority to government for that jury-selection act, permits the State's supported assertion of jurors' rights, and applies ordinary Batson burdens. Ordinary defense work remains private; no generalized State authority to enforce any citizen's rights follows. Neither a new speech-licensing standard nor a congressional power to require state regulation is supplied.
metadata.Kraft General Foods v. Iowa Department o: Domestic/foreign dividend discrimination is invalid on the specified comparison; partial incorporation of federal tax definitions is not congressional permission to discriminate, and administrative convenience does not overcome reasonable neutral alternatives. The rule preserves the distinction between actual congressional authorization and an inference from partial federal conformity. No general foreign-commerce or state-sovereignty rule decides an unpresented question.
metadata.Nordlinger v. Hahn: The Court retains ordinary rational-basis review, independently supports acquisition-value taxation on neighborhood continuity and existing-owner reliance, sustains the specified exceptions, and rejects assertion of absent travelers' rights without the necessary relationship and obstacle. Allegheny Pittsburgh is retained. Its personal-injury/third-party distinction remains relevant to identifying whose rights are at issue; it establishes no rule governing speech-license costs or federal direction of state governments.

metadata.Action and judgment: Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded, 7-1; suburban exclusion retained, name and whole-slate exclusions reversed.
metadata.Authority: Souter's opinion joined by seven of eight participating Justices.
metadata.Ballot-access holding and operative rule: Illinois may require meaningful support within each separate electorate, but it may not categorically prevent authorized candidates from expanding an existing party under its name or disqualify otherwise qualified countywide and city candidates solely because candidates in a different district lack sufficient signatures.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Moore v. Ogilvie* recognizes that election restrictions may retain legal consequences after ballots are counted. Here several candidates exceeded the five-percent threshold that may alter the party's qualification in later elections, and the challenged rules operate on a timetable too short for complete review before voting. The dispute therefore remains concrete. The Court decides the federal grounds actually used by the Illinois Supreme Court but does not supply an answer to the unaddressed judicial-candidate objection. *Bacchus Imports* supports returning that consequential state-law issue for authoritative construction. The Court neither revives the unappealed water-district candidates nor orders a new election.
metadata.Issues not reached: Constitutional, as-applied, merits, damages, enforcement, or other collateral questions expressly reserved in the public action were not decided.
metadata.Justiciability holding and operative rul: Completion of an election does not moot a ballot-access dispute where election results carry continuing party-qualification consequences and the short election cycle presents a reasonably recurring controversy that otherwise evades review.
metadata.Law after decision: Authorized party-name expansion and independently qualified slate components receive constitutional protection; separate-electorate support requirements remain permissible on this record.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Speech — escrow of an accused or convicted person's income from accounts of the crime
inventory_refs.caption: Simon & Schuster, Inc. v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's opinion joined by Stone, White, Stevens, Scalia, and Souter; six of eight participants.
metadata.Blackmun noncontrolling position: The statute also fails because it is underinclusive as well as overinclusive; noncontrolling elaboration.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The escrow obligation arises from what the work says and restrains payment to the source, which affects a publisher's access to protected expression even without a purpose to suppress ideas. *Arkansas Writers' Project* supplies scrutiny for a content-based financial burden, and *Leathers* confirms that general economic regulation differs from selective burdens keyed to expression. Victim compensation and recovery of crime proceeds are compelling at their strongest, but §632-a is not fitted to those interests. It captures all income under a covered contract when crime appears only incidentally and extends to voluntary admissions never followed by prosecution. Excluding victimless crimes and releasing limited production or legal expenses do not cure that breadth. Neutral restitution, forfeiture, attachment, and collection mechanisms show that compensation can be pursued without this subject-matter classification. The Court decides only this statute and leaves materially different laws, stolen property, general judgments, and victim claims open.
metadata.Court opinion: O'Connor writes for Stone, White, Stevens, Scalia, Souter, and herself. Stone assigned O'Connor as Chief Justice in the judgment majority.
metadata.Dates and route: Argued October 15 and decided December 10, 1991, on certiorari to the Second Circuit, 916 F.2d 777, which rejected the publisher's First Amendment challenge.
metadata.Dependency: *Gibson* protects disputed compelled dues before ideological use but does not replace scrutiny of this content-based financial burden.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A law that selects crime-related expression for a special financial escrow is content based and must be necessary and narrowly drawn to serve a compelling interest. Section 632-a fails because it burdens an entire covered contract, including incidental discussion and unprosecuted admissions, while leaving other assets outside its special reach; it therefore may not be enforced against this publishing contract.
metadata.Judgment: Second Circuit reversed, 8-0. All eight participating Justices support reversal.
metadata.Law after decision: Effective December 10, §632-a's content-based proceeds escrow is unconstitutional; neutral asset-recovery and creditor rules remain available.
metadata.Natural key: *Simon & Schuster, Inc. v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board*, 502 U.S. 105 (1991), No. 90-1059; merits decision; December 10, 1991; OT1991.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Arkansas Writers' Project* and *Leathers* are applied; *Caplin & Drysdale* is distinguished. *Gibson* remains confined to compelled bar financing.
metadata.Question and relief: Whether New York Executive Law §632-a unconstitutionally burdens speech by escrowing income from a person's account of crime. Simon & Schuster seeks a declaration of invalidity and an injunction against enforcement through §1983.
metadata.Remedy: The case returns for appropriate declaratory and injunctive relief against applying §632-a to the contract. No award to Hill or discharge of victim or creditor claims.
metadata.Separate writings: Blackmun concurs in the judgment, generally agreeing but emphasizing that the statute is underinclusive as well as overinclusive. Kennedy concurs in the judgment because direct content-based burdens on fully protected speech are forbidden here without the Court's compelling-interest balancing formulation.
metadata.Stage: Plenary merits review before decision; remand for declaratory and injunctive relief after reversal.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Appellate procedure — whether an appellate brief can serve as a Rule 3 notice of appeal
inventory_refs.caption: Smith v. Barry

metadata.Action and judgment: Reversed and remanded, 9-0, for examination of the brief's contents.
metadata.Authority: O'Connor's opinion joined by eight Justices supplies the controlling rationale; Scalia agrees with the judgment and the express form-or-title ground.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Torres* makes Rule 3 compliance mandatory while recognizing functional compliance with the information the Rule actually requires. *Foman* directs courts to read a notice in context where the intent to seek review is manifest. Rule 3(c) itself prohibits dismissal for informality of form or title, so an administrative expectation that a notice and brief arrive as separate papers cannot add a jurisdictional condition. Smith returned the clerk's informal-brief form within the valid filing period after attempting to appeal; responding to that form does not negate the objective notice his document may convey. Rule 4 also treats a notice mistakenly filed in the appellate court as filed in the district court upon receipt. The first notice remains ineffective under the then-current posttrial-motion rule. The Fourth Circuit must still determine whether the May 4 document actually contains each required item and what judgment or orders it fairly identifies.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A timely document styled as an appellate brief may serve as a notice of appeal if it objectively identifies the appealing party, the judgment or order appealed, and the appellate court as Rule 3(c) requires. Filing it in the court of appeals is governed by Rule 4's mistaken-filing provision; informal form or title alone cannot require dismissal.
metadata.Issues not reached: Constitutional, as-applied, merits, damages, enforcement, or other collateral questions expressly reserved in the public action were not decided.
metadata.Law after decision: Rule 3 looks to timely objective content, not a document's caption, while preserving every required item.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Maritime law — Jones Act seaman status of a worker in an LHWCA-enumerated occupation
inventory_refs.caption: Southwest Marine, Inc. v. Gizoni

metadata.Authority: White's opinion joined by all eight participating Justices.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The occupational definition and the crew exclusion must be read together. A ship-repair worker may fall outside LHWCA coverage if the worker proves crew status under *Wilander*, which requires a substantial employment-related connection to a vessel in navigation and contribution to the vessel's function without demanding traditional navigational duties. Gizoni's claimed assignment to floating platforms, his work aboard them, and his role during towing create genuine disputes that occupational labels, lack of propulsion, and absence of living quarters do not conclusively resolve. *Tipton* supplies the rule that voluntary compensation receipt does not decide seaman status. Congress provided mechanisms for moving between remedies and crediting payments, rather than an election rule forcing an injured worker to refuse immediate compensation. A final award, settlement, conclusive record, ultimate status, negligence, unseaworthiness, maintenance and cure, and damages remain open.
metadata.Dates and route: Argued October 15 and decided December 4, 1991, on certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 909 F.2d 385, which reversed summary judgment for Southwest Marine.
metadata.Dependencies: The December 3 *MCorp* statutory-channel holding is limited to §1818(i)(1) and does not create administrative priority under the LHWCA. The December 4 matters share their entering baseline.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Employment in an occupation listed by the LHWCA does not foreclose Jones Act seaman status because the LHWCA expressly excludes a vessel's master or crew. Receipt of voluntary LHWCA benefits without a final adjudication of status does not preclude a Jones Act suit; any overlapping recovery remains subject to statutory credit.
metadata.Judgment: Ninth Circuit affirmed, 8-0. Stone, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter support affirmance.
metadata.Law after decision: Effective December 4, listed occupational work and voluntary, unadjudicated LHWCA benefits are not categorical bars to a Jones Act status claim.
metadata.Natural key: *Southwest Marine, Inc. v. Gizoni*, 502 U.S. 81 (1991), No. 90-584; merits decision; December 4, 1991; OT1991.
metadata.Opinion: White writes for the unanimous participating Court. Stone assigned the opinion as Chief Justice in the judgment majority. No separate writing.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Wilander*, *Swanson*, and *Tipton* are applied and unchanged. *MCorp* is confined to its express banking-review statute and does not migrate to this scheme.
metadata.Question and relief: Whether work in an occupation enumerated by the Longshore and Harbor Workers' Compensation Act (LHWCA), or acceptance of voluntary LHWCA benefits, forecloses a Jones Act claim by a worker who may be a vessel crew member. Southwest Marine seeks reinstatement of summary judgment; Gizoni seeks adjudication of status and injury claims.
metadata.Remedy: Summary judgment remains reversed. The case returns for ordinary determination of status and any viable injury claims. The Court awards no damages and makes no ultimate status finding.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Freedom of Information Act — Exemption 6 privacy and identities of interviewed Haitian returnees
inventory_refs.caption: United States Department of State v. Ray

metadata.Action and judgment: Reversed, 8-0; identifiers remain withheld while segregated reports remain released.
metadata.Authority: Stevens's Court opinion; all eight participating Justices support the operative rule and judgment, while Scalia and Kennedy do not join the broader discussion of possible derivative public benefits.
metadata.Chronology: The event is processed on its manifest date. Same-day events use the common start-of-day baseline and are not treated as sequential doctrinal dependencies.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Exemption 6 requires a practical balance between the invasion of personal privacy and disclosure's contribution to public understanding of government operations. *Rose* supplies that balance and demonstrates that useful agency records may be disclosed after identifiers are removed; *Washington Post* confirms that information about particular persons falls within “similar files.” The released reports disclose the questions, answers, dates, sampling, and reported treatment, allowing scrutiny of the Department's monitoring. Adding names would connect intimate family, employment, and living information—and cooperation given under an accepted assurance of confidentiality—to identifiable returnees. On this record, the requesters identify only a general hope that renewed interviews might uncover inaccuracies, not concrete contradictory information or a demonstrated incremental contribution sufficient to outweigh that invasion. The Court does not require proof of government wrongdoing before invoking FOIA, decide that derivative investigation can never matter, or adjudicate Haiti's safety or any asylum claim.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Under FOIA Exemption 6, identifying information may be withheld when linking names to sensitive personal interviews would cause a substantial privacy invasion and the identifiers add little demonstrated value to public understanding of agency conduct after reasonably segregable substantive material has been released. A confidentiality assurance informs the privacy interest but does not itself create an exemption.
metadata.Issues not reached: Constitutional, as-applied, merits, damages, enforcement, or other collateral questions expressly reserved in the public action were not decided.
metadata.Law after decision: Effective December 16, the Exemption 6 balance measures the incremental public contribution of identifiers against their concrete privacy cost after segregated release; confidentiality is relevant but not dispositive.

metadata.Issue-specific statutory, constitutional: Ford v. Georgia, 498 U.S. 411, treats the substance of a pre-Batson objection grounded in a historical exclusion practice as an equal-protection claim despite imprecise citations. Batson, 476 U.S. 79, requires a race-neutral explanation after a prima facie showing and an ultimate determination of purposeful discrimination. Powers, 499 U.S. 400, removes the same-race bar. Griffith, 479 U.S. 314, applies new criminal-procedure rules to cases still on direct review; Teague, 489 U.S. 288, concerns collateral review. Holland, 493 U.S. 474, governs the distinct Sixth Amendment theory. Current Stringer does not change direct-review retroactivity; no current record displaces Ford or Powers. No operative opening Standards entry exists.
metadata.Material record and posture: Before the 1984 capital trial, Trevino alleged Texas’s historical racial use of peremptory challenges and sought to prohibit it. He renewed his objection after each of the only three Black prospective jurors was struck and referred to Swain. His December 19, 1985 appellate brief invoked the Fourteenth Amendment while renewing the same issue. Batson issued while direct review remained pending. The State answered with a same-race objection, while the Texas court treated the issue as Sixth Amendment only and rejected it under Holland; the conviction and death sentence were affirmed June 12, 1991, with rehearing denied September 18. Trevino is Hispanic. The present record establishes preservation, not the ultimate purpose of each strike.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Bankruptcy — ordinary-course preference exception and payments on long-term debt
inventory_refs.caption: Union Bank v. Wolas

metadata.Assignment: Stone assigns Stevens as Chief Justice in the unanimous judgment coalition.
metadata.Authority: Stevens's opinion states the proposition for all nine Justices; Scalia's separate writing agrees with the statutory holding and judgment.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Section 547(c)(2) contains no distinction between short- and long-term debt. Congress removed the former 45-day restriction and retained three express ordinary-course requirements, so a court may not recreate a maturity bar from legislative purpose or the amendment's perceived motivating examples. *Ron Pair* supplies the obligation to apply operative Code text when the result is not demonstrably contrary to congressional design. Equality of distribution and discouragement of destructive collection races coexist within the enacted preference rule and its exceptions; neither permits omission of the exception's words. Eligibility does not establish that these interest and commitment-fee payments were incurred and paid in both parties' ordinary course and according to ordinary business terms. Those questions, including appellate challenges not addressed under the categorical rule, remain for remand with the Bank bearing §547(g)'s burden.
metadata.Dates and route: Argued November 5 and decided December 11, 1991, on certiorari to the Ninth Circuit, 921 F.2d 968.
metadata.Dependencies: *MCorp* concerns bankruptcy's interaction with bank regulatory jurisdiction, not preferences. *Ardestani* concerns a distinct fee cross-reference. Neither alters §547.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Payments on long-term debt may qualify for the ordinary-course exception in the then-current §547(c)(2). Debt maturity is not an additional categorical exclusion, but the creditor must prove every enacted ordinary-course element for the particular payments.
metadata.Judgment: Reversed and remanded, 9-0. All nine Justices support the judgment.
metadata.Law after decision: Effective December 11, long-term debt payments are eligible for §547(c)(2), subject to all three contemporaneous statutory elements and the creditor's burden.
metadata.Natural key: *Union Bank v. Wolas*, 502 U.S. 151 (1991), No. 90-1491; merits decision; December 11, 1991; OT1991.
metadata.Opinion: Stevens writes for a unanimous Court, joined by Stone, White, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, and Thomas. Scalia also writes separately to rest the result directly on the enacted text without extended legislative-history or policy analysis.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Ron Pair* is applied. The Ninth Circuit's categorical *CHG International* construction is rejected; no Supreme Court precedent is overruled.
metadata.Published noncontrolling position: Scalia would decide from the unambiguous text without relying on legislative history or policy balancing. His statutory holding and judgment join are controlling; this methodological reservation is noncontrolling.
metadata.Question and relief: Whether payments on long-term debt may qualify for the then-current ordinary-course exception in 11 U.S.C. §547(c)(2). Union Bank seeks reversal of the categorical exclusion and review of remaining statutory issues.
metadata.Remedy: The Ninth Circuit must review any remaining challenges to application of all statutory elements. The Court does not itself restore judgment for the Bank.
metadata.Stage: Plenary merits review; reversal and remand to the Ninth Circuit afterward.

metadata.Component application: Each numbered holding below operates on this snapshot; its identified authorities supply the applicable triggers, burdens, presumptions, exceptions and scope. metadata.Effective state: March 24 completed-law baseline (ledger entries 1–51); Suter remains stopped. No March 25 event supplies law to another March 25 event. Holmes remains unadjudicated; no RICO/SIPA law is assumed. Wyoming’s January 22 injunction and retained implementation jurisdiction remain, without a new filing.
metadata.Issue-specific statutory, constitutional: The Fifth Amendment bars a second prosecution for the same offense. Blockburger, 284 U.S. 299, compares statutory elements; Grady, 495 U.S. 508, prohibits proving essential elements through conduct constituting a previously prosecuted offense but rejects a same-evidence test. Dowling, 493 U.S. 342, distinguishes evidentiary use from a second prosecution. Bayer, 331 U.S. 532, Pinkerton, 328 U.S. 640, and Iannelli, 420 U.S. 770, preserve conspiracy as distinct from substantive offenses. Garrett, 471 U.S. 773, warns against mechanically translating a single-incident analysis to multilayered conduct. Current Griffin (December 3) concerns alternative objects, not offense identity; Estelle (December 4) leaves the general propensity question open. Neither supplies a new evidence exemption or displaces Grady. No operative opening Standards entry exists.
metadata.Material record and posture: The Missouri prosecution concerned attempted manufacture during August 26–31, 1987. Evidence of the earlier Oklahoma manufacturing operation was admitted to establish intent; that evidentiary use did not enlarge the charged Missouri offense. The later Oklahoma prosecution concerned the earlier completed acts and a broader agreement. The Tenth Circuit reversed counts 1–6 under Grady but affirmed the travel convictions, counts 9–10, with sentencing proceedings. No prior acquittal or issue-preclusion finding controls this record.

inventory_refs.caption: United States v. Ibarra

metadata.Application and remedy: The January 30 notice followed the January 3 denial within thirty days. The dismissal is vacated and the appeal returns to the Tenth Circuit.
metadata.Authority: Per curiam opinion joined by Stone, White, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter; unanimous participating Court.
metadata.Case: *United States v. Ibarra*, 502 U.S. 1 (1991); No. 90-1713; OT1991.
metadata.Chronology: First OT1991 Court event; no earlier current-term law.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court applies *United States v. Healy*, which supplies the rule that a timely criminal rehearing request suspends finality, and *United States v. Dieter*, which rejects classifications based on the kind or strength of error asserted. The Government filed one motion within thirty days of suppression and then appealed within thirty days after denial. Its earlier abandonment of consent may bear on the merits, but the motion still asked the District Court to alter adjudicated rights. Making appellate time depend on an advance assessment of whether the renewed argument was strong, preserved, or likely to succeed would leave litigants guessing about the jurisdictional date. *Department of Banking v. Pink* remains distinct because the filing there did not seek substantive alteration. The Court therefore decides only when appellate finality attached. It leaves open bad-faith motions, successive motions, the substantive effect of the Government's abandonment, and the Fourth Amendment validity of the search.
metadata.Court below / question / relief: Tenth Circuit, 920 F.2d 702; whether a timely Government reconsideration motion renewing an abandoned ground postponed appellate finality. The Government sought vacatur and appellate consideration, not a suppression ruling.
metadata.Event: Petition granted, judgment vacated, and case remanded on October 15, 1991. The official reporter supplies the date. The matter was decided without argument on the petition record.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A single timely motion asking a district court to alter a suppression ruling renders that ruling nonfinal for appeal purposes until the motion is decided, even when the motion renews a ground the Government earlier abandoned. The full appeal period begins upon disposition of the motion; this rule does not determine whether the renewed ground remains waived on the merits.
metadata.Law after decision: The holding above enters simulated law effective October 15, 1991. Existing appeal periods and preservation rules are unchanged.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *Healy* is applied to all timely substantive reconsideration motions; *Dieter* forecloses a merits-strength exception; *Pink* is distinguished as involving no request to alter adjudicated rights.
metadata.Stage: Petition pending before; concluded here after summary merits disposition. The Tenth Circuit must conduct further proceedings.
