metadata.Event: referred application to vacate execution stay and impose a further-stays condition; user-added docket matter inserted into chunk 8.
metadata.Further-stays snapshot: No entering Court holding already requires the requested restriction. Kennedy's Delo concurrence, joined by Scalia, identifies §1651's aid-of-jurisdiction function and prompt appellate resolution as support for protection from injurious unsupported stays. That separate writing is a Justice-specific source, not a controlling rule compelling this remedy. The actual completed panel and Court sequence supplies the case-specific occasion; the requested direction retains an avenue to seek this Court's order. The separate issue is whether to require that avenue before another federal stay, leave lower courts free to apply ordinary standards to genuinely new claims, or deny the entire application. The rule for mandamus and the Rules' routing provisions supply no automatic universal prohibition.
metadata.Reporter locator: historical order at 503 U.S.1000; the docket/date identify this simulated event without inventing an official reporter citation.
metadata.Strongest supported alternatives and bou: Vacatur is supported by the demonstrated completed Court sequence and the absence of a shown materially new basis; a Harris-only authorization condition preserves the Court's ability to evaluate a further request while giving effect to its existing orders. The strongest objection is that the State has not established insufficiency of the actual unknown stay ground, and a Court-only condition displaces lower-court consideration that might identify a new claim before irreversible harm. A mixed path vacates this stay but preserves lower-court availability for a genuinely new jurisdictionally proper claim; another possible narrower path would restrict only repetitive grounds. The six non-Stone grant-side Justices regard the demonstrated sequence and retained permission route as sufficient for both requested components despite the disclosed limitation. Blackmun and Stevens regard that limitation and the loss of lower-court assessment as sufficient to deny both. Stone grants vacatur but rejects the blanket permission condition under his approved core. No participant's disposition is grounded in a finding of judicial defiance, actual impossibility of novelty, or an invented future claim. The order is unexplained, so these internal grounds become no public substantive holding.
metadata.Submission: emergency application at the April 21 action; no oral argument or exact submission time is established.
metadata.Vacatur snapshot: The unchanged opening trackers and 62 pre-April21 records enter, followed by Gomez and the actually committed A-766 order: 64 prior records in this dependent snapshot. A-766 grants vacatur of its distinct April 20 stay, 7–2, by unexplained order and adds no substantive doctrine. Alaska, Barker, Department of Energy and Taylor are independent April21 siblings; they do not enter this sequence. No May4 law enters. Gomez's six-Justice per curiam permits independent equitable assessment of unjustified delay and State enforcement interests on its gas-method record, while reserving the final method issue, channel and abuse-of-writ extensions and abstention. Its particular findings do not identify A-768's unknown grounds.

metadata.Authority: White's opinion joined by all eight participating Justices.
metadata.Controlling explanation: *Terry* supplies both the historical-analogue inquiry and the more important classification of the remedy. Wooddell seeks replacement for earnings he says retaliation prevented him from obtaining, not return of identified funds held by the union or backpay incidental to reinstatement in a former job. That compensation has the character of legal damages. The combined request for injunctive relief does not permit a court to withhold a jury from the legal claim; the forum instead sequences legal and equitable issues consistently with the Seventh Amendment. The holding resolves entitlement to the factfinder, not whether retaliation occurred or what amount, if any, is recoverable.
metadata.Dates and route: Argued October 16 and decided December 4, 1991, on certiorari to the Sixth Circuit, 907 F.2d 151.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A union member's claim for wages and benefits lost because hiring-hall referrals allegedly were withheld is a claim for compensatory legal relief carrying a Seventh Amendment jury right. Accompanying equitable requests do not eliminate the jury right on the legal issues.
metadata.Judgment: Reversed and remanded, 8-0. All eight participating Justices support both components.
metadata.Judgment under review: The Sixth Circuit restored the retaliation claim but denied a jury and sustained dismissal of the union-constitution claim. Wooddell seeks reversal on both reviewed issues.
metadata.Natural key: *Wooddell v. International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local 71*, 502 U.S. 93 (1991), No. 90-967; merits decision; December 4, 1991; OT1991.
metadata.Opinion: White writes for the unanimous participating Court, assigned by Stone as Chief Justice in the majority. No separate writing.
metadata.Questions: Whether Wooddell has a jury right on his LMRDA damages claim and whether LMRA §301 permits his claim as a member-beneficiary alleging breach of an international-local union constitution.
metadata.Remedy: Restore the union-constitution claim for §301 proceedings and permit a jury on the LMRDA legal damages claim. No liability or damages are awarded.
metadata.Stage: Plenary review before decision; remand for adjudication afterward. Same-day baseline shared with the other December 4 matters.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Court procedure — in forma pauperis status of pro se petitioners under Rule 39.8
inventory_refs.caption: Zatko v. California

metadata.Authority: Per curiam opinion joined by White, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, and Souter; majority of the eight participating Justices.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Rule 39.8 supplies discretion to deny fee-waived filing when the Court is satisfied that a current petition or application is frivolous or malicious. The Court finds that predicate here in the grouped submissions and considers the applicants' extraordinary histories—73 petitions for Zatko and more than 45 for Martin—evidence that the present filings continue an abuse of process. *In re McDonald* and *In re Sindram* supply authority for targeted responses that preserve judicial resources for substantial claims. The Court does not adopt a numerical threshold, make prior denials alone conclusive, or close the courthouse prospectively. Instead it denies the pending fee motions and permits each applicant to place the petitions on the paid docket by November 25 in the required form. The Court leaves ordinary screening available if they comply and does not reach any underlying conviction, claim, petition merits, or constitutional entitlement to unrestricted free filing.
metadata.Event: Decision on seventeen in-forma-pauperis motions under Rule 39.8, November 4, 1991; no underlying petition merits were before the Court.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: When the Court is satisfied that the pending submissions are frivolous and the applicants' repeated frivolous filings constitute extreme abuse of its process, Rule 39.8 permits denial of in-forma-pauperis status. Denial may require payment of the docketing fee and compliance with ordinary petition form rules by a stated deadline; it does not decide the petitions' merits or impose a broader prospective filing ban.
metadata.Law after decision: Rule 39.8 remains discretionary; this decision establishes that extreme repetitive frivolous use can warrant fee denial for identified current submissions.
metadata.Precedent treatment: *McDonald* and *Sindram* are applied as authority for tailored process protections; neither is extended to a categorical ban.
metadata.Stage: Fee motions pending before; denied with a November 25 opportunity to pay docketing fees and submit compliant petitions. Underlying submissions proceed only upon compliance.

metadata.Material record: Austin pleaded guilty to a South Dakota cocaine-possession-with-intent-to-distribute charge and received a state prison sentence. The United States separately sought the mobile home and auto-body shop under the federal forfeiture provisions. The account links a cocaine transaction to the two properties. The lower court did not undertake an Excessive Fines determination, and the Supreme Court record does not supply findings sufficient to fix their value, the constitutionally relevant proportionality, or the final forfeitable extent.
metadata.Question: Whether the Excessive Fines Clause applies to federal civil in rem forfeiture under 21 U.S.C. §§ 881(a)(4) and (a)(7), and the proper consequence if constitutional coverage exists.
metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: This is a federal forfeiture, so incorporation against States is not presented. The nature of an extraction for Excessive Fines coverage is separate from Double Jeopardy, criminal-procedure coverage, innocent ownership, and the merits of statutory forfeiture. The question is not whether every civil loss of property is a fine. Appellate review of the categorical exclusion does not authorize invented valuation findings.
metadata.Relief sought: Austin seeks reversal of the ruling that the Clause does not reach the forfeitures and an opportunity to contest excessiveness. The United States seeks affirmance on the theory that these civil in rem forfeitures fall outside the Clause.

metadata.Material facts and record limits: Liggett developed lower-priced generic cigarettes. Brown & Williamson's rebate campaign allegedly used below-cost sales to discipline Liggett, increase generic prices, and preserve branded-cigarette profits. metadata.Material record: Buckley alleges that prosecutors sought a favorable bootprint identification after other laboratory examinations failed reliably to connect him to the crime, using an expert allegedly willing to fabricate evidence. The fabrication and wrongdoing allegations are accepted at this pleading stage, not adjudicated facts. The challenged preliminary evidence work preceded probable cause to arrest or initiate proceedings against him.
metadata.Question: Whether prosecutors have absolute immunity from § 1983 damages claims for allegedly fabricating evidence during preliminary investigation and making false statements at a press conference announcing an indictment.
metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: Absolute immunity is the issue, not final constitutional liability or qualified immunity. The function of each challenged act must be identified separately. Neither the eventual use of evidence in court nor the prosecutor’s title retroactively converts all investigation into advocacy. Conversely, an out-of-court act is not necessarily investigative merely because it occurs outside a courtroom.
metadata.Relief sought: Buckley seeks reversal of the immunity dismissal and further proceedings on his damages claims. The prosecutors seek affirmance of absolute immunity.

metadata.Material record: Two children with limb-reduction birth defects and their parents allege that maternal Bendectin use caused the defects. metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: Federal evidence rules govern admissibility in this removed diversity action; state substantive causation requirements and summary-judgment sufficiency remain separate. The reported question does not call for a general rule about every form of specialized knowledge or a comprehensive appellate standard for all future gatekeeping decisions.
metadata.Relief sought: The children and their parents seek vacatur and reconsideration under the Federal Rules. Merrell Dow seeks affirmance because the proposed evidence lacks an adequate scientific foundation and cannot support causation.

metadata.Current rule: Section 1305(a)(1) preempts state enforcement having a connection with or reference to covered air-carrier rates, routes or services. General applicability does not avoid that express relation, and §1506's general remedies clause preserves remedies outside the specific prohibition without undoing it. Fare-marketing requirements that directly regulate fare descriptions, restrictions, availability, surcharges and round-trip pricing fall within that construction. Independently, the identified package of compelled disclosures and advertising restrictions is preempted because it substantially constrains the marketing of restricted fares and significantly affects fares themselves. Directly covered requirements need not conflict with an existing federal rule; consistency alone does not defeat the express prohibition.

metadata.Material record: Nineteen States and private plaintiffs filed 36 complaints alleging concerted changes in commercial general liability insurance and reinsurance, including policy forms, pollution exclusions, and terms of coverage. The allegations include withholding broader reinsurance business to compel adoption of disfavored terms, as well as joint drafting without alleged refusal to deal. Other counts concern London reinsurers’ coordinated terms for American risks. These are allegations on motions to dismiss, not proven cartels. The London defendants invoke a British regulatory regime permitting their practices; they do not identify British law requiring conduct that American law forbids.
metadata.Question: Whether domestic insurers lose McCarran-Ferguson antitrust protection by alleged agreement with foreign reinsurers; which pleaded conduct falls within the boycott exception; and whether international comity bars the Sherman Act claims against the London defendants. No. 91-1111 presents the two McCarran-Ferguson questions. No. 91-1128 presents extraterritorial application to the foreign conduct. These are distinct reviewed components of the same listed consolidated matter.
metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: The two Supreme Court dockets are one CASE LIST matter; No. 91-1128 is the related Merrett petition within this consolidated review. Distinguish federal judicial power over nonfrivolous Sherman Act claims, the statute’s substantive foreign reach, the insurance exemption, and any comity limitation. Personal jurisdiction is not contested. State-law claims are not within this review. The foreign-defendant counts and the domestic exemption counts must not be merged.
metadata.Relief sought: Domestic defendants seek reinstatement of dismissals under the insurance exemption. The London defendants seek dismissal of the foreign-conduct claims on comity grounds. State and private plaintiffs seek continued litigation of the challenged conspiracies.

inventory_refs.caption: Heller v. Doe

metadata.Material record: Kentucky required proof of dangerousness, likely benefit from treatment, and a least restrictive placement predicate in the relevant commitment proceedings. For the category described in the then-operative statute as “mental retardation,” proof was clear and convincing and guardians or immediate family could participate as parties. For mental illness, proof was beyond a reasonable doubt and that party status was not supplied. The class challenged these differences. The medical and developmental distinctions offered as rationales concern typical onset, diagnostic history, prediction, and the information held by families; they are not individual findings that any class member is dangerous or incompetent.
metadata.Question: Whether Kentucky’s different burdens of proof and family-participation rules for involuntary commitment of persons with intellectual disability and persons with mental illness violate equal protection, and whether family party status violates procedural due process.
metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: The class litigated equal protection below on rational-basis review and first requested heightened scrutiny in its Supreme Court merits brief. The preserved due-process issue is family participation, not a claim that Addington itself requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt in every civil commitment. Existing grounds not before the Court must not be silently erased.
metadata.Relief sought: Kentucky seeks reversal of the challenged federal rulings. The committed class seeks affirmance. Other district-court grounds outside the questions under review remain separate.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Voting rights; equal protection — racial gerrymandering challenge to North Carolina congressional districts
inventory_refs.caption: Shaw v. Reno

metadata.Material record: After the 1990 census, North Carolina received a twelfth congressional seat. The Attorney General objected to its initial one-majority-Black-district plan under § 5; the State then adopted a two-majority-Black-district plan. The Attorney General’s objection identified a possible additional district in the southeast; the revised second district instead followed roughly 160 miles of the Interstate 85 corridor farther north. Forty counties were covered by § 5, and the State did not pursue the alternative declaratory-judgment preclearance route. The complaint alleges arbitrary concentration by race rather than ordinary geographic criteria. Its five Durham County voters include two assigned to District 12 and three to adjacent District 2. Racial purpose, a legally sufficient remedial predicate, and the actual relationship between the challenged boundaries and voting-rights compliance have not been resolved at trial.
metadata.Question: Whether the complaint states an Equal Protection claim against North Carolina officials for allegedly arbitrary racial construction of congressional districts, notwithstanding the asserted Voting Rights Act purpose; separately, whether the claims against federal preclearance officials may proceed in this district.
metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: Separate personal injury from generalized disagreement with race-conscious government. Two plaintiffs reside in District 12 and three in District 2; that division must be preserved when identifying each claim and requested remedy. Allegations concerning a statewide scheme do not themselves establish personal injury from every district. The legal sufficiency of the alleged assignment injury is disputed and is not identical to proof of dilution. The appeal concerns dismissal, not an established constitutional violation. VRA § 14(b) and Morris v. Gressette separately constrain relief against federal officers. The complaint does not assert a one-person-one-vote or partisan-gerrymandering claim, and those theories may not be substituted.
metadata.Relief sought: The voters seek reversal of dismissal, declaratory relief, and an injunction against the challenged plan. State officials seek affirmance; federal officials defend the jurisdictional and preclearance-review bars.

metadata.Material record: Hicks, a Black correctional officer and shift commander, was demoted and discharged. He sued St. Mary's under Title VII and superintendent Steve Long under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 for the alleged racial discrimination. Following a bench trial, the district court found a prima facie case, found the employer’s articulated disciplinary explanations unworthy of belief, but did not find racial motivation proved. It suggested personal animosity rather than race. The court of appeals did not complete ordinary clear-error review of that finding because it treated rejection of all offered reasons as dispositive. Whether the alternative explanation is supported and was fairly litigated is distinct from the abstract burden rule.
metadata.Question: Whether a Title VII plaintiff is entitled to judgment as a matter of law once the factfinder rejects all of the employer’s stated nondiscriminatory reasons, or must still persuade the factfinder of intentional discrimination.
metadata.Reachability and reserved issues: The case concerns individual intentional disparate treatment under Title VII, not a disparate-impact claim. Burdens of production and persuasion must remain separate. A rule permitting an inference of discrimination does not necessarily compel it, and rejection of compulsion does not require additional independent evidence in every case. The court of appeals treated the purposeful-discrimination element of the § 1983 claim against Long as the same as that of the Title VII claim against St. Mary's; neither side challenges that premise. Applicability of the McDonnell Douglas framework to that companion claim may be assumed for this case without collapsing the causes of action.
metadata.Relief sought: The employer seeks reversal of the automatic-liability rule. Hicks seeks affirmance or review of the adverse factual finding under the correct evidentiary framework.

metadata.Chronology: Law through 1993-04-20 enters this uncoordinated date group. Brecht, Withrow and Easterwood use the common April 20 baseline. Display order creates no earlier same-day authority. Their decisions operate prospectively within their stated scopes. No historical post-divergence grant or unsupplied follow-on event is admitted by implication.
metadata.Issue-specific Law-Entering Snapshot: Section 2254 authorizes constitutional habeas review, with ordinary gates intact. Powell, 428 U.S. 465, is a prudential limit on Fourth Amendment exclusionary claims after a full and fair opportunity, not a withdrawal of jurisdiction. Miranda, 384 U.S. 436, protects the trial self-incrimination privilege; Jackson, 443 U.S. 307, Rose v. Mitchell, 443 U.S. 545, and Kimmelman, 477 U.S. 365, declined other proposed Powell extensions. Rule 15(b), through habeas Rule 11, permits issues actually tried by express or implied consent; the two theories do not automatically supply such consent. Connelly, 479 U.S. 157, requires police coercion for due-process involuntariness, with the totality assessed under existing law. Simulated Herrera supplies no universal innocence gate. Common entering baseline April 20: the same-day Brecht decision is not an earlier premise. No actual same-day sequence is established.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Labor law — NLRB reinstatement and backpay for an employee who lied under oath
inventory_refs.caption: ABF Freight System, Inc. v. NLRB

metadata.Authority: Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; seven Justices. Scalia and O'Connor agree with the lawfulness of the result in a separate judgment concurrence.
metadata.Case and dockets: ABF Freight System, Inc. v. NLRB; No. 92-1550.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Congress assigned this remedial choice to the Board, within the Act's limits. Section 10(c) authorizes affirmative action that effectuates labor policy and separately withholds reinstatement and backpay when the actual suspension or discharge was for cause. Phelps Dodge places the relationship between remedy and labor policy primarily within the Board's competence. Virginia Electric preserves judicial review when relief pursues ends outside that policy. False testimony is serious, but a court cannot convert that concern into a forfeiture command Congress did not enact. The remedy addresses an established employer violation and the public interest in lawful labor relations, as well as the employee's loss. Precision Instrument's equitable refusal of relief does not displace the statutory allocation of authority here. The Board may address misconduct through its lawful remedial discretion, and independently authorized sanctions remain available. The Court neither awards automatic employee entitlement nor orders a criminal sanction; the accepted unlawful-discharge premise remains outside this limited review.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Under NLRA section 10(c), an employee's deliberate false testimony at the remedial hearing does not automatically forfeit reinstatement or backpay for an established unfair labor practice; the Board may withhold relief for supported misconduct but is not required to apply a categorical forfeiture rule. The separate statutory prohibition applies when the employee was actually suspended or discharged for cause; later hearing testimony does not itself establish that earlier discharge ground.
metadata.Result: Tenth Circuit enforcement judgment affirmed, 9–0; reinstatement and backpay remain enforceable.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Civil rights — §1983 claim for prosecution without probable cause under substantive due process
inventory_refs.caption: Albright v. Oliver

metadata.Case and dockets: Albright v. Oliver; No. 92-833.
metadata.Explanation of authority and limits: The Court affirms the dismissal, but no opinion supplies five votes for a sufficient legal explanation. The plurality applies Graham's specific-source approach to the alleged seizure-related liberty burdens while preserving Soldal and James Daniel Good's independent protections. Kennedy and Thomas distinguish arrest from prosecution and consider the nature of the asserted due-process interest, including the conditional significance of Illinois's remedy for unauthorized malicious prosecution. Souter asks whether the complaint supplies a substantial deprivation outside the protection ordinarily afforded by the Fourth Amendment. These inquiries are not interchangeable. A claim involving an additional substantial injury, a properly presented procedural defect, or an established substantive right could divide those approaches differently. Marks does not permit adding their votes to announce the plurality's rule, the state-remedy rationale, or a new synthesized test. The Court does not adopt the Seventh Circuit's requirement of incarceration, employment loss or another palpable consequence. Nor does it decide the abandoned Fourth Amendment theory, its accrual, immunity, municipal attribution or a general fabrication claim.
metadata.Judgment without controlling rationale: Dismissal of Albright's presented substantive-due-process claim is affirmed, 7–2. O'Connor's specific-source plurality has four votes: O'Connor, Stone-Zsela, Scalia and Ginsburg. Kennedy and Thomas adopt a distinct prosecution/due-process analysis; Souter adopts a distinct absence-of-additional-substantial-injury ground. The judgment binds the parties, but neither a general Fourth Amendment displacement rule nor a general state-remedy bar becomes law.
metadata.Precedent treatment: Marks v. United States supplies the governing fractured-decision inquiry; no rationale here is established as a controlling logical subset. Graham, Collins, Soldal, James Daniel Good, Williams, Medina, Costello, Gerstein, Paul, Parratt and Hudson retain their existing force; the uses of those decisions in the separate rationales do not establish a new majority construction.
metadata.Result: Seventh Circuit affirmed, 7–2; dismissal of the presented substantive-due-process claim stands; no opinion supplies a controlling rationale.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Dormant Commerce Clause — state use tax on out-of-state goods exceeding some local sales taxes
inventory_refs.caption: Associated Industries of Missouri v. Lohman

metadata.Authority: Thomas's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg; eight direct joins. Blackmun agrees with the judgment without joining this full framework.
metadata.Case and dockets: Associated Industries of Missouri v. Lohman; No. 93-397; 511 U.S. 641.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that compensation must concern the competing transaction. Henneford v. Silas Mason permits complementary sales and use taxes, while Oregon Waste requires an identified domestic burden, rough approximation without excess, and substantially equivalent taxable events. Sale and use are equivalent events here; the defect is the excess over the actual local counterpart. Halliburton requires the appropriate comparison, and Armco rejects discrimination concealed by an unrelated burden. Missouri's aggregate figures show favorable treatment for many interstate purchases, but those figures impose no corresponding tax on the local purchase competing with a disadvantaged interstate transaction. Fort Gratiot prevents substate boundaries from curing discrimination, and Carbone preserves that principle in a different service setting. Administrative complexity and lawful delegation of local taxing power do not authorize the State's unequal exaction. General American Tank Car does not supply an unrestricted averaging defense. This holding neither requires raising lower interstate burdens nor determines a replacement tax system or every taxpayer's transaction.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Missouri's additional 1.5% use tax discriminates against interstate commerce to the extent it exceeds the corresponding local sales-tax burden on an equivalent purchase where the goods are used; greater sales taxes on other transactions elsewhere in the State cannot compensate that excess. The ordinary matched 4.225% statewide taxes remain outside this challenge, and equal or lower interstate burdens are not invalid merely because other localities impose discriminatory excesses.
metadata.Result: Missouri Supreme Court reversed and remanded, 9–0.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Bankruptcy — fraudulent transfers; whether a noncollusive foreclosure sale price is reasonably equivalent value
inventory_refs.caption: BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp.

metadata.Authority: Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens and Ginsburg; five Justices directly adopt the proposition and explanation. No fractured-decision synthesis is needed.
metadata.Case and dockets: BFP v. Resolution Trust Corp.; No. 92-1370; 511 U.S. 531.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Congress's value condition does work beyond checking foreclosure procedure. Section 101(54) expressly includes foreclosure of the debtor's equity of redemption, and §548 reaches voluntary and involuntary transfers. Treating every compliant price as equivalent would collapse the substantive value inquiry into a different state's procedural requirements. Butner v. United States respects state-created property interests where federal bankruptcy law supplies no contrary consequence; it does not eliminate the consequence Congress expressly provided here. Owen v. Owen likewise requires giving the federal avoidance provision its own operation. Dewsnup protects an allowed lien against the particular Chapter 7 strip-down it considered, while Nobelman protects specified mortgage rights in Chapter 13. Neither decided this separate avoidance question. Title stability and the effect of uncertainty on bidding are substantial concerns, but they cannot supply a conclusive exception to the enacted condition. The limited avoidance period, required statutory predicates, claimant's burden and applicable transferee protections remain. The Court reverses the categorical value ground without finding this sale avoidable or resolving recovery.
metadata.Controlling proposition: A noncollusive mortgage foreclosure of real property that complies with state law does not conclusively establish reasonably equivalent value under 11 U.S.C. §548(a)(2)(A); when the statutory avoidance claim is timely and otherwise properly presented, the bankruptcy court must assess the value exchanged independently under that federal requirement. Procedural compliance remains relevant evidence, and rejection of conclusiveness establishes neither insolvency nor any other avoidance predicate, entitlement to recovery, or a defect in the debtor's property interest.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit categorical value ruling reversed and remanded on both consolidated routes, 5–4.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Admiralty — contribution claims by nonsettling defendants against a settling joint tortfeasor
inventory_refs.caption: Boca Grande Club, Inc. v. Florida Power & Light Co.

metadata.Authority: Stevens’s opinion for the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine Justices adopt this application of McDermott.
metadata.Case and dockets: Boca Grande Club, Inc. v. Florida Power & Light Co., No. 93-180.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that McDermott’s settlement-credit rule resolves the contribution question. McDermott reduces the claim against a nonsettling defendant by the settling defendants’ proportionate responsibility, leaving the benefit or shortfall of their bargain with its parties. The nonsettler therefore needs no contribution claim to avoid bearing the settler’s share. The contrary circuit approach addressed the danger of excessive payment under a different credit mechanism. Combining that remedy with equitable-share reduction would undo the settlement without supplying a missing protection. Reliable Transfer’s comparative-fault principle continues to require a meaningful allocation, and no percentage is fixed on this record. Edmonds concerns a distinct statutory allocation and does not compel a different result for a voluntary settlement shortfall. The Court vacates for application of the governing mechanism. It does not decide a distinct contractual indemnity obligation, settlement fraud or invalidity, exoneration, limitation of liability, total damages, or a shortfall unrelated to the settlement bargain.
metadata.Controlling proposition: In a general maritime tort action governed by proportionate-share settlement credit, the plaintiff’s claim against nonsettlers is reduced by the settling tortfeasor’s equitable share, and a nonsettler may not recover contribution from the settler merely because the settlement price is less than that share. The lower court must permit meaningful litigation and reliable determination of comparative responsibility; it may not withhold equitable-share protection while invoking settlement finality to bar contribution.
metadata.Result: Vacated and remanded, 9–0.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Federal habeas — presumption of correctness for state witness-immunity finding; counsel conflict of interest
inventory_refs.caption: Burden v. Zant

metadata.Authority: The per curiam Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg; all nine participants support this narrow record-correction rule and remand. No fractured-opinion synthesis is needed.
metadata.Case and dockets: Burden v. Zant; No. 92-8836.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that appellate deference cannot supply a missing factual determination. The district court distinguished formal immunity from an informal undertaking not to prosecute Dixon. Its rejection of formal transactional immunity did not decide whether such an undertaking existed. The court of appeals nevertheless treated both propositions as findings and overlooked evidence supporting an informal arrangement. The earlier Burden decision, 498 U.S. 433, requires faithful consideration of the state immunity determination under the governing factual-presumption statute; it does not permit an invented federal finding to replace the actual record. Cuyler v. Sullivan supplies the merits inquiry: an actual conflict must adversely affect counsel's performance. Neither the absence of formal immunity nor successor counsel's cross-examination resolves whether pretrial counsel sacrificed Burden's interests while representing Dixon. The manifest record mistake alone requires reversal. The Court does not decide whether the state proceeding inadequately developed material facts under §2254(d)(3), whether the conflict predicates are established, or whether a writ ultimately must issue.
metadata.Controlling proposition: A federal habeas judgment resting on deference to a district-court finding that the district court never made must be reversed when that mistake leaves the actual conflict claim unadjudicated. Absence of formal transactional immunity does not establish absence of an informal nonprosecution agreement; on remand the courts must determine whether counsel had an actual conflict that adversely affected his performance under Cuyler v. Sullivan, without presuming those predicates from joint representation alone.
metadata.Event and date: Summary merits decision — 1994-01-10; October Term 1993, chunk 1.
metadata.Result: Leave to proceed without prepaying fees and certiorari granted; judgment reversed and remanded, 9–0.

inventory_refs.caption: Caspari v. Bohlen

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; eight Justices. Stevens disagrees with fair inclusion and would decline the defense under Rule 14.1(a).
metadata.Case and dockets: Caspari v. Bohlen; No. 92-1500.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court separates preservation from the question actually accepted for review. Missouri asserted nonretroactivity throughout the relevant proceedings and described it in the petition, so the late-defense concern addressed in Schiro is absent. That observation alone does not settle Rule 14. Yee and Izumi require distinguishing an argument within a presented question from a related independent question. Here Teague limits whether the particular constitutional rule supporting this same habeas judgment may be applied to the final conviction. It is not a request to reverse an additional party-status order or decide another constitutional claim. The Court treats that confined remedial limit as subsidiary and therefore needs no exceptional-circumstances bypass. Stevens correctly identifies different legal inquiries into constitutional merits and retroactivity, but their difference does not make this limit on the same claimed writ an independent question. The holding neither makes nonretroactivity jurisdictional nor turns a State's preserved defenses into a general exemption from the Court's question-presentation rules.
metadata.Controlling proposition: In this habeas case, Missouri's consistently asserted Teague defense is fairly included as a subsidiary limit on applying the very constitutional rule and granting the writ challenged by the petition, although the stated question names the double-jeopardy issue rather than Teague. The Court therefore considers that nonjurisdictional defense; preservation, disclosure in the petition's body or logical priority alone does not make every independent omitted question reviewable.
metadata.Result: Eighth Circuit habeas judgment reversed, 8–1, under Teague; the constitutional merits remain unresolved.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Environmental law — RCRA household-waste exclusion and ash from municipal waste incinerators
inventory_refs.caption: City of Chicago v. Environmental Defense Fund

metadata.Authority: Scalia’s opinion for the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; seven Justices adopt the statutory rule and its stated limits.
metadata.Case and dockets: City of Chicago v. Environmental Defense Fund, No. 92-1639.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that protection of specified facility activities is not an exemption for every output. Section 6903 separately defines generation as producing hazardous waste. Its management definition lists collection, source separation, storage, transportation, processing, treatment, recovery and disposal, but not generation. Section 3001(i) protects the facility in its listed activities while leaving that distinct category intact. One incineration process can receive one protection and remain subject to another obligation. The earlier household-waste regulation, the clarifying title and the committee’s reference to generation support the contrary reading, but cannot add an omitted activity to the enacted exclusion. Congress’s methane-recovery provision expressly includes generation, confirming the distinction. Chicago’s mixed inputs did not enjoy the earlier pure-household waste-stream protection; the later statute does not create the asserted output exemption. The statutory rule also reaches household-only resource-recovery facilities. The Court leaves open the regulation’s validity for such facilities before §3001(i) took effect and the regulation of household waste outside resource-recovery facilities. It does not find all ash hazardous.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Section 3001(i) protects an energy-recovery facility using mass burning of municipal solid waste from being deemed to treat, store, dispose of or otherwise manage hazardous waste when it receives and burns only household waste from single or multiple dwellings, hotels, motels and other residential sources, and commercial or industrial solid waste containing no hazardous waste identified or listed under §3001; it must not accept identified or listed hazardous waste, and its owner or operator must establish contractual requirements or other appropriate notification or inspection procedures to assure that hazardous waste is neither received nor burned. Those distinct conditions and alternative safeguards protect the listed facility activities, not generation: ash that actually meets the hazardous-waste criteria receives no §3001(i) waste-stream exemption, including ash from an exclusively household-waste resource-recovery facility.
metadata.Result: Affirmed, 7–2; statutory facility exclusion does not exempt generated hazardous ash.

inventory_refs.caption: Custis v. United States

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg; six direct joins to this statutory ground.
metadata.Case and dockets: Custis v. United States; No. 93-5209; 511 U.S. 485.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that an attack on a predicate conviction's constitutional validity must be distinguished from an objection to the federal enhancement's own requirements. Section 924(e) identifies previous convictions, while §921(a)(20) recognizes expungement, setting aside, pardon and civil-rights restoration under its express conditions. Congress expressly supplied a procedure for challenging convictions under the different enhancement scheme in 21 U.S.C. §851(c); it supplied no comparable general procedure here. Lewis v. United States distinguishes an operative conviction from an unresolved collateral objection, although its firearms-disability setting does not decide every sentencing question. Beecham v. United States identifies the jurisdiction whose law governs the removal of a conviction's effect; it does not create a collateral-review forum. Custis's Maryland predicates remained operative. The importance of ineffective-assistance and involuntary-plea claims does not itself create authority to decide them at this sentencing. This conclusion does not find those convictions constitutionally sound, import §851's procedure into the ACCA, or prevent challenges to identification, counting, statutory exclusion, or classification of a predicate.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Under 18 U.S.C. §924(e), a defendant may not use the federal sentencing proceeding to litigate these constitutional attacks on operative state convictions for ineffective assistance and involuntary counseled pleas. The statute does not supply a general collateral-review procedure; the distinct exception for an unconstitutional complete denial of appointed counsel remains, as do objections to whether the enhancement itself satisfies its statutory requirements.
metadata.Result: The Fourth Circuit is affirmed, 6–3.

metadata.Authority: Souter's Opinion of the Court is joined by all nine Justices. The statutory-preclusion ground alone commands the Court; a four-Justice concurrence on recommendation finality is not controlling.
metadata.Case and dockets: Dalton v. Specter; No. 93-289; 511 U.S. 462.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the particular relief sought is foreclosed by the enacted closure scheme. Michigan Academy supplies a strong presumption of review, while Block permits a contrary congressional design to emerge from statutory structure. No single deadline, military subject, presidential role or absence of express review would suffice here. Together, the temporary process, indivisible presidential approval, congressional disapproval opportunity and mandatory implementation establish a selection that the requested injunction would reopen. The separate, time-limited NEPA channel reinforces the distinction between selection and implementation review. The contrary argument properly emphasizes that courts ordinarily enforce statutory procedures. This holding preserves that principle without treating it as authority to undo this completed package. Franklin concerns a completed census determination followed by prescribed transmission and leaves presidential APA status open; it does not decide this statute's preclusion. Thunder Basin likewise requires attention to the actual scheme, and its different later-review route cannot substitute for this analysis. Alleged procedural violations remain allegations. The Court leaves distinct timely procedural claims, genuine constitutional claims and unauthorized additions for a case that presents them.
metadata.Controlling proposition: The 1990 Base Closure Act precludes the present APA challenge seeking to stop implementation of an approved indivisible closure selection because of alleged antecedent selection-process defects. Its combined package-approval structure, strict deadlines, temporary Commission, mandatory implementation, congressional review and expressly confined implementation review overcome the presumption of review for this relief; they do not erase every earlier procedural duty or decide distinct constitutional or unauthorized-action claims.
metadata.Result: The Third Circuit is reversed and the case remanded for dismissal of the presented selection challenge, 9–0.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Federal labor relations — union requests for employee home addresses; Privacy Act and FOIA
inventory_refs.caption: Department of Defense v. Federal Labor Relations Authority

metadata.Authority: Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine Justices adopt this statutory coordination and precedent-based explanation.
metadata.Case and dockets: Department of Defense v. Federal Labor Relations Authority; No. 92-1223.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court gives each enacted condition its function. Congress recognized the public value of collective bargaining and required necessary information, while expressly preserving prohibitions imposed by other law. The Privacy Act's invoked exception asks what FOIA requires, not what another statute makes useful. Reporters Committee supplies the retained statutory precedent measuring the ordinary third-party disclosure interest by public understanding of government operations. Applying that rule here does not decide whether it was the only possible original reading of FOIA. The unions' strongest argument relies on a congressionally selected representational duty, not merely their preferred use of information. But that duty does not change the terms of the exception Congress incorporated. Treasury/IRS confirms that administration of the labor statute remains bounded by enacted limits. The Court therefore preserves the accepted necessity determination while applying FOIA's own inquiry. It decides only the asserted FOIA exception; the subject's written request or consent and any independently applicable exception remain separate questions, without an order requiring their approval.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Section 7114(b)(4)'s duty to supply qualifying bargaining data operates only to the extent disclosure is not prohibited by law; when the asserted exception to the Privacy Act is §552a(b)(2), the question is whether FOIA itself requires disclosure. Retained Reporters Committee precedent governs the ordinary third-party public-interest inquiry, so collective-bargaining utility alone does not enlarge the incorporated FOIA balance; the Court does not decide that this precedent's restriction was inevitably compelled by FOIA's original text.
metadata.Operative statutory qualifications: The labor duty concerns requested data normally maintained by the agency in its regular course of business, reasonably available and necessary for full and proper discussion, understanding and negotiation of subjects within collective bargaining, and not guidance, advice, counsel or training provided for management officials or supervisors relating to collective bargaining. These conditions are not independently disputed or newly adjudicated here. For a record contained in a system of records, §552a(b) bars agency disclosure absent a written request by, or prior written consent of, the individual to whom it pertains, or an applicable enumerated exception. A union request is not the subject individual's request or consent. Routine use under §552a(b)(3) and other exceptions are distinct and undecided; their applicability is not guaranteed.
metadata.Result: Fifth Circuit enforcement judgment reversed, 9–0 on both Gulfport and Lowry components; the asserted Privacy Act FOIA exception does not authorize compelled release of these home addresses.

inventory_refs.caption: Department of Revenue of Oregon v. ACF Industries, Inc.

metadata.Authority: Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; eight Justices adopt the statutory definition as the premise of the exemption ruling.
metadata.Case and dockets: Department of Revenue of Oregon v. ACF Industries, Inc.; No. 92-74.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court reads the comparison definition together with the protections it serves. Congress prohibited discriminatory assessment ratios, collection on those assessments, and rates of taxes based on property value by specifying the property with which railroad property is compared. Section 11503(a)(4) excludes transportation property and agricultural or timber-growing land and also confines commercial and industrial property to property subject to a levy. In this setting, that means property actually taxed, not everything the State has abstract power to tax. The same levy language in subsection (c)'s assessment provision confirms that meaning. Sorenson supports giving repeated words in one Act a consistent meaning. Burlington Northern applies the enacted assessment protection; it does not authorize replacing Congress's comparison class with all potentially taxable property. Respondents' broader reading would deprive the levy qualification of operative effect. The conclusion establishes a statutory classification, not a finding that exempt and railroad property have equal economic burdens or a decision on an assessment or rate challenge not presented here.
metadata.Controlling proposition: For §11503(b)(1)–(3), the §11503(a)(4) commercial-and-industrial comparison class consists of property devoted to commercial or industrial use and actually subject to a property-tax levy, excluding transportation property and land used primarily for agriculture or timber growing. Property exempt from that levy is outside the comparison class; these paragraphs therefore do not require ordinary exemptions granted to nonrailroad property to be extended to railroad property.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded, 8–1; ordinary exemptions within the generally applicable property tax do not support this §11503(b)(4) challenge. Stevens dissents and would vacate and remand for discrimination and remedy review.

metadata.Authority: The per curiam opinion and order, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine Justices grant the motion on this bounded ground.
metadata.Case and dockets: In re Anderson, No. 93-8312.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court grants financial leave after examining this submission. Martin distinguishes an arguable current question from a defective companion paper; it does not make every reference to access sufficient. Demos v. Storrie likewise permits a particular allegation of official interference to clear the filing threshold without proving that allegation or excusing an underlying default. Anderson identifies concrete obstacles to review and appends an order vacating a filing injunction because the record did not show whether notice and an opportunity to be heard had been afforded. That order also affirms dismissal of the complaint and establishes neither lack of notice nor continuing obstruction. The petition faces serious contrary rulings on counsel, trial claims and the adequacy of local remedies, but financial permission is distinct from success under Rule 20. The Court finds no financial deficiency or sufficient basis to characterize this entire paper as frivolous or malicious. It neither accepts the allegations as true nor decides the writ.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Rule 39.8 permits denial of financial leave when the Court is satisfied that the particular submission is frivolous or malicious; prior unsuccessful filings do not by themselves supply that finding. Anderson’s affidavit supports inability to prepay, and the present petition’s specific, partly corroborated access-to-review contention supports granting this motion despite substantial independent obstacles to the requested extraordinary writ; the grant establishes no entitlement to that writ.
metadata.Event and date: 1994-05-02; Rule 39 fee and prospective-control order; October Term 1993, chunk 4.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Equal protection — gender-based peremptory challenges in jury selection
inventory_refs.caption: J.E.B. v. Alabama ex rel. T.B.

metadata.Authority: Blackmun’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter and Ginsburg; six Justices adopt the rule and explanation. Kennedy concurs in the judgment and independently supports the operative prohibition on individual-right grounds.
metadata.Case and dockets: J.E.B. v. Alabama ex rel. T.B.; No. 92-1239.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that a citizen’s sex cannot substitute for individual qualification to serve as a juror. Craig and Hogan require an important objective substantially advanced by a sex classification and protect men as well as women. Batson provides the prohibition on discriminatory peremptories in the racial setting; the Court extends its protection here through sex’s own heightened scrutiny. Powers, Edmonson and McCollum explain the prospective juror’s independent equal-protection interest. Alabama itself exercised these strikes, so its state action is direct. An adversary’s wish for sympathetic jurors cannot justify excluding a citizen on a generalized expectation of male or female views. Even a population-level correlation does not establish this individual juror’s partiality, and voir dire permits inquiry into actual attitudes. The decision does not assume that men and women have identical experiences, abolish peremptory challenges, or require proportional representation. Taylor’s fair-cross-section principle concerns a distinct guarantee; the all-female result is evidence to consider, not itself the constitutional violation. Whether sex requires a stricter classification rule is unnecessary to this decision.
metadata.Controlling proposition: The State may not strike a prospective juror because of sex or the assumption that sex itself predicts competence or impartiality. Under the equal-protection requirement that a sex classification substantially serve an important governmental objective, a generalized prediction that men will favor the alleged father does not justify this exclusion; genuine individual, sex-neutral reasons remain available.
metadata.Result: Alabama Court of Civil Appeals reversed and remanded, 7–2, for the equal-protection jury-selection inquiry and a new trial if the strikes cannot lawfully be sustained.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: ERISA — plan-asset status of insurer general-account funds under a group annuity contract
inventory_refs.caption: John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Harris Trust & Savings Bank

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg's opinion for the Court, joined by Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, and Souter. Six Justices adopt the component-specific construction and its application to the disputed free funds.
metadata.Case and dockets: John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co. v. Harris Trust & Savings Bank, No. 92-1074
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that an insurer cannot remove nonguaranteed plan investments from ERISA merely by placing them in a general account. Section 401(b)(2) confines its exclusion to the extent that the policy supplies benefits whose amount the insurer guarantees. That language requires attention to the particular component, not a choice between exempting or regulating every asset associated with a mixed contract. United Benefit supplies the useful distinction between investment risk borne by the purchaser and a genuine insurance guarantee; ERISA's own text fixes this exclusion. This contract includes guaranteed benefits and a residual floor, but those features do not guarantee the amount of benefits payable from the disputed free funds. A guaranteed reasonable return and fixed conversion protection are significant indicators, not an exhaustive mandatory formula. Commingling, administrative difficulty, and the possibility of later annuity purchases cannot erase the statutory limitation. The Court therefore affirms the status ruling while leaving the separate fiduciary-function, breach, loss, and relief questions for their proper application below.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Under ERISA §401(b)(2), a guaranteed-benefit policy itself is a plan asset, while the insurer's underlying assets are not deemed plan assets solely because it issued the policy to the extent the policy genuinely guarantees the amount of benefits. The disputed nonguaranteed free-funds component is not excluded: its plan-asset character subjects Hancock to fiduciary obligations to the extent it exercises authority or control over management or disposition of those assets under §3(21)(A), without deciding breach, causation, loss, or remedy.
metadata.Result: Affirmed, 6–3; further proceedings on the fiduciary claims.

metadata.Authority: Stevens’s general-framework portion, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Souter and Ginsburg; five Justices adopt this organizing rule. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas concur on a distinct relevant-activity approach, not as additional joins at this level of generality.
metadata.Case and dockets: Landgraf v. USI Film Products, No. 92-757.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court begins with Congress’s direction, not a slogan that every pending case receives either old law or new law. Kaiser makes the enacted temporal instruction the first inquiry. Bowen supplies the presumption against attaching new obligations to completed conduct, and Bennett preserves substantive obligations fixed under earlier law. Bradley remains effective in its litigation-fee setting, where applying the later provision did not impose the new primary liability presented here. A statute is not retrospective merely because its application involves earlier facts or disappoints an expectation. The court must identify the legal consequence being changed. Rules governing future conduct or the court’s present power may operate in pending proceedings; procedural changes likewise do not necessarily alter past legal consequences, although they do not automatically undo a completed trial. Harper governs judicial decisions applied to litigants and does not command backward application of later legislation. The Court leaves constitutional limits on expressly retrospective legislation for a case presenting them.
metadata.Controlling proposition: When Congress has prescribed a civil statute’s temporal reach, courts apply that direction subject to constitutional limits; absent sufficient direction, they ask whether applying the provision would impair rights possessed when a party acted, increase liability for past conduct, or impose new duties concerning completed transactions. If it would, the provision does not govern those events without clear congressional intent; a pending case or reference to earlier facts alone does not establish such an effect, and prospective relief, jurisdiction, procedure and collateral matters require examination of what the particular provision actually changes rather than an automatic reopening of completed acts.
metadata.Event and date: 1994-04-26; merits decision before Rivers; October Term 1993, chunk 4.
metadata.Result: Affirmed, 8–1; five-Justice general temporal framework.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Admiralty — allocating damages between settling and nonsettling defendants
inventory_refs.caption: McDermott, Inc. v. AmClyde

metadata.Authority: Stevens’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone, Blackmun, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; all nine adopt the rule and its settlement-specific limits.
metadata.Case and dockets: McDermott, Inc. v. AmClyde; No. 92-1479.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court adopts a proportionate-share rule within its established authority to develop maritime law. Reliable Transfer supplies allocation by comparative responsibility, but did not decide settlement credit. Dollar credit with contribution exposes a settling defendant to renewed litigation and undermines the peace bought by settlement. Dollar credit coupled with a contribution bar instead makes the nonsettler’s obligation turn on another party’s bargain. A good-faith hearing cannot reliably eliminate that distortion without duplicating much of the liability inquiry. Under proportionate credit, the injured party receives the benefit of a favorable settlement and bears the loss from an unfavorable one. The settlement price purchases certainty; it is not a finding of fault or damages. A possible excess over the later valuation therefore does not require dollar credit. Fault attributable to absent settlers must be reliably determined when material, with an opportunity to present evidence. The rule preserves ordinary challenges to fraudulent or invalid settlements and does not prescribe a credit method for every statutory or nonmaritime action.
metadata.Controlling proposition: When an injured party settles with some alleged joint tortfeasors in a general maritime action, the claim against the nonsettlers is reduced by the settling tortfeasors’ equitable share of the obligation, not by the settlement dollars. Plaintiff and settlers bear their bargain’s gain or shortfall; the nonsettler owes its adjudicated responsibility and has no contribution claim against the settler for that voluntary settlement shortfall.
metadata.Result: Fifth Circuit reversed as to River Don’s dollar settlement credit and remanded, 9–0; the AmClyde contract ruling remains undisturbed.

inventory_refs.caption: McKnight v. General Motors Corp.

metadata.Authority: Per curiam Opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine direct joins.
metadata.Case and dockets: McKnight v. General Motors Corp.; No. 92-1113; 511 U.S. 659.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that losing under circuit precedent does not by itself make preservation of a substantial question frivolous. Mozee and Luddington bound the Court of Appeals on retroactivity, but that court's rejection was a necessary step toward review here. When counsel acted, district courts disagreed and this Court had not answered the question; no favorable circuit decision then existed. The later answer in Rivers does not retrospectively change that setting. The order invoked appellate Rule 38 and Circuit Rule 38, referred to the motion and response, and imposed a penalty on counsel without stating an independent abusive act. Willy permits a distinct collateral sanctions inquiry; it does not establish frivolity or furnish the source of this appellate penalty. Reconsideration must respect that distinction. Nothing here immunizes objectively baseless claims or independently established misconduct, orders reimbursement, or decides the local rule's general authorization beyond the presented sanction ground.
metadata.Controlling proposition: If the only basis for sanctioning counsel was that controlling circuit precedent foreclosed an otherwise substantial, unresolved argument preserved for Supreme Court review, the sanction was improper: counsel had to take the appellate step to seek that review. The $500 sanction against attorney John S. Williamson, Jr., is vacated for reconsideration; an independent sanction ground requires its own lawful basis and actual support, and none is supplied by inference here.
metadata.Result: Counsel sanction vacated and remanded, 9–0; underlying employment disposition undisturbed.

inventory_refs.caption: Morgan Stanley & Co. v. Pacific Mutual Life Insurance Co.

metadata.Authority: Thomas's Opinion of the Court is joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter. Five participating Justices directly join this as-applied Article III rule and the limited remedy; no aggregation of separate rationales is necessary.
metadata.Case and dockets: Morgan Stanley & Co. v. Pacific Mutual Life Insurance Co.; No.93-609; 511 U.S.658.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that a final limitations dismissal is a judicial resolution even though it does not determine whether fraud occurred. Robertson v. Seattle Audubon Society permits changed law in pending litigation but expressly reserves completed judgments. McCullough v. Virginia recognizes the significance of completed adjudication, and United States v. Klein protects the judicial function against legislative prescription. Congress genuinely changed the limitations rule here; that answers neither the finality objection nor the separate command to reinstate. The contrary argument emphasizes restoration of earlier filing expectations and the courts' continued control over fraud findings. But treating that remaining work as sufficient would allow any completed case to be reopened by changing its rule of decision. Wheeling Bridge concerns continuing prospective relief, not this final dismissal. Chase Securities addresses legislative revival under due process and does not settle Article III. Pacific Mutual allowed direct review to end before enactment. The Court withholds only this reopening application, leaving §27A(a), general severability, the underlying claims and independently authorized judicial reopening undecided.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Article III prevents application of §27A(b) to require reinstatement of this private securities action after its dismissal with prejudice became final, without appeal, before the statute was enacted. Congress may change governing law, but that power does not authorize this command to reopen a completed federal judgment; pending litigation, prospective injunctions and independently lawful judicial reopening remain distinct.
metadata.Result: Fifth Circuit reversed; deny §27A(b) reopening on remand, 5–3; O'Connor absent.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Labor law — NLRA supervisor status of nurses; 'in the interest of the employer' test
inventory_refs.caption: NLRB v. Health Care & Retirement Corp. of America

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg's Opinion of the Court is joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens and Souter. All five directly adopt the permissible-construction ground; Stone-Zsela's proposed mandatory construction appears only in his concurrence.
metadata.Case and dockets: NLRB v. Health Care & Retirement Corp. of America; No. 92-1964; 511 U.S. 571.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the employer's economic benefit from patient care does not alone answer whether skilled direction constitutes supervisory authority. Sections 2(3), 2(11), 2(12) and 9(b) preserve both employee coverage and genuine supervisory exclusion. Fall River Dyeing requires respect for a rational Board construction consistent with that scheme and an application supported by substantial evidence. Yeshiva University recognizes that professional and institutional interests can coincide, while distinguishing ordinary professional work from management; its managerial exclusion does not replace this statutory inquiry. The Board examined limited direction, established assignment patterns and administrators' continuing availability, rather than relying on a nursing title. Those findings make its functional rationale discernible under Chenery and Boston & Maine. The opposing reading risks making ordinary skilled instruction itself a supervisory role. Yet the Board may not discard assigning or responsibly directing, demand hiring power in every case, or deny that professional judgment can be independent judgment. Lechmere's statutory limits remain. The Court sustains this permissible interpretation, without holding it the only lawful construction or supplying an unpresented alternative independent-judgment ground.
metadata.Controlling proposition: The Board permissibly interprets NLRA §2(11), in the context of the Act's protection of skilled and professional employees, to distinguish direction incidental to skilled patient care from genuine supervisory authority exercised for the employer. On this record, its functional construction and supported determination that the four licensed practical nurses are employees must be sustained; no occupational exemption or independent judicial substitute for the agency's rationale is adopted.
metadata.Result: The Sixth Circuit is reversed on the supervisory-status issue and the case remanded, 5–4.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: RICO — whether an economic motive is needed for racketeering enterprise; clinics' standing
inventory_refs.caption: National Organization for Women, Inc. v. Scheidler

metadata.Authority: Blackmun's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine Justices adopt this threshold ruling.
metadata.Case and dockets: National Organization for Women, Inc. v. Scheidler; No. 92-780.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court assesses the two clinics' own alleged injuries. Simon requires named plaintiffs to establish their own standing even when they seek class treatment; no class was certified here, and NOW did not assert the RICO counts. Allen requires injury fairly traceable to the challenged conduct. The clinics allege that force and threats drove away staff and patients and harmed their businesses, including a threat of reprisals against one clinic's administrator. Those allegations connect the asserted injury to respondents' conduct. Hishon requires sustaining a complaint when relief could follow from facts proved consistently with its allegations. Respondents' demand for more at this stage would treat an untried pleading as a completed evidentiary record. Holmes's factual and proximate-cause requirements remain operative; today's threshold ruling does not find a pattern, an extortionate obtaining of property or the direction of an enterprise. It permits the two clinics to proceed on their own claimed injury while leaving proof and each defendant's responsibility for further proceedings.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Delaware Women's Health Organization and Summit Women's Health Organization have standing at the Rule 12(b)(6) stage on allegations that respondents' threatened and actual force against staff and patients caused injury to the clinics' own business or property. Under the governing pleading standard, the allegations suffice where relief could be granted on facts consistent with them; this neither supplies standing to NOW on an unasserted RICO count nor establishes liability, a certified class or final proof of causation.

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's plurality, joined by Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, permits this application under a broader valid-conviction rule; Souter's concurrence in the judgment expressly permits this Guidelines application on the narrower reliability-and-opportunity ground. Five Justices support the stated permission at this level; no complete rationale has five joins, and Souter supplies no fifth vote to overrule Baldasar generally.
metadata.Case and dockets: Nichols v. United States; No.92-8556; 511 U.S.738.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court permits this use within the sentencing framework actually presented. Scott leaves the original fine-only conviction valid; the question is the consequence of that conviction in a later counseled prosecution. Section 4A1.1(c) assigns one point to a prior sentence not included under its more serious categories, subject to its cap, and the commentary expressly includes DUI rather than treating it as a minor traffic infraction. The framework also provides an opportunity to contest sentencing information and permits a downward departure for significant overrepresentation under §4A1.3. A claim that every such Guidelines use is forbidden therefore does not prevail here. Nichols did not present that overrepresentation contention, and the Court invents neither a departure nor independent proof of the DUI conduct. Baldasar involved a different later misdemeanor-to-felony use and yielded incompatible rationales; its judgment cannot be turned into five identical reasons governing this case. The shared permission is confined to these conditions. The broader justification, automatic-enhancement question and proposed general overruling retain their distinct voting support.
metadata.Controlling proposition: An uncounseled misdemeanor conviction valid under Scott because no imprisonment was imposed may supply the otherwise authorized criminal-history point in the Guidelines setting presented here: the later prosecution is counseled and the sentencing framework provides a genuine opportunity to contest reliability, relevance and significant overrepresentation through its lawful procedures, including a permitted §4A1.3 departure. This limited permission neither makes a departure mandatory nor adopts a general rule for a scheme that conclusively requires enhanced incarceration without that opportunity.
metadata.Result: Sixth Circuit affirmed, 5–4, on fractured grounds; general Baldasar overruling lacks five votes.

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter; seven Justices adopt this threshold reasoning. Thomas independently accepts jurisdiction, the limited assumption and preservation of both corrections, but does not join the Court's statutory merits rationale.
metadata.Case and dockets: Northwest Airlines, Inc. v. County of Kent; No. 92-97.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court has federal-question jurisdiction over the asserted federal claims; it does not assume that power. Bell v. Hood and Burks v. Lasker distinguish jurisdiction from the existence of a statutory claim for relief. The Airport and the United States raise a substantial question whether the airlines instead must begin before the Transportation Department. That question need not be settled to reject the appealed claims. Thigpen permits a prevailing respondent to defend a judgment on an alternative ground, but Thurston requires cross-review when the respondent seeks to change it. The Airport lost the crash, fire and rescue allocation issue below. A ruling that the entire AHTA action was unavailable would undo that favorable relief as well as preserve the Airport's victories. Its failure to cross-petition therefore matters. The Court assumes the action only for this decision, preserves both existing corrections, and leaves the unreviewed AAIA action question and unbriefed primary-jurisdiction question undecided.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Federal-question jurisdiction under §1331 is distinct from whether the AHTA creates a private action; the Court assumes that nonjurisdictional action solely to reject the airlines' appealed claims without deciding that it exists. An alternative ground may defend the judgment, but the Airport's failure to cross-petition prevents using its no-action argument to eliminate the airlines' favorable crash, fire and rescue allocation remand; the separately unappealed parking correction also remains in force.
metadata.Result: Sixth Circuit judgment affirmed, 7–1 overall; the appealed AHTA claim fails 8–0 on different grounds, and the constitutional challenge fails 7–1. The unappealed parking correction and crash, fire and rescue allocation remand remain intact.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Environmental law — Clean Water Act §401 certification and state minimum stream-flow conditions on hydroelectric projects
inventory_refs.caption: PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County v. Washington Department of Ecology

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg; seven direct joins to this proposition and its explanation.
metadata.Case and dockets: PUD No. 1 of Jefferson County v. Washington Department of Ecology; No. 92-1911; 511 U.S. 700.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the trigger and the scope of necessary conditions perform different statutory work. Section 401(a)(1) identifies activities involving possible discharges; subsection (d) then requires assurance of the applicant's compliance. Petitioners concede construction and tailrace discharges, so no general rule classifying every diversion as a discharge is needed. EPA's §121.2(a)(3) requires reasonable assurance concerning the activity, a reasonable reading entitled to deference under Chevron within the delegation recognized here. Subsection (a)(4)'s reference to conditions concerning the activity's discharge supplies a substantial contrary argument, but it does not erase the statute's broader applicant-compliance language. Arkansas v. Oklahoma supports respect for a permissible interpretation of this water-quality scheme without transferring its distinct §402 proof rules. Health Care likewise requires examination of the particular text, not automatic deference. The construction permits necessary water-quality protection, not unrelated land-use or energy policy. The Court does not adopt the Government's alternative discharge-nexus argument or a general test governing every State-law condition.
metadata.Controlling proposition: When an activity requiring a federal license or permit may result in a discharge into navigable waters, §401(a)(1) triggers certification, and §401(d) permits limitations and monitoring on the applicant's activity as necessary to assure compliance with its listed federal requirements and other appropriate State-law requirements stated in the certification. Conditioning authority is not confined to the particular triggering discharge, but it remains tied to those lawful compliance requirements; EPA's reasonable activity-compliance interpretation reinforces this reading without creating authority to contradict the statute.
metadata.Result: Washington Supreme Court affirmed, 7–2; minimum-flow certification condition sustained.
