inventory_refs.caption: Rivers v. Roadway Express, Inc.

metadata.Authority: Stevens’s opinion, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Souter and Ginsburg; these five adopt the complete explanation. Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas reach the same temporal result through their separate relevant-activity and textual-command method.
metadata.Case and dockets: Rivers v. Roadway Express, Inc., No. 92-938.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court applies Landgraf to the particular provision before it. Section 101 enlarges the contractual conduct for which §1981 imposes liability; it does not merely change the procedure for deciding an unchanged claim. The coverage extends beyond employment and beyond employers subject to Title VII, so the amendment cannot be reduced to a new remedy for an identical preexisting duty. Section 402(a) makes the Act effective upon enactment except as otherwise specifically provided. Section 109(c) separately confines its extraterritorial amendments to later conduct. Section 402(b) excludes disparate-impact cases whose complaints preceded March 1, 1975 and whose initial decisions followed October 30, 1983. These distinct provisions do not direct the broader application sought here. Section 3(4)’s expansion purpose likewise identifies a substantive aim, not temporal reach. Bowen and Bennett support the protection against new consequences for completed conduct; Bradley’s collateral-fee setting does not eliminate that inquiry. The existing contract-enforcement claim remains available under the earlier statute, subject to its own elements and the proceedings already ordered below.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Section 101’s expansion of §1981’s making-and-enforcing-contracts coverage to include making, performance, modification, termination, and enjoyment of all benefits, privileges, terms and conditions of the contractual relationship does not govern conduct completed before November 21, 1991: it adds substantive legal consequences without sufficient congressional direction for that reach. This provision-specific rule does not eliminate a claim already covered by old §1981 or decide a separate dispute over subsection (c)’s protection against nongovernmental discrimination and impairment under color of state law.
metadata.Event and date: 1994-04-26; merits decision after Landgraf; October Term 1993, chunk 4.
metadata.Result: Affirmed and remanded, 8–1; existing old-law enforcement jury remand preserved.

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg, seven Justices. Blackmun and Stevens also agree with merits reach, but their agreement is unnecessary to the opinion's controlling authority.

metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court declines to decide the State's late nonretroactivity defense. Collins v. Youngblood establishes that Teague does not limit subject-matter jurisdiction and need not be raised by the Court on its own. That distinction permits attention to the way a case was presented. Indiana defended the judgment in the lower courts and opposed review without invoking Teague. Its later merits brief does not make consideration of that defense compulsory. The fully presented double-jeopardy questions can therefore be resolved without deciding whether Schiro seeks a new rule or whether a Teague exception would permit it. This exercise of discretion does not establish that every omission permanently forfeits nonretroactivity, or that a reviewing court may never consider the question on its own. The State's legitimate interest in finality does not turn a nonjurisdictional defense into an unavoidable threshold in this procedural posture.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Teague nonretroactivity is not jurisdictional. When the State omitted that defense in the lower courts and in its opposition to certiorari and first raised it in merits briefing, the Court may decline to consider it; the Court exercises that discretion here and reaches the presented double-jeopardy claims.
metadata.Result: Seventh Circuit affirmed, 7–2; no habeas relief on the presented claims.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Criminal procedure — Miranda custody and officers' undisclosed suspicion of the person questioned
inventory_refs.caption: Stansbury v. California

metadata.Authority: The per curiam opinion, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; all nine adopt the rule and reversal with remand.
metadata.Case and dockets: Stansbury v. California, No. 93-5770.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the custody inquiry concerns the restraint a reasonable person would understand, not a police officer’s private plan. Miranda requires warnings for custodial interrogation. Mathiason and Beheler explain that questioning at a station, even of a suspect, is not custody without arrest or comparable restraint. Berkemer makes the inquiry objective because an undisclosed intention cannot affect the person’s understanding of freedom to leave. Beckwith likewise rejects investigative focus as a substitute for custody. California nevertheless gave weight to the officers’ view that Stansbury was initially a witness rather than a suspect. That legal criterion was mistaken. A reassuring label cannot overcome objective restraint; a communicated accusation does not alone establish it. The state court must assess the circumstances actually presented, including the manner of questioning and conditions at the station. The Court does not decide whether custody began before the warnings, whether any particular statement must be excluded, or whether any established error would require further relief.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Miranda custody exists upon formal arrest or restraint on freedom of movement of the degree associated with formal arrest, assessed from all objective circumstances as a reasonable person in the interviewee’s position would understand them; an officer’s uncommunicated view that the person is or is not a suspect, and the interviewee’s undisclosed subjective belief, have no independent role. An officer’s words or conduct conveying suspicion matter only to the extent they affect that objective understanding: communicated suspicion is not automatically custody, and undisclosed beliefs bearing on a witness’s credibility do not thereby become independent custody factors.
metadata.Result: Reversed and remanded, 9–0.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Criminal law — National Firearms Act mens rea for possessing an unregistered automatic weapon
inventory_refs.caption: Staples v. United States

metadata.Authority: Thomas's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy and Souter, supplies five direct joins to this rule and its explanation. Ginsburg, joined by O'Connor, independently concurs in the judgment on the same narrow factual-knowledge requirement; the Court's authority does not depend on combining different rationales under Marks.
metadata.Case and dockets: Staples v. United States; No. 92-1441; 511 U.S. 600.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that knowledge must reach the characteristic distinguishing this machinegun from an ordinary semiautomatic rifle. Morissette v. United States preserves the traditional presumption of criminal fault when a statute is silent, and United States v. United States Gypsum Co. requires examination of the particular offense before dispensing with it. United States v. Freed concerned knowing possession of grenades and ignorance of their registration status; it did not resolve ignorance of the physical feature that places an otherwise ordinarily possessed rifle within this Act. The Government's reliance on a gun's dangerous character does not alone establish that Congress eliminated knowledge of that feature. Ordinary lawful rifle possession and the substantial statutory penalty support the narrower construction together; neither establishes a categorical rule for all dangerous objects or all felonies. Here the instruction expressly allowed conviction without knowledge of the defining characteristics. Staples's testimony does not establish that he lacked knowledge, and modifications or firing behavior may supply circumstantial proof. Further proceedings must apply the correct requirement while preserving ordinary sufficiency and retrial constraints.
metadata.Controlling proposition: To convict a defendant under 26 U.S.C. §5861(d) for possessing an unregistered machinegun in the circumstances presented here, the Government must prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant knew the characteristics bringing the rifle within the complete-weapon machinegun definition—a weapon that shoots, is designed to shoot, or can be readily restored to shoot automatically more than one shot, without manual reloading, by a single function of the trigger; circumstantial evidence may establish that knowledge. It need not prove knowledge of nonregistration, the registration requirement, or illegality, and the omitted-element instruction requires reversal and remand without a finding of evidentiary insufficiency or an order of acquittal.
metadata.Result: Tenth Circuit reversed and remanded, 7–2.
metadata.Version / lineage: Initial decision; supersedes no earlier adjudication. inventory_refs.area_of_law: Capital sentencing — felony-murder aggravator duplicating offense elements and Eighth Amendment narrowing
inventory_refs.caption: Tennessee v. Middlebrooks

metadata.Authority: Justice O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Blackmun, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg; all nine Justices support the rule and its application. No combination of separate opinions is necessary.
metadata.Case and dockets: Tennessee v. Middlebrooks; No. 92-989.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court reviews judgments, not abstract statements of federal law. Herb v. Pitcairn forbids a federal correction that cannot affect the judgment; Coleman v. Thompson recognizes that adequate, independent state grounds impose that jurisdictional limit on direct review. Michigan v. Long respects a clear state ground even when a state court also discusses federal law. Tennessee's original opinion did more than cite its Constitution. It relied on Tennessee's prohibition of duplicative enhancement in noncapital sentencing and independently construed Article I, §16 to prohibit the aggravator's use here. Howell's majority then expressly explained that this state provision required Middlebrooks's result and that the federal discussion considered an additional constitutional ground. The extended Eighth Amendment analysis therefore does not make the state judgment dependent on federal law. Correcting that analysis would leave the resentencing requirement intact. This conclusion rests on the original reasoning and the state court's explicit clarification together, not on counsel's assertion or a rule that any later footnote defeats review. The Court decides neither finality under Cox nor the federal sentencing merits.
metadata.Event and date: Jurisdictional dismissal after argument — 1993-12-13; October Term 1993, chunk 1.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: The Court lacks jurisdiction to review a state judgment when an adequate state constitutional ground independent of federal law requires the same judgment whatever the answer to the federal question. The Tennessee Supreme Court's original state constitutional analysis in Middlebrooks, expressly confirmed by its subsequent majority opinion in Howell, independently requires this resentencing judgment, so the writ is dismissed for want of jurisdiction.
metadata.Result: Writ of certiorari dismissed for want of jurisdiction, 9–0; the Tennessee Supreme Court's resentencing judgment remains undisturbed.

inventory_refs.caption: United States v. Alvarez-Sanchez

metadata.Authority: Thomas’s opinion for the Court, joined in full by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg; all nine adopt the same bounded rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. Alvarez-Sanchez, No. 92-1812.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that delay presupposes a duty that has arisen. McNabb and Mallory concern federal presentment, and §3501(c) identifies an officer empowered to commit persons for federal or District of Columbia offenses. Reading any law-enforcement officer to include state officers does not erase that context. The case reaches the Court on a state-only-custody premise, with the statement preceding the later federal arrest. Ordinary notice of counterfeit currency does not alone establish an improper holding arrangement, and later failure to prosecute state charges does not automatically transform earlier custody. Anderson v. United States preserves the serious concern about using state detention to evade federal duties. The Court neither presumes that such arrangements are rare nor decides §3501’s effect on Anderson’s rule. The District Court’s reported no-collusion finding describes the posture below; this Court does not review or endorse its factual correctness. Actual detention governs, while the limits of disputed arrangements remain open.
metadata.Controlling proposition: In a federal or District of Columbia prosecution, detention solely on state charges does not itself start §3501(c)’s federal-presentment period; the period concerns delay in performing the duty to bring the person before an officer empowered to commit defendants for federal or District of Columbia offenses. Any law-enforcement officer can hold a person on a basis or arrangement engaging that duty, but suspicion of a federal offense, ordinary interagency notification or a state label alone does not decide it; the Court does not make formal federal charges or arrest indispensable in every possible arrangement.
metadata.Result: Reversed and remanded, 9–0; all nine join the bounded opinion.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Civil forfeiture — pre-seizure notice and hearing for real property; timeliness of forfeiture action
inventory_refs.caption: United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property

metadata.Authority: Kennedy's opinion for the Court, Pre-seizure process portion, joined by Stone, Blackmun, Stevens, Souter, and Ginsburg. These six adopt the same rule, its exigency qualification, and its application.
metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. James Daniel Good Real Property, No. 92-1180
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that taking control of land and its rents requires a separate inquiry into fair procedure. Soldal establishes that protection against unreasonable seizure does not displace another constitutional safeguard. Mathews directs attention to the owner's interest, the danger of error and value of additional procedures, and the Government's interests and burdens. Good's tenants remained, but the Government controlled occupancy and received their rent. An ex parte probable-cause determination does not answer every ownership defense or substitute for an opportunity to contest forfeiture. Doehr and Fuentes explain why notice and adversarial participation can prevent wrongful deprivation. Calero-Toledo permitted postponement for movable property and exceptional governmental needs; land ordinarily can be preserved without first taking possession or income. Its immovability does not eliminate waste, transfer, or unlawful use, but those risks require an actual showing that narrower safeguards are inadequate. None was made here. The Court therefore affirms the hearing ruling for civil real-property forfeiture, while reserving criminal forfeiture and the ultimate forfeiture merits.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Before seizing real property for civil forfeiture, the Government must ordinarily give the owner notice and a meaningful opportunity to be heard; a Fourth Amendment warrant does not itself satisfy this independent Fifth Amendment requirement. To bypass prior process for exigent circumstances, the Government must show that less restrictive measures, such as notice of the pending claim recorded against the property, a restraining order, or a bond, would not prevent sale, destruction, or continued unlawful use; emergency seizure remains possible on that showing with appropriate subsequent process.
metadata.Result: Affirmed in part (pre-seizure process, 6–3), reversed in part (statutory timing, 9–0), and remanded.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Speech — public employee discharge; whose account of disputed workplace speech governs the Connick inquiry
inventory_refs.caption: Waters v. Churchill

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's plurality opinion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Souter and Ginsburg, adopts this sufficient condition; Scalia's concurrence in the judgment, joined by Kennedy and Thomas, expressly accepts it under their broader genuine-ground rule. Seven Justices agree at this precise level; only four adopt the full objective-inquiry framework.
metadata.Case and dockets: Waters v. Churchill; No.92-1450; 511 U.S.661.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court's common rule permits reliance on a genuine, reasonable account without requiring perfect reconstruction of a workplace conversation. Pickering balances protected public criticism against effective public service, and Connick permits reasonable forecasts of disruption in the actual employment setting. An employer need not await a breakdown, but the account must describe speech the legal balance permits it to discipline. Givhan protects private expression without eliminating the relevance of its manner, time and place. These principles do not protect an asserted belief that was not the real reason for discharge. Mt. Healthy requires attention to actual causation rather than a reason that merely could have justified the result. Here the reported attack on supervisory authority and discouragement of transfer could permissibly prompt discipline because of its threatened disruption, even assuming some public-concern value. That conditional legal conclusion neither finds the reported words true nor establishes genuine reliance. The separate patient-care criticism and asserted management hostility leave the actual basis for discharge disputed.
metadata.Controlling proposition: A public employer does not violate the employee's substantive speech right by disciplining her because of a genuinely held, objectively reasonable account of speech that the Pickering–Connick balance permits it to discipline, even if that account is later shown mistaken. The protection requires actual reliance on the permissible ground; it does not protect a reasonable investigation used to conceal retaliation for different protected speech.
metadata.Result: Vacate and remand, 7–2; defendants' summary judgment remains set aside; fractured rationales.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Military justice — Appointments Clause and due process for military judges' appointment and tenure
inventory_refs.caption: Weiss v. United States

metadata.Authority: Part A of Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Blackmun, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; nine Justices support the confined existing-commission and germane-duty proposition.
metadata.Case and dockets: Weiss v. United States; No. 92-1482, including Hernandez under Rule 12.2.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court examines the office and duties, not merely Congress's choice of the word detailing. Buckley establishes that persons exercising significant federal authority must hold constitutionally authorized appointments. These judges already possess presidential commissions confirmed by the Senate. Shoemaker permits germane additional responsibilities within a validly conferred office; it does not permit an unauthorized official to fill a distinct federal office by renaming appointment as assignment. Administering military discipline has long belonged to commissioned officers' responsibilities. Congress's judicial qualifications and separation of judging from command make that function more independent without removing its connection to the military office. Articles 26 and 66 accordingly provide for detailing or assignment of qualified officers rather than a second appointment. The constitutional objection fails on that bounded combination of existing appointment and germane duties. Neither administrative convenience nor the initial commission alone would establish authority to assign an unrelated office, and civilian appellate judges are outside the facts before the Court.
metadata.Controlling proposition: The Appointments Clause applies to military judges, but the already commissioned officers serving as trial and appellate judges in these cases require no second appointment: their judicial duties are germane to the military offices conferred by presidential appointment and Senate confirmation. Assignment by a Judge Advocate General does not itself confer a new, unrelated federal office; the holding does not authorize that result or decide civilian appellate appointments or assignment to principal offices.
metadata.Result: Both Court of Military Appeals judgments affirmed, 9–0 on appointment and fixed-tenure components.

inventory_refs.caption: Adarand Constructors, Inc. v. Peña

metadata.Authority: Threshold portion of Justice Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; five Justices adopt the proposition. Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas independently agree with this threshold conclusion in their dissenting positions.
metadata.Case and dockets: Adarand Constructors, Inc. v. Peña, No. 93-1841.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that unequal opportunity to compete is an injury even when the award remains uncertain. Northeastern Florida identifies the governmental barrier, rather than proof of the award that would follow its removal, as the relevant competitive injury. Adarand submitted the low bid, but the prime contractor selected a certified disadvantaged business in response to the financial incentive. The contractor could decline that incentive; its optional character does not remove its effect on competitive opportunity. Lujan requires the connection to be concrete and the requested relief appropriate to a continuing or threatened injury. Adarand's recurring bids and the likelihood of encountering the challenged clause again satisfy that prospective requirement on this record. The Court does not infer a guaranteed future award, an entitlement to damages, or a waiver of sovereign immunity. Nor does accepting this competitive injury establish that the challenged preference is unconstitutional; justification remains a separate question.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A bidder able and ready to compete suffers a personal injury when a governmental racial preference denies equal competitive opportunity; it need not prove that it would have received the contract. Prospective relief also requires a real, sufficiently imminent renewed exposure to that preference, which Adarand's repeated bidding and continuing opportunity to encounter the challenged incentive establish here.
metadata.Result: The Tenth Circuit judgment is affirmed, 5–4.

metadata.Authority: The Court's per curiam opinion, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer; all nine adopt this threshold rule and its application.
metadata.Case and dockets: Anderson v. Green; No. 94-197; 513 U.S. 557
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the present controversy cannot support a constitutional judgment. California law makes the necessary federal approval a condition of this benefit provision's operation. Beno removed that approval, and no replacement has been established. Regional Rail Reorganization Act Cases requires assessment of ripeness when the Court acts; Hall v. Beals prevents a decision based on conjectural future events. California's request for administrative reconsideration does not establish what program could lawfully operate or what terms a new approval might impose. Church of Scientology preserves a controversy when meaningful partial relief remains available, but this record identifies no comparable continuing effect that a constitutional ruling could remedy. The presence of a statute and a class including future recipients cannot substitute for the missing implementation prerequisite. The Court therefore leaves the travel and equal-treatment questions unanswered. It neither restores the removed approval nor determines the validity of any later authorization.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A constitutional challenge to this approval-dependent benefit program is not ripe when the necessary federal authorization has been removed and no replacement authorization is established. The mere possibility of a new approval does not permit adjudication of the constitutionality of a program whose operative terms remain contingent.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit judgment vacated, 9–0; remand for vacatur of District Court preliminary judgment and dismissal without prejudice as unripe.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Endangered Species Act — whether 'harm' in the take prohibition reaches habitat modification
inventory_refs.caption: Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon

metadata.Authority: Souter's Opinion of the Court, Part I; Stone, Stevens, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg, and Breyer join this statutory proposition. Seven votes make it controlling independently of Part II's deference rationale.
metadata.Case and dockets: Babbitt v. Sweet Home Chapter of Communities for a Great Oregon, No. 94-859
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the enacted definition permits this bounded construction. Congress included harm alongside hunting, shooting, wounding, and killing; harm therefore can reach injury caused through a change in the conditions on which animals depend. The regulation does not turn every land-use decision into a taking. It requires significant habitat modification and actual death or injury through significant impairment of essential behavior. The incidental-take permit provisions reinforce the distinction between causing injury and acting with injury as one's purpose. The separate federal-agency provisions protect against jeopardy and destruction of critical habitat under different conditions; their existence does not erase the individual-animal protection of section 9. MCI requires statutory authority before an agency acts, and that requirement is satisfied here by the enacted definition and the connected provisions. The contrary reading gives the definition's broad injury term too little independent work. The Court decides facial validity, leaving proof of particular violations for appropriate proceedings.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: The ESA permits the Secretary to define harm to include significant habitat modification or degradation that actually kills or injures protected wildlife by significantly impairing essential behavioral patterns, including breeding, feeding, or sheltering. Habitat change without the required animal injury is outside this clause.
metadata.Result: 7–2; reverse the facial invalidation and remand.

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined at this level by Stone-Zsela, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Ginsburg; six support the general connection rule. Stevens, Thomas and Breyer concur only in the judgment on their different actual-crew approach.
metadata.Case and dockets: Chandris, Inc. v. Latsis; No. 94-325.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that contribution and substantial employment connection are distinct requirements. Wilander removes any requirement that a seaman perform navigational duties, while retaining the line between a vessel's workforce and land-based employees incidentally aboard. Gizoni rejects occupational labels and voluntary compensation as conclusive substitutes for that employment inquiry. Nature and duration together identify whether the relationship ordinarily exposes the worker to the vessel's work as part of its company. The lower court's duration-or-nature formula does not preserve both dimensions. The parties stipulated that Latsis contributed to the mission, but disputed the nature and extent of his shipboard assignment. Neither that stipulation nor his presence on the injury voyage settles the remaining connection. A genuinely new essential assignment is evaluated on its own activities; prior shoreside years cannot mechanically defeat a newly established shipboard role. Conversely, later employment cannot retroactively create a relationship absent when injury occurred. The Court leaves actual status to proper factual evaluation and decides neither negligence nor damages.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Jones Act seaman status requires work contributing to a vessel's function or mission and an employment-related connection to a vessel in navigation or identifiable fleet that is substantial in both duration and nature. The actual assignment governs; a job label or isolated moment aboard is not conclusive, and a genuine change of essential assignment is assessed on the new position rather than mechanically diluted by earlier shoreside service.
metadata.Participation and authority: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer; nine participants, quorum satisfied, five votes required for a controlling proposition. metadata.Authority: Ginsburg's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Breyer: six direct votes.
metadata.Case and dockets: City of Edmonds v. Oxford House, Inc.; No. 94-23
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the exemption addresses crowding rather than the membership of a household. Section 3607(b)(1) preserves reasonable restrictions on the maximum number of people occupying a dwelling, while section 3604(f) supplies protection against disability discrimination and requires reasonable accommodation within its terms. Edmonds permits any number of people related by genetics, adoption or marriage, yet limits unrelated people to five. That operation identifies who may live together, not how many occupants the dwelling can safely hold. The City's strongest response is that five is a real maximum for the unrelated household. But a numerical feature does not change the subject of this rule: unlimited related occupancy remains permitted. Reading the exception in its enacted setting keeps genuine crowding controls distinct from household definitions. The Court decides only the exemption. It does not invalidate single-family zoning, find discrimination, order a particular accommodation or determine ultimate relief.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: The FHA exemption for reasonable restrictions regarding the maximum number of occupants permitted to occupy a dwelling does not cover Edmonds' family definition, which permits an unlimited number of related residents while limiting unrelated residents to five. The definition regulates household composition, so the absolute exemption does not foreclose the ordinary FHA discrimination and accommodation inquiry.
metadata.Result: The Ninth Circuit is affirmed, 6-3.

inventory_refs.caption: City of Milwaukee v. Cement Division, National Gypsum Co.

metadata.Authority: Stevens's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; all eight participating Justices adopt the complete rule and affirm the calculation remand.
metadata.Case and dockets: City of Milwaukee v. Cement Division, National Gypsum Co., No. 94-788
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that prejudgment interest compensates rather than punishes. The Scotland preserves equitable judgment in admiralty, but that discretion must serve compensation for the claimant's lost use of money. Reliable Transfer assigns collision damages in proportion to comparative responsibility. Here principal already reflects National Gypsum's two-thirds fault and the City's one-third responsibility; denying interest because both were at fault would make the same circumstance reduce compensation again. An honest disagreement about liability is likewise common in litigation and does not eliminate the eventual loss of use. The City's discretion argument therefore rests on legally insufficient reasons. No statute displaces the traditional maritime rule, and uncertainty of amount does not create a fixed liquidated-claim prerequisite. Genuine supported exceptional circumstances, including undue delay attributable to the claimant, remain relevant on their actual record. The principal was settled and paid with interest expressly reserved. The Court neither rewrites that bargain nor converts the claimant's requested interest into an award; calculation remains for further proceedings.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Maritime prejudgment interest ordinarily compensates loss of use of an otherwise compensable amount; departure requires a legally sufficient exceptional circumstance supported by the record. Mutual fault already reflected in principal damages and a genuine ordinary liability dispute, without more, do not justify denial; undue claimant-caused delay can qualify, but the Court adopts no exhaustive list, fixed liquidated-claim prerequisite, rate, period, compounding rule or sum.
metadata.Precedent treatment: The Scotland, 118 U.S. 507, is applied to compensatory equitable discretion, not unbounded fairness. United States v. Reliable Transfer Co., 421 U.S. 397, is applied to proportional collision fault and the avoidance of a second deduction for that same fault. McDermott and Boca Grande retain their separate maritime settlement/contribution rules; neither creates an interest exception.
metadata.Result: Affirmed, 8–0; Breyer takes no part.

metadata.Authority: Stevens's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer; five directly support the causal holding. Scalia concurs only in the judgment and supplies no vote for this explanation.
metadata.Case and dockets: Commissioner v. Schleier; No. 94-500.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that these receipts are taxable because their compensating purpose does not satisfy the statutory causal condition. Section 61 begins with inclusion; § 104(a)(2) and Treasury Regulation § 1.104-1(c) require both a qualifying claim and qualifying injury-related receipts. The nature of a legal wrong cannot alone settle what each payment redresses. The backpay here replaces earnings lost through the employment deprivation, rather than wages lost because a demonstrated personal injury prevented work. Thurston supplies the ADEA liquidated amount's punitive purpose; Hazen Paper makes knowledge or reckless disregard the willfulness trigger. That multiplier responds to the employer's conduct, not the extent of personal harm. Missel's compensatory treatment of a different FLSA provision does not control this ADEA award. Discrimination may cause dignitary or emotional injury, but that possibility does not identify these payments as compensation for it. The Court assumes tort-type rights and leaves their general ADEA classification open. It does not exclude all wage-measured injury damages or decide a general punitive-damages tax rule.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Under the applicable § 104(a)(2), a taxpayer must satisfy both the regulation's tort-or-tort-type-right requirement and the statute's independent requirement that the particular damages be received on account of personal injuries or sickness; amounts attributable to deductions allowed under § 213 in a prior year remain excepted from the exclusion. Assuming the ADEA claim satisfies the first requirement, these backpay and willfulness-based liquidated damages fail the second and must be included in gross income.
metadata.Participation and authority: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, Breyer; nine participants, quorum satisfied, five votes required for a controlling proposition. Review proceeds in the user-admitted merits posture, not through a new certiorari poll. The separate simulated grant date and verbatim grant order are not supplied and are not invented. Operational questions are reconstructed scope, not quotations from a Court order.
metadata.Result: The Fifth Circuit judgment excluding the ADEA backpay and liquidated damages is reversed, 6–3, and the case is remanded for lawful tax treatment.

metadata.Case and dockets: First Options of Chicago, Inc. v. Kaplan; No. 94-560.

metadata.Same-term premise control: References below to a decision or rule in an earlier OT1994 matter are conditional on the Court actually adopting that proposition before this event. metadata.Stone's Legal Position: Stone applies ordinary consent principles. Courts independently decide whether parties agreed to submit arbitrability to the arbitrator unless clear and unmistakable evidence shows that delegation. Merely arguing arbitrability to the panel while objecting to jurisdiction does not establish consent. Appellate review of the district court’s legal conclusion is ordinary, not specially deferential.
metadata.Stone's Proposed Holding: Courts decide arbitrability independently absent clear and unmistakable agreement to delegate that question, and a party does not consent merely by presenting an objection to the arbitrators while preserving it.
metadata.Stone's Reasoning and Record Application: Arbitration rests on agreement. Silence and defensive participation cannot supply the delegation. Once the court properly determines no agreement existed, ordinary standards govern appellate review of that judicial determination.

metadata.Authority: Kennedy’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg; five Justices adopt the same advancement-and-fit ground.
metadata.Case and dockets: Florida Bar v. Went For It, Inc.; No. 94-226
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that protecting privacy does not dispense with the State’s burden to connect the restriction it chose to actual harm. Central Hudson requires material advancement and reasonable fit; Board of Trustees v. Fox does not demand the least restrictive conceivable means. Shapero distinguishes a mailed communication that the recipient can discard from the coercive pressure of an in-person encounter. Florida’s study summary and complaints show disapproval of immediate solicitation and concern for professional reputation. They do not establish that truthful, identified mail deprives recipients of choice or that suppressing all such mail during the fixed period protects privacy in a way proportionate conduct rules cannot. Existing restrictions can address deception, coercion, harassment, unwilling recipients and misuse of confidential information. Lanphere and Rubin require the actual causal connection while permitting supported predictive judgments. The Court requires no numerical study or least-restrictive-means showing. A materially different record establishing concrete injury and fit remains open.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: On this record, Florida may not forbid truthful, nonmisleading targeted direct-mail solicitation about lawful legal services until an accident or disaster is more than thirty days old. The asserted privacy and professional-confidence interests are substantial, but Florida has not established that this categorical silence materially and proportionately addresses concrete harm; the referral-service rule is likewise invalid insofar as it incorporates that restriction.
metadata.Result: Eleventh Circuit affirmed, 5–4, on the targeted-mail waiting period and its referral-service incorporation; injunction remains in force.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Federal Tort Claims Act — judicial review of Westfall Act scope-of-employment certification
inventory_refs.caption: Gutierrez de Martinez v. Lamagno

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy and Breyer; six Justices adopt the statutory review rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: Gutierrez de Martinez v. Lamagno; No. 94-167
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Congress did not clearly entrust final adjudication of employment scope to the Executive. Abbott Laboratories supplies the ordinary presumption that executive action affecting legal rights remains reviewable. Section 2679 directs initial substitution when certification issues but expressly makes the certificate conclusive only for removal. Reading that limitation as finality for every purpose would confuse the litigation procedure with the predicate for employee immunity. Certification can eliminate a private tort action when the United States is immune under an FTCA exception, making impartial determination of the predicate important. United States v. Smith preserves employee exclusivity once scope is established; it does not decide who conclusively determines that scope. The express employee petition following refusal of certification does not clearly bar a plaintiff’s ordinary judicial challenge. The district court must review scope under applicable law with appropriate evidence and procedure. The Court determines neither actual scope nor liability and creates no federal damages action.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A Westfall Act scope-of-employment certification is judicially reviewable before substitution of the United States becomes final. metadata.Authority: Souter’s Opinion of the Court, joined by all eight other Justices; nine Justices adopt the as-applied private-expression holding.
metadata.Case and dockets: Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian and Bisexual Group of Boston; No. 94-749
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the right to speak includes control over the composition of a private expressive presentation. Barnette prohibits compulsory affirmation, and Tornillo protects editorial choice against compelled inclusion. Turner preserves the importance of a speaker’s selection within a particular medium; its separate cable context is not mechanically imported here. A parade presents expression through the groups and messages its organizers choose, even if those selections are permissive or varied. GLIB’s bannered unit has its own protected message, but that protection creates no entitlement to insert it into another private speaker’s presentation. Use of public streets under a neutral permit does not convert this parade into a governmental forum. Roberts and PruneYard concern access without the same compelled alteration of expression. Independent review of intertwined expression characterizations, with credibility deference, rejects the conclusion that absence of a single theme eliminates protection. The Court invalidates only this compelled expressive inclusion, without finding every customer identity a message or requiring proof that spectators endorse each contingent.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Applying a public-accommodations law to compel private parade organizers to include an identified contingent conveying a message they do not choose violates the First Amendment. A parade remains expression despite broad admissions, multiple themes and the absence of a single precise message; the rule does not exempt ordinary nonexpressive goods or services from nondiscrimination law.
metadata.Result: Massachusetts Supreme Judicial Court reversed and case remanded, 9–0; compelled-inclusion injunction shall be dissolved.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Federal jurisdiction — interlocutory appeal of qualified-immunity denials resting on evidence sufficiency
inventory_refs.caption: Johnson v. Jones

metadata.Authority: Justice Breyer's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; all nine adopt this bounded rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: Johnson v. Jones, No. 94-455.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that a disputed factual defense does not become a collateral legal issue because the defendant invokes qualified immunity. Cohen requires separateness from the merits; Mitchell recognizes immediate review of the legal immunity question on assumed facts, not appellate reconsideration of ordinary evidentiary sufficiency. Petitioners dispute their presence or participation in the alleged beating. They do not contend that losing that factual dispute would leave them immune; counsel's characterization confirms the nature of this appeal without proving the beating or participation. Deciding whether the evidence warrants trial would duplicate the ordinary summary-judgment inquiry and intermingle appellate review with the merits. Digital Equipment preserves cumulative category requirements rather than an exception for costly litigation, and Swint rejects convenience as a source of additional appellate power. Immunity's protection against suit remains important, but that purpose does not admit every factual defense to immediate review. The Court decides no ultimate constitutional violation, evidence sufficiency or liability, and does not categorically exclude genuine legal portions of mixed orders.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A denial of qualified immunity is not immediately appealable under §1291 insofar as it determines only whether the pretrial evidence presents a genuine factual dispute about the official's participation in the alleged conduct. Mitchell's immediate appeal remains available for the separable legal question whether the conduct, on the relevant assumed facts, violated clearly established law; the present excessive-force participation dispute does not meet that condition.
metadata.Result: The Seventh Circuit judgment dismissing the reviewed immediate excessive-force appeal is affirmed, 9–0.

metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the challenged evidence rule presents a question of law distinct from the truth of Kimberlin's allegations. Mitchell v. Forsyth permits interlocutory review of a legal entitlement to immunity; it does not supply a trial of disputed facts on appeal. Elder v. Holloway requires independent examination of relevant contemporaneous law while preserving the proper summary-judgment record. Digital Equipment preserves finality by demanding a genuinely separable legal question. The D.C. Circuit made the form of motive evidence dispositive. That prerequisite can be examined without deciding who ordered a detention, why an official acted, or which witness should be believed. The officials' entitlement to protection from unsupported litigation remains important, but it does not make their contested account the appellate record. The Court therefore reaches the categorical legal rule alone. It leaves actual motive, personal responsibility, causal sufficiency and each episode's independently available immunity defense for lawful consideration below.
metadata.Controlling proposition: An interlocutory qualified-immunity appeal may resolve whether the law permits a categorical direct-evidence condition without deciding disputed motive, participation or causation. Review of that separable legal condition does not authorize appellate selection between contested factual accounts.

metadata.Authority: O’Connor’s opinion for the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. All nine adopt this proposition and explanation; it is a direct majority holding.
metadata.Case and dockets: McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co., No. 93-1543
metadata.Controlling explanation: The ADEA forbids discharge because of age and gives courts authority to grant relief that serves the statute’s purposes. Hazen Paper requires age actually to motivate the challenged decision and have a determinative influence on it; a reason the employer did not know cannot have motivated it. Mt. Healthy and Price Waterhouse address lawful and unlawful reasons operating in the actual decision, so their same-decision inquiry does not transform later discovery into an original cause. The Banner assumed discrimination only to obtain summary judgment and relied on documents discovered after McKennon’s dismissal. That discovery cannot erase an otherwise proved violation. The contrary rule would remove compensation for an unlawful period and weaken enforcement whenever later investigation uncovered a sufficient ground for termination. The employee’s misconduct nevertheless matters to remedy, which the next holding addresses. The Court does not find age discrimination, change the employee’s ultimate burden, or decide whether the violation was willful.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Misconduct unknown to the employer when it discharged an employee cannot defeat liability for an age-discriminatory discharge or categorically bar every remedy. The employee must still establish an ADEA violation under the governing liability rules; an employer’s assumption of discrimination for summary judgment is not a final liability finding.
metadata.Precedent treatment: Hazen Paper’s actual-motive requirement remains controlling; Mt. Healthy and Price Waterhouse are distinguished because they concern reasons involved in the challenged decision. St. Mary’s Honor Center retains its existing proof framework and does not make rejection of an employer’s explanation an automatic liability judgment.
metadata.Result: Reversed and remanded, 9–0.

metadata.Authority: Justice Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight Justices adopt the construction and bounded reversal/remand.
metadata.Case and dockets: Metropolitan Stevedore Co. v. Rambo, No. 94-820.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the condition relevant to this nonscheduled award is injury-related earning incapacity, not bodily impairment alone. Sections 2(10) and 8(c)(21) tie compensation to economic disability. Reading section 22 to require medical change would preserve an award after the very incapacity it compensates had genuinely changed. O'Keeffe and Banks resist extra-textual restrictions on the modification provision's distinct fact-correction ground; they do not independently decide this economic-change question. Potomac Electric and Bath Iron Works preserve the different operation of scheduled compensation and therefore do not convert this award into a fixed impairment payment. Finality matters, but Congress supplied qualifying grounds and a deadline rather than a physical-only restriction. The employer's actual assessment and reimbursement stake permits this challenge despite Fund payments; Newport News does not equate it with the Director's general administrative interest. The Court removes the categorical barrier without deciding the ultimate capacity finding, terminating benefits itself, or authorizing perpetual reopening.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Section 22 permits modification of a nonscheduled disability award upon a demonstrated change in injury-related earning capacity even when physical impairment is unchanged. Modification remains limited to the enacted grounds of changed conditions or mistake in a determination of fact, within one year after the last compensation payment, whether or not a compensation order issued, or within one year after rejection of a claim; true §8(i) settlements remain distinct.
metadata.Result: The Ninth Circuit judgment is reversed and the case remanded, 8–1.

metadata.Authority: Breyer’s opinion for the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, and Ginsburg. All nine adopt this construction and its limits.
metadata.Case and dockets: Milwaukee Brewery Workers' Pension Plan v. Jos. Schlitz Brewing Co., No. 93-768
metadata.Controlling explanation: Section 1399 expressly separates an assumed payment schedule from the actual commencement of payments. Its calculation directs the first assumed payment to the opening of the plan year after withdrawal and each later payment to the opening of a successive year. Amortization includes interest, but that word alone does not answer when this statutory obligation is treated as outstanding for computation. The Plan’s earlier valuation date measures the withdrawal amount; it does not authorize an additional year of interest while the employer was still contributing. Brown v. Gardner requires attention to enacted conditions before adding a condition the text does not supply. Concrete Pipe’s separate treatment of facts, actuarial assumptions, and legal rules likewise leaves this statutory date for judicial construction. The Plan’s appeal to complete actuarial equivalence cannot displace Congress’s explicit assumptions. The Court resolves the demanded additional year, without recalculating the agreed amount, reopening the allocation method, or deciding a distinct default or collection-delay controversy.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Under 29 U.S.C. §1399(c)(1)(A)(i), the withdrawal-liability installment calculation uses the first day of the plan year after the withdrawal year as the assumed first-payment and computational-interest starting point; it does not capitalize interest for the preceding withdrawal year. Actual payment commencement, overdue-payment interest, default acceleration, prepayment, and mass-withdrawal rules retain their separate statutory triggers and qualifications.
metadata.Precedent treatment: Concrete Pipe and Products of California, Inc. v. Construction Laborers Pension Trust retains its independent arbitration, factual-review, and actuarial-review rules; this legal date question changes none of their burdens. Brown v. Gardner’s attention to statutory text and context is applied without creating a broader agency-deference rule.
metadata.Result: Affirmed, 9–0.

metadata.Authority: Thomas’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; nine Justices adopt this remedial rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: National Private Truck Council, Inc. v. Oklahoma Tax Commission; No. 94-688
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that a federal right and the relief available to enforce it are distinct questions. Dennis v. Higgins recognizes an enforceable Commerce Clause right; it does not abolish the established limits on federal tax equity. Dows, Matthews and Great Lakes supply that tradition: courts ordinarily withhold tax injunctions and parallel declarations when legal relief affords effective protection. Section 1341 directly addresses federal district courts and therefore cannot itself withdraw this state court’s jurisdiction. Nor does a State’s preference for uniform procedure defeat federal law. Here the taxpayers obtained invalidation of the discriminatory taxes and an adequate state-law refund remedy. Additional federal equity is unnecessary on that record. The rule preserves extraordinary relief for irreparable injury, a cloud on title or a genuine risk of numerous suits between the same parties involving the same law or facts. It does not impose general exhaustion, decide damages, or permit withdrawal of an actually promised refund.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Section 1983 does not authorize injunctive or declaratory interference with state tax administration where an adequate legal remedy actually protects the claimant. The limitation arises from federal equitable principles informing §1983, not direct application of 28 U.S.C. §1341 to state courts, and does not restrict otherwise lawful state-law equitable relief.
metadata.Result: Oklahoma Supreme Court affirmed on federal equitable relief and §1988 fees, 9–0; tax invalidity and state-law refunds remain undisturbed.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Indian tax immunity — state fuel tax on tribal retailers; income tax on tribal employees
inventory_refs.caption: Oklahoma Tax Commission v. Chickasaw Nation

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg’s Opinion of the Court, joined by all eight other Justices; nine Justices support the fuel-incidence rule and application.
metadata.Case and dockets: Oklahoma Tax Commission v. Chickasaw Nation; No. 94-771
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that legal incidence must be identified before a State relies on economic pass-through or collection machinery. Moe and Potawatomi distinguish a direct tax on an immune tribe from collection of a valid tax on nonmembers. Yakima requires attention to the particular tax Congress authorized; Attea permits reasonable collection controls for valid nonmember taxes, not taxation of the Tribe itself. Here distributors remit on retailers’ behalf, receive credits for retailer taxes they cannot collect, and receive an exemption for the distributor’s own sale. Comparable consumer liability or a mandatory pass-through does not appear in that arrangement. These features support the lower court’s reasonable construction that the retailer bears legal liability; they are not an express statutory declaration naming incidence. The late Hayden-Cartwright argument was not presented below or in the petition and will not be decided first here. A tax lawfully shifted to non-Indians would still require its own federal-preemption and collection analysis.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Without clear congressional authorization, Oklahoma cannot enforce a tax whose legal incidence falls on the Tribe or tribal members for Indian-country sales. Under the reviewed statute’s payment, remittance and credit arrangement, incidence falls on the tribal retailer, so the fuel tax is barred in that application.
metadata.Result: Tenth Circuit affirmed on motor-fuels tax, 9–0; reversed on off-country-resident tribal-wage exemption, 5–4; remanded.

metadata.Result: Reverse the color-only registration bar and cancellation direction, 9–0; ordinary further proceedings; independent §43(a) relief intact.
metadata.Stone's Controlled Judgment or Dispositi: REVERSE the Ninth Circuit and REMAND.
metadata.Stone's Legal Position: Stone applies the statute’s broad definition of a mark. A color can identify source after acquiring secondary meaning, and trademark protection then serves the same informational function as words or symbols. The functionality doctrine prevents control of useful or competitively necessary color features.
metadata.Stone's Proposed Holding: A color may be protected as a trademark when it has acquired source-identifying significance and is not functional.
metadata.Stone's Reasoning and Record Application: The green-gold dry-cleaning press-pad color can distinguish Qualitex’s goods without performing a utilitarian function. Existing doctrines address shade confusion, depletion, and competitive need rather than imposing a categorical ban absent from the Act.
metadata.Stone's Remedy and Remand Instruction: The lower courts shall recognize color as potentially registrable and determine infringement, secondary meaning, and functionality under ordinary Lanham Act rules.
metadata.Threshold and Merits Reach: Stone finds no jurisdictional, preservation, or vehicle bar and reaches the question presented.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Retroactivity — applying Bendix tolling-statute ruling to pending pre-Bendix tort claims in state court
inventory_refs.caption: Reynoldsville Casket Co. v. Hyde

metadata.Authority: Breyer's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg: seven direct votes; Kennedy and O'Connor concur in the judgment.
metadata.Case and dockets: Reynoldsville Casket Co. v. Hyde; No. 94-3
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Ohio cannot preserve the legal operation of its unconstitutional tolling provision solely for claims accruing before Bendix. Bendix establishes the interstate-commerce defect in that provision. Harper requires a federal rule applied to the original litigants to govern still-open cases within its substantive scope. Beam supplies the distinction between applying the rule and deciding an independently supported remedy. Ohio's reliance ground is tied to the date of Bendix and continues the invalid tolling rule for earlier claims. Calling that treatment a remedy does not create an independent legal basis. Reliance can matter to an actual equitable doctrine with its own lawful prerequisites; this judgment establishes none. Finality, valid procedural bars, immunity, an independently justified equitable rule or a constitutional remedial requirement can present different grounds. Reich concerns withdrawal of an apparent tax remedy and does not guarantee survival of this tort action. The Court remands without deciding whether another valid ground supports relief.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A state court must apply a controlling federal constitutional rule to a case still open on direct review and cannot withhold that rule merely because a litigant relied on the invalidated statute. Independently valid procedural or remedial rules may determine relief, but cannot reproduce selective prospectivity under a different label.
metadata.Result: The Supreme Court of Ohio is reversed, 9-0, and the case remanded.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Speech and Establishment Clause — university student-fee funding of a religious student publication
inventory_refs.caption: Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia

metadata.Authority: Kennedy’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia and Thomas; five Justices adopt the program-specific viewpoint rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia; No. 94-329
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the University’s decision to support independent student expression does not make each publication its own speech. Perry permits definition of a limited forum and its subjects, but not discrimination against a religious perspective on otherwise included subjects. Lamb’s Chapel and Widmar supply religious-viewpoint equality in genuinely opened private-expression channels. Here the broad publication program leaves editing with the students, requires independence disclaimers and pays approved outside printing expenses. The denial treats primarily religious belief or manifestation as a forbidden activity while allowing comparable student perspectives. That operation excludes viewpoint rather than neutrally defining a government message. The Court does not erase the distinction between recognition, facilities, distribution and money, or equate every expenditure with a speech forum. Nor does it find the organization ineligible under a separate organizational rule. The religious-viewpoint exclusion must be removed; other lawful program terms remain. Actual payment amounts and properly available independent defenses remain subject to the federal viewpoint holding.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: The University may not exclude an otherwise eligible private student publication from its generally available printing benefit because its editorial viewpoint is religious. The rule applies to this privately edited, independently attributed publication program on its otherwise lawful eligibility, payment and administrative terms; it does not require funding every religious activity or every subject.
metadata.Result: Fourth Circuit reversed and remanded, 5–4; religious-viewpoint exclusion removed from the printing benefit on otherwise lawful terms.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Appointments Clause — Coast Guard appellate military judges and the de facto officer doctrine
inventory_refs.caption: Ryder v. United States

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg's opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer; nine Justices adopt this bounded rule and remedy.
metadata.Case and dockets: Ryder v. United States, No. 94-431
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Ryder's timely challenge requires meaningful relief. Buckley identifies constitutional appointment routes but its treatment of past civil acts does not make every direct challenger remedyless. Glidden distinguishes substantial constitutional qualifications for adjudicators from technical assignments, and Freytag preserves appointment accountability. Two civilian judges deciding Ryder's appeal lacked lawful appointments, and he objected before their judgment became final. Ball, McDowell and Ward concerned different collateral or statutory-assignment settings; their continuity rationale cannot answer this preserved constitutional challenge to his own tribunal. A new military appellate hearing protects both lawful authority and institutional continuity without adjudicating drug guilt anew or dismissing the trial judgment. Weiss's treatment of germane assignments for commissioned officers leaves these civilian appointments open. The Court does not prescribe general collateral reopening, invalidate ministerial acts, decide the rights of litigants who failed to use an available challenge channel, or resolve every possible officers-and-departments classification. Its remedy is limited to the lawful review Ryder was denied.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A litigant who timely challenges a substantial constitutional defect in the appointments of officers adjudicating his own case and pursues that objection on direct review is entitled to a fresh adjudication by lawfully appointed officers; the de facto officer doctrine cannot validate the defective panel’s judgment against him. Ryder must receive new Article 66 review by a properly appointed military appellate panel, without automatic dismissal or reversal of his trial conviction.
metadata.Precedent treatment: Buckley v. Valeo is distinguished as a universal de facto remedial defense. Glidden Co. v. Zdanok and Freytag are applied to substantial constitutional adjudicator qualifications. Ball v. United States, McDowell v. United States and Ex parte Ward are distinguished by collateral or technical-assignment settings. The completed Weiss decision retains its commissioned-officer/germane-assignment scope and leaves civilian appointments open.
metadata.Result: Reversed and remanded, 9–0.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Prisoners' rights — due process liberty interest in disciplinary segregation
inventory_refs.caption: Sandin v. Conner

metadata.Authority: Breyer’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg; five Justices adopt this sufficient, nonexclusive state-entitlement rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: Sandin v. Conner; No. 93-1911
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that legal substance matters more than a regulation’s drafting conventions. Hewitt supplies the recognition that substantive state constraints may create protected liberty; Thompson distinguishes genuine predicates from procedures that do not require a particular substantive outcome. The Court narrows reliance on mandatory words alone without discarding real constraints simply because they operate inside prison. The complete scheme must be considered: defined misconduct, an impartial adjudicative process, valid evidence and the relationship between guilt and a significant sanction can confine official authority even when officials retain discretion to select a commensurate penalty afterward. Wolff distinguishes substantial protected liberty from routine management and supplies the separate inquiry into appropriate process. Mere mandatory administration, routine transfers or brief inconveniences do not automatically create entitlements. Nor is this an exclusive requirement of state codification for intrinsic constitutional liberty, an unexpected restraint or a sentence-duration interest. The Court adopts no new multifactor hardship test and leaves the ultimate application to the district court under the stated rule.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A State creates protected prison liberty when substantive law meaningfully restricts officials’ authority to impose a significant deprivation. Mandatory wording alone is insufficient: courts must examine the genuine constraint in the whole disciplinary scheme and the meaningful restraint, without making state codification necessary for directly protected constitutional liberty.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit affirmed in the reviewed respect and case remanded, 5–4; genuine constraint, meaningful deprivation and process must be determined; no liability finding.

metadata.Result: Vacate the adverse federal prospective-enforcement determination and remand under RFRA, 5–4; no final exemption; constitutional claim reserved.

metadata.Stone's Controlled Judgment or Dispositi: AFFIRM the Supreme Court of Alaska.
metadata.Stone's Legal Position: Government may not prescribe or punish religious belief, including religious moral judgments expressed publicly. But RFRA does not require an exemption from a neutral commercial housing-nondiscrimination law when the requested exemption would operate by withdrawing from an identified applicant the statutory protection the law confers and no accommodation preserving that protection in the regulated transaction has been identified. The compelling interests are protecting each member of the covered class from being denied an otherwise available commercial housing opportunity because of the prohibited status and preserving equal access to the covered rental market without forcing applicants to absorb the religious objections of individual landlords.
metadata.Stone's Remedy and Remand Instruction: The state enforcement judgment remains in force. No separate remedial instruction is required.
metadata.Threshold and Merits Reach: Stone assumes without deciding that application of the housing law substantially burdens Swanner’s religious exercise and reaches RFRA’s compelling-interest and least-restrictive-means requirements.

metadata.Authority: Justice Kennedy's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Souter, and Ginsburg. Six Justices adopt the same rule and explanation; no aggregation of separate rationales is needed.
metadata.Case and dockets: Tome v. United States, No. 93-6892
metadata.Controlling proposition: Under original Federal Rule of Evidence 801(d)(1)(B), a prior statement offered substantively to rebut an express or implied charge of recent fabrication or improper influence or motive must have been made before the particular charged fabrication, influence, or motive arose. The declarant must testify and be subject to cross-examination concerning the statement, and the statement must be consistent with that testimony and offered for that specified rebuttal purpose; general relevance or repetition alone does not satisfy this nonhearsay rule.
metadata.Result: The Tenth Circuit judgment is reversed and the case remanded, 6–3.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Congressional qualifications — state term-limit ballot-access restriction on congressional incumbents
inventory_refs.caption: U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton / Bryant v. Hill

metadata.Authority: Stevens's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: six direct votes, in both consolidated dockets.
metadata.Case and dockets: U.S. Term Limits, Inc. v. Thornton / Bryant v. Hill; Nos. 93-1456, 93-1828
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Arkansas cannot use prior congressional service to disqualify otherwise eligible candidates from the ordinary ballot. Powell establishes the fixed character of congressional qualifications and protects electors' choice of constitutionally eligible representatives against additional substantive exclusions. The national offices created by Article I do not become state offices subject to a reserved power to alter their qualifications. The Elections Clause allows administration of the manner of elections; it does not authorize a service-based disability on who may represent the people. Arkansas answers that a candidate may still seek write-in votes and that Powell concerned Congress rather than a State. But the State deliberately excludes the candidate from the ordinary ballot for a personal eligibility characteristic, achieving indirectly the additional qualification it lacks authority to impose directly. Storer preserves genuine election regulation rather than such additions. The Court leaves neutral filing, petition, support and ballot-management requirements, and Arkansas's separate state-office provisions, outside this holding.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: A State may not deny an otherwise constitutionally qualified congressional candidate ordinary ballot access because of prior congressional service when that restriction adds a substantive personal qualification. The exclusive Article I qualifications cannot be supplemented indirectly through the ballot; genuine time, place and manner administration remains distinct.
metadata.Result: The Arkansas Supreme Court is affirmed in both dockets, 6-3.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Federal criminal law — obstruction of justice and wiretap disclosure by a federal judge
inventory_refs.caption: United States v. Aguilar

metadata.Authority: Ginsburg’s §1503 portion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Souter and Breyer; six Justices adopt this statutory nexus and application.
metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. Aguilar; No. 94-270
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the omnibus clause concerns the due administration of judicial justice, rather than every investigation a federal officer conducts. Pettibone supplies the requirement of a known pending proceeding and a connection between the endeavor and that work. The word endeavor permits punishment even when interference fails; it does not dispense with the statutory object. The conduct must have the natural and probable relation to interference with the proceeding, and the defendant must know it is likely to affect that proceeding. Here the charged false denials were made to FBI investigators not shown to be directed by or subpoenaed before the grand jury. A speculative possibility that their later testimony would relay the statements does not establish the required nexus. The Court does not create a categorical subpoena condition, implied repeal of all witness-related obstruction by section 1512 or a privilege to lie. Direct grand-jury lies and knowingly channeled statements remain distinct. The charged conviction’s reversal stands.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Section 1503 requires a relationship in time, causation or logic between the endeavor and a pending judicial or grand-jury proceeding, including knowledge that the conduct is likely to affect that proceeding. An unsuccessful endeavor can qualify, but false statements to investigators do not suffice merely because they might later testify.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit affirmed on §1503 reversal, 6–3; reversed on §2232(c) expiration bar, 8–1; remanded for preserved claims.

inventory_refs.area_of_law: Criminal procedure — jury determination of materiality in false-statement prosecutions
inventory_refs.caption: United States v. Gaudin

metadata.Authority: Scalia’s Opinion of the Court, joined by all eight other Justices; nine Justices adopt the element-allocation rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. Gaudin; No. 94-514
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the jury must decide every element necessary to establish criminal guilt, including application of an instructed legal standard to the charged facts. Winship supplies proof beyond a reasonable doubt; the constitutional jury guarantee places that determination with the jury. Materiality asks whether a statement has a natural tendency or capacity to influence the relevant governmental decision. That application does not become an abstract legal question simply because legal instruction is needed. Historical practice and functional convenience cannot reserve an offense element to the judge. Sinclair’s contrary criminal pertinency allocation cannot stand to that extent. Kungys concerns a civil denaturalization proceeding and a different appellate allocation, not this criminal jury guarantee. Here the Government concedes materiality is an element and did not challenge the lower court’s error classifications. Those premises preserve this reversal without deciding whether every section 1001 clause includes materiality or every withheld element is structural error. Statutory interpretation and threshold evidentiary sufficiency remain judicial functions.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: When materiality is an element of the charged criminal false-statement offense, the Fifth and Sixth Amendments require the jury to determine it beyond a reasonable doubt. The judge states statutory meaning and the governing legal standard; labeling its application a mixed question does not remove an element from the jury.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit affirmed, 9–0; reviewed false-statement convictions remain vacated; retrial under proper jury instructions remains available.

metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. Mezzanatto, No. 93-1340
metadata.Controlling proposition: Rules 410 and 11(e)(6) permit a defendant knowingly and voluntarily to agree before plea discussions that his statements may be used to impeach his own inconsistent trial testimony; absent an affirmative indication that this agreement was entered unknowingly or involuntarily, the limited waiver is enforceable. Supported challenges based on ignorance, fraud, coercion, involuntariness, or the agreement's scope remain subject to individual review, and inconsistency alone creates no nonconsensual impeachment exception.
metadata.Result: The Ninth Circuit judgment is reversed, 7–2. Six Justices enforce the limited impeachment waiver under the Court's affirmative-challenge rule; Chief Justice Stone-Zsela concurs in reversal and remand under his separate Government-proof requirement.
