metadata.Authority: Justice O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, joined in full by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. All nine directly adopt this construction and its application; no fractured-opinion analysis is necessary.
metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. Shabani; No. 93-981; 513 U.S. 10
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Congress made the unlawful agreement the completed conspiracy offense. Section 846 contains no additional overt-act language, while 18 U.S.C. §371 expressly requires an act to effect the conspiracy’s object. Nash supplies the common-law understanding of conspiracy, and Singer shows why Congress’s omission of an extra act requirement matters when it uses that settled term. This reading does not punish a thought: the agreement itself is conduct, and the Government must prove knowing participation in it. The Ninth Circuit’s contrary element cannot rest on circuit precedent when the governing statute supplies none. Felix’s treatment of successive prosecutions did not decide this statutory question and cannot add the omitted element. Nor does lenity supply it; ordinary construction resolves the question without the residual ambiguity addressed in Ratzlaf. The refused overt-act instruction therefore supplies no ground for reversal of the conviction. The Court leaves the appeal’s reserved sufficiency and other claims to the court of appeals.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Section 846 of Title 21 requires neither an allegation nor proof of an overt act beyond the unlawful narcotics agreement. The Government must still prove the unlawful agreement and the defendant’s knowing participation beyond a reasonable doubt; neither mere association nor awareness of another person’s plan is enough.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit reversed and remanded, 9–0; §846 requires no additional overt act.

metadata.Authority: Part I of Scalia's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; nine Justices adopt the search and no-waiver rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: Vernonia School District 47J v. Acton; No. 94-590.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that obtaining urine and examining its chemical contents intrudes on interests the Fourth Amendment protects. Skinner recognizes both physical collection and analysis as searches; neither step becomes ordinary nonconstitutional administration merely because the subject is a child. T.L.O. permits school officials to act without a warrant or ordinary probable cause when the school setting justifies that adjustment, but it does not extinguish the student's protection against unreasonable searches. Student athletes accept coaching, examinations directed to fitness, changing facilities and safety rules. Those practices bear on expectations within the activity; they do not amount to surrender of privacy in bodily functions or medical information. The District's permission form therefore cannot settle the constitutional question by describing participation as voluntary. The Court must examine the actual need, intrusion and safeguards. This threshold conclusion does not determine whether the particular program is reasonable, and it does not authorize unrelated medical investigation or police use.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: Collection and chemical analysis of a student's urine are Fourth Amendment searches. Enrollment or voluntary athletic participation does not waive that protection; the school and athletic setting instead informs the reasonableness inquiry.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit judgment vacated and remanded, 5–4; federal interscholastic-athlete policy sustained, independent Oregon question reserved.

metadata.Authority: Kennedy’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; seven participating Justices adopt this statutory coexistence ground.
metadata.Case and dockets: Vimar Seguros y Reaseguros, S.A. v. M/V Sky Reefer; No. 94-623
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that a change in forum is not itself a surrender of the carrier obligations Congress protected. COGSA invalidates contractual relief from or lessening of specified liability; it does not guarantee the cheapest forum for enforcing those obligations. The FAA separately enforces maritime arbitration agreements. Those commands can coexist without treating either as an implied repeal or giving arbitration automatic priority over statutory rights. Mitsubishi preserves the distinction between submitting a federal claim to arbitration and prospectively waiving the protected entitlement. Indussa’s increased-cost inference for foreign courts is not adopted for this arbitration clause; its arbitration reservation matters here. Allied-Bruce, Mastrobuono and First Options retain their actual coverage, agreement and judicial-review limits, without deciding COGSA. The certified question permits rejecting the categorical foreign-arbitration objection. It permits no reopening of the excluded adhesion defense or adjudication of cargo liability. True foreign-court selection clauses, practical foreclosure on a materially different record and demonstrated substantive waiver remain outside this holding.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: COGSA §3(8) does not invalidate the Tokyo arbitration clause merely because the selected forum increases inconvenience or enforcement expense. The FAA does not override nonwaivable COGSA substantive protection; the statutes operate together while that protection remains available.
metadata.Result: First Circuit arbitration stay affirmed and case remanded, 7–1; district court must retain the underlying action.

metadata.Authority: Justice O'Connor's opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Ginsburg; all eight participants adopt the rule.
metadata.Case and dockets: Wilton v. Seven Falls Co., No. 94-562.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that Congress made the declaration a discretionary remedy. Section 2201 authorizes a court to declare rights; it does not oblige a declaration whenever ordinary jurisdiction exists. Brillhart gives effect to that choice by requiring attention to whether parallel state litigation can satisfactorily resolve the controversy. Here the Travis County proceeding includes the insurers, permits the coverage defenses and counterclaims, and encompasses the same state-law dispute. The District Court could therefore avoid duplicative adjudication while retaining the federal case. Colorado River's exceptional-circumstances standard addresses a different duty to adjudicate ordinary coercive claims and does not silently replace the declaratory statute. The insurers' earlier federal filing does not make the remedy obligatory, and the subsequent filing sequence supplies no automatic state priority. A stay also protects against needless loss of a forum if the state action proves inadequate. The Court decides neither coverage liability nor any breach of the advance-notice agreement.
metadata.Holding and operative rule: In a declaration-only state-law coverage action with adequate parallel state proceedings, §2201 and Brillhart permit a reasoned stay without Colorado River's exceptional-circumstances showing. The court must consider the state case's scope, defenses, interested and necessary parties and amenability to process; it retains federal jurisdiction and may resume if the state case fails to resolve the controversy.
metadata.Result: The Fifth Circuit judgment affirming the stay is affirmed, 8–0.

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's Opinion of the Court, constitutional-characterization discussion, joined by Stone-Zsela, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; six support this rationale. Scalia and Thomas affirm only in the judgment on the narrower distinct-prosecution ground.
metadata.Case and dockets: Witte v. United States; No. 94-6187.
metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court holds that the first judgment punished the marijuana attempt, although the cocaine facts materially increased its Guidelines calculation. Williams v. Oklahoma permits consideration of other criminal conduct when fixing punishment for the offense before the sentencing court; McMillan distinguishes lawful sentencing considerations from a separate offense, subject to independent safeguards. The statutory range was five to forty years, the calculated Guidelines range 292 to 365 months, and the actual substantial-assistance sentence 144 months. Those distinct quantities show why the sentencing label alone is not the answer: real aggravation occurred, but it calibrated one legally authorized marijuana punishment rather than imposed a separate cocaine penalty. Felix supplies the distinction between evidentiary use and prior prosecution, applied here by analogy rather than equating all sentencing with trial evidence. Dixon retained Grady's essential-conduct protection; the cocaine offenses were not previously prosecuted, and their conduct did not constitute the later marijuana attempt. Kurth Ranch involved a distinct punitive exaction and remains intact. The Court decides no guilt or future sentence.
metadata.Controlling proposition: Consideration of relevant uncharged conduct in selecting a sentence within the authorized statutory range for the offense of conviction does not itself constitute prosecution or independent punishment for the uncharged offense. Witte's marijuana-attempt sentence therefore does not bar the distinct cocaine indictment under the retained Grady rule; this holding does not approve a separate disguised penalty, punishment beyond statutory authority or disregard of independent sentencing safeguards.

metadata.Case and dockets: Young v. Northern Illinois Conference of United Methodist Church, No. 93-1917
metadata.Controlling proposition: The Religion Clauses bar the application of Title VII to Young's race, sex, and retaliation claims challenging her advancement and retention as a probationary minister, because deciding those claims or imposing the requested relief would subject the church's choice of its religious leadership to civil review. The defense covers reinstatement, compelled reconsideration, and financial liability resting on that same selection decision; it does not exempt every religious employee or independently actionable secular conduct from civil law.
metadata.Result: The jurisdictional judgment is vacated and the case remanded for dismissal of the stated Title VII ministerial-selection claims on the merits. All nine agree on the defense and jurisdiction; eight join that mandate, while Chief Justice Stone-Zsela would also affirm the dismissal on its corrected merits basis.

metadata.Authority: Part I-B of Souter's opinion, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. Eight directly adopt this alternative ground. Stone-Zsela does not join this additional rationale.
metadata.Case and dockets: Allridge v. Scott; Fifth Circuit No. 93-9137; judgment below reported at 41 F.3d 213 (1994)
metadata.Controlling explanation: Teague requires claim-specific identification of law dictated at finality. Simmons's separate legal-ineligibility premise cannot establish a broader forecast right where ordinary parole remains available. The record supplies no prefinality requirement for that proposed prediction instruction. As Gilmore v. Taylor and Caspari v. Bohlen explain, the then-existing exceptions concern substantive limits on the State's power to punish and watershed procedures essential to accuracy and fundamental fairness. The requested forecast instruction regulates the jury's information; it does not remove Allridge's conduct, a class to which he belongs, or his punishment from the State's substantive power. Nothing establishes it as a watershed accuracy-and-fairness procedure; asserted usefulness in answering future-danger evidence does not itself meet that demanding category. Neither exception supplies a route to this requested extension. A properly presented claim about a fixed legal minimum would require its own preservation and retroactivity inquiry; this decision does not resolve such a claim.
metadata.Event and date: Merits review of federal habeas judgment; 1996-01-15; October Term 1995.
metadata.Operative rule: Federal habeas relief on a proposed constitutional entitlement to a favorable parole-improbability instruction is unavailable here because no basis establishes that this different rule was dictated when Allridge's conviction became final before Penry in 1989, or that either then-existing Teague exception applies: rules excluding conduct, classes of persons, or punishments from the State's substantive power, or watershed procedures essential to accuracy and fundamental fairness. This is an independent ground for rejecting the proposed extension, not a new rule governing accurate information about a fixed statutory minimum.
metadata.Participation and channel: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer participate. All nine seats are occupied; no case-specific nonparticipation is established. The six-Justice quorum is satisfied. A dispositive order, merits judgment, or controlling proposition requires five participating votes; a petition grant alone uses the Rule of Four. No additional petition, argument, or stay event is inferred.
metadata.Precedent treatment: Teague's dictated-at-finality requirement and its two then-existing exceptions are applied at the scope preserved in Gilmore and Caspari; neither exception is created, abolished, or generally narrowed. Simmons is not enlarged into a parole-forecast rule.

Historical post-divergence Supreme Court opinions are comparators only. The frozen source handoffs distinguish verified record facts, earlier simulated law, and assembly inferences. No new external source fact is added here.

metadata.Case and dockets: Ayers v. Fordice; lower-court No. 4:75CV009-B-O; 879 F. Supp. 1419. No authenticated current Supreme Court docket is assigned.
metadata.Entering-law cutoff: Immediately before March 25, 1996; effective current-term public law through March 20. The [dated neutral projection](../entering-law/OT_1995CHUNK5_NEUTRAL_AFTER_1996-03-25.md) records no prior Ayers action. Its old broader preparation stop is not a judgment and does not override the released limited packet. No later event supplies law, urgency, authorship fit or factual support. Retrospective dependency review and coordinated workspace publication belong to the controlling operator; this Record does not silently revise later adjudications.
metadata.Event and date: Dismissal of certiorari before appellate judgment, 1996-03-25; October Term 1995, chunk 5.
metadata.Fordice, June 26, 1992: The State must demonstrate dismantlement; good faith and facial neutrality do not discharge that burden. Traceable policies with continuing segregative effects must be eliminated when practicable consistently with sound education. The inquiry includes interacting missions and properly challenged allocations; no fresh intent is needed for such remnants, but racial imbalance alone is insufficient. Remedies remain tied to the established violation. Identical institutions, funding parity, a fixed expenditure and closure based on racial identifiability alone do not follow. Existing findings survive a legal correction unless properly displaced.
metadata.Freeman, March 31, 1992: A defendant seeking partial release must show full and satisfactory compliance, practicable elimination of relevant vestiges, whole-decree good faith and the necessary causal and remedial connections; retained control necessary or practicable for other compliance and nonobstruction of remaining relief must be assessed. Release may follow the complete showing. Independent demographics need not be counteracted perpetually. No release request is presented, and denial of additional relief is not a release.
metadata.Jenkins, June 12, 1995: Necessary instructional and noninstructional salary support is permissible on sufficient segregation-caused educational-injury and personnel-necessity findings. An implementation expense need not itself constitute a separate violation, and incidental voluntary attraction does not defeat an independently sufficient repair ground. The decision supplies no present library finding, general educational-improvement guarantee or automatic future expenditure.
metadata.Result: Writ dismissed as improvidently granted, 8–1. Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer support dismissal; Stone-Zsela dissents and would vacate only the denial of additional library relief and remand. No decree provision is affirmed on its merits.
metadata.Review and remedy: Legal standards and burden allocation receive legal review; supported factual findings receive clear-error review; remedial discretion operates within lawful bounds. Section 2106 permits correction of the ruling properly before the Court, without authorizing new appellate findings of injury, necessity, feasibility or cost. Title VI's established related dismantlement duty remains on Fordice's terms; no new disparate-impact action or §602 agency-enforcement procedure is adopted.

inventory_refs.caption: Bailey v. United States / Robinson v. United States

metadata.Authority: O'Connor's Part I, joined by all eight other Justices named in Opinion Topology, supplies nine direct votes for this rule, its application and reversal of the use-based appellate affirmances.
metadata.Case and dockets: Bailey v. United States; Robinson v. United States, Nos. 94-7448 and 94-7492; 516 U.S. 137; October Term 1995.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Congress used a conduct word and separately referred to carrying. Reading use as every way a gun's availability may support a criminal enterprise would erase the difference between actual employment and possession. Smith holds that offering a firearm in exchange for drugs employs it in the transaction even though as merchandise. That example broadens the purposes for which a gun may be actively used; it does not eliminate the act of using it.
metadata.Operative rule: Under the applicable §924(c)(1), a defendant uses a firearm only by actually and actively employing it as an operative instrument of the predicate offense. Possession, proximity, accessibility, protective storage, emboldening or placement for possible later employment does not by itself satisfy use; firing or employment as a weapon is not required, and Smith's actual firearm barter remains use.
metadata.Result: Reverse both use-based appellate affirmances, 9–0; remand for bounded carrying consideration without immediate trial-conviction vacatur, 8–1, Stone-Zsela dissenting on that remedial difference.

metadata.Assignment authority and accounting: The Chief joins the unanimous judgment coalition and assigns its single coordinated opinion to **Stevens**. This is Chief assignment **73**, bringing Stevens to **6**. Root confirmed the preceding assignments through Degen at `3615a4e` (Chief 72, Scalia 4), following Whren at `2f48aa6` (Chief 71, Thomas 7) and the preceding Richards assignment 70 to Stone. The verified pre-Exxon count is O'Connor 20, Souter 14, Ginsburg 10, Kennedy 8, Thomas 7, Stevens 5, Scalia 4, Stone 3 and Breyer 1, total 72. After Exxon, Stevens has 6 and the total is 73, with every other count unchanged. The [Chunk7 assignment reference](../freeze/OT_1995CHUNK7_ASSIGNMENT_REFERENCE.md) supplies the verified prior-term count: 93 Chief assignments, maximum 18 to any Justice, so the two-consecutive-term concentration ceiling is not triggered.
metadata.Case and dockets: Exxon Co., U.S.A. v. Sofec, Inc., No. 95-129, 517 U.S. 830; October Term 1995.
metadata.Case-specific fit and comparison: The coalition already shares sufficiently settled ground, so expansion is unnecessary. Stevens's actual *McDermott*, *Boca Grande* and *City of Milwaukee* opinions show directly relevant craftsmanship in separating maritime allocation and compensation from their liability predicates and preserving reliable apportionment where it belongs. This opinion's central work is explaining why those protections do not abolish genuine legal causation, without reviving the major-minor shortcut or folding contractual liability into a tort label. That demonstrated fit makes Stevens the best author.
metadata.Entering law: [Completed June 3 public law](../entering-law/OT_1995CHUNK7_PRE_JUNE10_NEUTRAL_PROJECTION.md) at `e1bc5d6`, SHA-256 `0f48b37716f9c1aa116cf34fe4734a8fc6641cabc90ff0316d3d0714bff707ac`, and the [chronology clarification](../entering-law/OT_1995CHUNK7_PRE_JUNE10_CHRONOLOGY_NOTE.md) at `8fb1ac9` fix the common baseline. The relevant [opening maritime slice](../entering-law/OT_1995CHUNK7_C_OPENING.md) at `d69c51d` and the neutral's verified intervening public opinions complete the issue-specific law. Smiley's eight-Justice temporal holding controls within its stated banking setting, but supplies no maritime causal rule or unquoted contract term. Ornelas supplies no universal mixed-question review standard; Quackenbush does not guarantee success on a contract claim or expand these questions. June 10 peers affect neither law nor procedure here. Assignment bookkeeping is separate.
metadata.Event and lawful channel: The inventory-authorized June 10 merits review follows argument March 19. The Ninth Circuit, 54 F.3d 570, affirmed the Rule 54(b) judgment against Exxon for stranding damages after phase one of a maritime bench trial. The Court reviews the submitted tort/comparative-fault and distinct warranty questions, including the legal contention that comparative fault categorically forecloses a separate superseding-cause inquiry. It does not decide the excluded free-standing abuse-of-discretion or due-process challenge to this bifurcation. Supreme Court Rules 14.1(a) and 24.1(a) retain that boundary. No jurisdictional defect or additional companion event is established. Breakout oil-spill claims remain untried.
metadata.Participation: The full roster participates at argument and decision: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer. No case-specific nonparticipation is established. Nine provide a quorum; five suffice for the ordinary merits judgment and holdings. All nine affirm both submitted components and join each controlling proposition.
metadata.Result: Ninth Circuit affirmed, 9–0, on the submitted tort and warranty components of the stranding-only judgment. Stevens writes for the unanimous Court; all nine join Parts I–V throughout.

Hodge's Court damages holding is immunity-only and reserves constitutional informational/family merits; its prospective ruling is claim-specific mootness. These holdings do not change the present statutory or review-classification issue, the supported frozen grounds or the bounded remedy. [Tuggle's October 30 decision](../records/Tuggle_v_Netherland_summary_merits_1995-10-30.md) is effective earlier law. The limited sentence-review disposition is vacated and remanded; the actual violation, applicability and choice of a collateral harmless-error standard, actual effect and ultimate relief remain undecided. metadata.Case and dockets: Klinger v. Department of Corrections; Eighth Circuit No. 93-2928, 31 F.3d 727; Supreme Court docket not supplied; October Term 1995.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Equality does not require identical institutions before any particular deprivation may be examined. The women's institution is smaller than the Nebraska State Penitentiary and houses prisoners with different sentence lengths and security characteristics. Those circumstances may explain particular choices; they do not establish that sex is irrelevant to every challenged opportunity. Hogan requires scrutiny of the actual sex distinction rather than a broad institutional label. Turner preserves attention to legitimate prison administration and resources; it does not exempt an actual sex classification from the governing equality rule.
metadata.Operative rule: In an equal-protection challenge to prison programs, whether prisoners are similarly situated must be assessed in relation to the treatment challenged. Population, security, confinement duration, feasible delivery and actual resource choices may materially distinguish a particular program; general differences between entire institutions cannot categorically defeat every comparison of the benefits provided.
metadata.Precedent treatment: Hogan's real-justification inquiry and Turner's attention to actual operational constraints are applied together; neither becomes a rule of identical services or a prison-program immunity.
metadata.Result: Affirm reversal of existing equal-protection liability; vacate categorical dismissal and remand the preserved program claims, 9–0 on each component.

metadata.Authority: Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas and Ginsburg; seven Justices adopt the rule, explanation and limits.
metadata.Case and dockets: Lane v. Peña, No. 95-365; October Term 1995.
metadata.Chronology and route: Certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, which summarily affirmed denial of compensatory damages after denying initial en banc consideration of Dorsey. The District Court, 867 F. Supp. 1050, had found a Rehabilitation Act violation and ordered reinstatement, first permitting damages with amount deferred, then vacating that ruling after Dorsey v. Department of Labor, 41 F.3d 1551. The Government did not contest the injunction. The question is whether the enacted Rehabilitation Act provisions unequivocally consent to compensatory damages for this federally conducted academy program. The event date and argument date come from the approved neutral packet and authenticated published chronology. The case is at merits judgment before this action and concluded in this Court afterward, subject to the ordinary mandate.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Congress imposed §504(a)'s nondiscrimination duty on programs conducted by Executive agencies and the Postal Service. Section 505(a)(2), however, supplies Title VI remedies to persons aggrieved by recipients or federal providers of financial assistance. That assistance-related formulation does not unequivocally expose every federal program operator to compensatory damages. Nordic Village requires enacted consent to the particular money judgment; Ohio requires an incorporated remedial provision's limits to receive independent effect. A substantive prohibition and an affirmative obligation to pay from the Treasury are distinct.
metadata.Entering law: The frozen neutral packet and `../entering-law/OT_1995CHUNK9_JUNE20_LANE_LAW.md` supply the actual pre-June20 federal-immunity and remedies rules. Nordic Village's original-§106(c) remedy-specific clarity requirement, Ohio's incorporated-remedy distinctions, Meyer's separate waiver/cause/recovery inquiries, and Franklin's established-action remedial rule retain their exact scopes. The current-term Hercules and Seminole Tribe public positions do not create a general federal statutory waiver. Gray and every June20 peer are excluded as entering authority. Operative statutory language appears in the frozen packet, including §§504(a), 505(a)(1), 505(a)(2), 505(b) and §1003; distinct facility-accessibility and employment provisions do not resolve this question.
metadata.FDIC v. Meyer, 510 U.S. 471 (1994): Preserves the separate inquiries into waiver, substantive cause and recovery, including the effect of a genuinely broad sue-and-be-sued clause. No such clause supplies this academy claim's waiver; no agency Bivens question is decided.
metadata.Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schoo: Preserves appropriate relief in the established Title IX action and distinguishes that remedial inquiry from federal sovereign consent. Compensation still requires proved intentional discrimination, recipient responsibility, causation and compensable loss; their satisfaction is not decided here.
metadata.Judgment and opinions: Affirm the judgment rejecting this compensatory-damages claim, 7–2. Supporting: Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg. Opposing: Stevens, Breyer, who would reverse the categorical bar and remand. Souter writes the Opinion of the Court, joined in full by the six other affirmers. Stevens writes a dissent joined in full by Breyer. There are no partial joins, judgment-only joins, or fractured propositions. No Marks inquiry arises.
metadata.Material record: Lane entered the United States Merchant Marine Academy in July 1991 after satisfying appointment requirements, including a Defense Department physical examination. He reported diabetes diagnosed during his first year. Following a September 1992 medical hearing, the Academy separated him in December because the condition disqualified him for the identified reserve commissions. The Department of Transportation operates the Academy through the Maritime Administration. These are published record recitations. No new medical finding, concession, or assistance-provider transaction is inferred.
metadata.Participation: Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision; no case-specific nonparticipation is established. Nine participating Justices supply a quorum; five votes suffice for a majority. The lawful channel is the granted certiorari merits review, not an independently added claim.
metadata.Result: Affirmed, 7–2, on the federal compensatory-damages waiver question; existing reinstatement undisturbed.
metadata.Stone fixed core and implementation: The approved Lane block in `../runtime/OT_1995CHUNK9_STONE.md` directs affirmance of rejection of Treasury compensatory damages under this asserted waiver, preserving the substantive duty and independently lawful prospective relief. Stone joins the whole common opinion because its remedy-specific text analysis and reservation of existing relief express that fixed core. No new officer action, implied cause or Article I immunity rule is added. No fallback vote is needed: the reviewed damages disposition and preservation of independently established relief are expressly addressed. Attorney-fee discretion is stated as statutory context; no fee application is adjudicated by fallback or otherwise.
metadata.United States Department of Energy v. Oh: Applies the distinction between federal substantive or adjudicatory coverage and the limits of incorporated monetary-remedy provisions; no pollution-remedy question is reopened.
metadata.United States v. Nordic Village, Inc., 5: Applies the requirement of unequivocal enacted consent to the particular affirmative monetary remedy; a plausible narrower statutory operation defeats the asserted waiver. The original §106(c) holding and its limits remain unchanged.

metadata.Authority: Justice Kennedy's Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg, and Breyer. All nine adopt the rule, its limits, and affirmance.
metadata.Case and dockets: Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers v. Atchison, Topeka & Santa Fe Railroad Co., No. 94-1592; 516 U.S. 152
metadata.Controlling explanation: Transportation describes the undertaking of returning the crew, including awaiting the vehicle that carries it. Nothing in the specific return provision confines that undertaking to minutes of physical movement. The general reporting-to-final-release rule in §21103(b)(1) must leave room for the express return category in §21103(b)(4). Otherwise the general language would defeat the exception Congress placed beside it.
metadata.Operative qualifications: Section 21103(a)'s ordinary eight-consecutive-hours-off requirement within the preceding twenty-four hours, and its ten-consecutive-hours-off requirement after twelve consecutive hours on duty, remain. Section (c)'s distinct emergency permission for a wreck or relief crew allows up to four additional hours in twenty-four for emergency-related work and ends when the track is cleared and the line reopened; that permission is not invoked here. Sections (b)(5)–(6) count interim rest outside a designated terminal, or shorter than four hours at a designated terminal, as duty. Section (b)(7) separately excludes an interim period available for at least four hours of rest at a place with suitable food and lodging facilities when a casualty, track obstruction, act of God, or derailment or major equipment failure prevents the employee from reaching the designated terminal; for derailment or major equipment failure, the cause must have been unknown and unforeseeable to the carrier or its officer or agent in charge of that employee when the employee left the designated terminal. Those predicates are neither found nor excused by this decision.
metadata.Operative rule: Waiting genuinely incident to transportation from a completed duty assignment to final release falls within 49 U.S.C. §21103(b)(4)'s return-transportation interval and counts as neither on-duty time nor required off-duty rest. Time engaged in or connected with movement of a train remains duty time under §21103(b)(2), as does any other service for the carrier during a twenty-four-hour period in which the employee is engaged in or connected with train movement under §21103(b)(3); transportation to a new duty assignment remains on duty.

metadata.Relief and limits: On remand use the existing Gingles/Holder/De Grandy inquiry, matched to each challenged jurisdiction and actual minority preference, then determine whether the proved violation admits a lawful, practicable correction. The existing subsidiary findings are not erased. If those facts support no dilution under the corrected legal inquiry, judgment may again favor the State. The remand is warranted by the identified legal premises; it does not add a new statistical formula, mandate more expert studies or guarantee proportional results. No intent requirement is added to §2.
metadata.Result: Eleventh Circuit judgment vacated and remanded, 5–4; no present finding of Section 2 liability or electoral restructuring.

Historical petition 95-647 identifies this same SCLC controversy; the corrected identifier changes neither the simulated merits assignment nor Stone’s disposition, reasoning or remedy. [Public judicial record](https://openjurist.org/56/f3d/1281) supplies facts, posture and argument; the same-matter historical outcome remains in Section III. These are individual legal positions. Only an effective validated simulated decision supplies governing law.
metadata.Stone’s disposition: Vacate and remand for application of §2's actual results inquiry and a lawful remedy analysis. Identify the legal errors affecting both the ultimate dilution finding and the separate remedy rationale; do not direct liability or impose subdistricts now.
metadata.Stone’s reasoning and application: The appellate discussion asks whether voters supported a candidate because of that candidate's race and begins by emphasizing the absence of discriminatory enactment or maintenance. Section 2 instead protects minority voters' opportunity to elect their preferred candidates; it does not require that the preferred candidate be Black or that plaintiffs prove racially motivated individual ballots or discriminatory legislative intent. Incumbency, qualifications, partisanship and actual preference remain relevant contextual evidence, but cannot become a substitute legal prerequisite of racial motivation. The aggregate treatment must be applied to the actual challenged electoral units. Stone would correct that legal framing while leaving supported subsidiary historical facts intact; he would not simply choose the plaintiffs' expert over the State's expert.
metadata.The independent remedy ground: Alabama's linkage of electoral and judicial territorial jurisdiction and its qualified-candidate pool deserve concrete weight. They do not confer categorical immunity from §2 or make every racially aware remedial district constitutionally suspect. The lower opinion invokes historical Shaw's racial-message rationale; actual simulated Shaw and Miller do not make racial design alone an equal-protection violation. Holder requires an appropriate benchmark and workable remedy, not an automatic override of statutory opportunity whenever the State prefers its existing structure. Reject both automatic subdistricting and the claim that no adequate remedy can exist merely because judges are independent decisionmakers.

metadata.Controlling explanation: Thermtron requires reading the review restriction with the grounds listed in §1447(c). A procedural-remand motion must be made within thirty days after removal; lack of subject-matter jurisdiction is a distinct covered ground. The district court remanded this action for untimely removal, and the remand request was timely raised. The actual stated ground thus falls within the ordinary bar. Gravitt makes clear that an asserted error in a covered remand ground does not open an appeal to decide its correctness.
metadata.Operative rule: When a removed case is remanded to the State court from which it came because of a timely raised defect in removal procedure or lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, §1447(d), read with §1447(c), bars appellate review even if removal also invoked §1452. An order remanding a case removed pursuant to §1443 may be reviewed on appeal or otherwise; that then-applicable exception is not implicated here. The rule does not declare every bankruptcy remand unreviewable.

inventory_refs.caption: United States v. Reorganized CF&I Fabricators of Utah, Inc.

metadata.Authority: Part I of Souter's Opinion of the Court, joined by Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer; eight Justices adopt the rule and complete explanation.
metadata.Case and dockets: United States v. Reorganized CF&I Fabricators of Utah, Inc., No. 95-325; October Term 1995.
metadata.Chronology and route: On writ of certiorari to the Tenth Circuit, 53 F.3d 1155, which affirmed the district court's affirmance of the bankruptcy court. The two submitted questions concern excise-tax priority under the governing pre-1994 section 507(a)(7)(E) and the sufficiency of the section 510(c) equitable-subordination ground. The United States seeks priority or, alternatively, ordinary-unsecured treatment. CF&I defends the lower ranking. The approved neutral packet and published record establish the argument and decision dates. Supreme Court merits review ends with this judgment; bankruptcy proceedings continue on remand through the court of appeals.
metadata.Controlling explanation: Feiring requires federal bankruptcy characterization by statutory operation. United States v. New York applies that inquiry to federal exactions and recognizes that a revenue tax can encourage conduct without becoming a penalty. Sotelo looks beyond a penalty label where the assessment represents taxes already withheld and not paid. Those decisions make the governing legal operation decisive, rather than importing another statute's terminology or treating every regulatory purpose as disqualifying.
metadata.Controlling proposition: The allowed 1989 section 4971(a) assessment is a noncompensatory penalty, not an excise tax entitled to priority under the governing pre-1994 section 507(a)(7)(E). When the Bankruptcy Code does not direct adoption of an external classification, the exaction's actual statutory operation controls its bankruptcy tax characterization; neither a tax label nor a deterrent purpose alone resolves that inquiry.
metadata.Entering law and statute: The frozen neutral packet, `../entering-law/OT_1995CHUNK9_JUNE20_CFI_LAW.md` and the full public reading copy of Noland, May 13, 1996, supply the pre-June20 baseline. No Gray or June20 peer enters. Feiring, New York and Sotelo govern bankruptcy characterization by operation. Actual Noland's administrative-priority holding is distinct from its limit on class-based equity; both retain their qualifications. Actual Keystone concerns section 4975's sale-or-exchange issue and supplies no holding that this section 4971 claim receives bankruptcy tax priority. Actual BFP, Wolas, Taylor, Nobelman and Rake support the recorded Justice-specific statutory methods only within their own scopes.
metadata.Judgment by component: Eight Justices preserve denial of excise-tax priority: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer. Thomas would reverse that determination. All nine set aside the stated equitable subordination and require remand; Thomas's preferred remand would also require tax treatment. The Tenth Circuit's judgment is vacated and the case remanded with its denial-of-priority legal conclusion preserved. No other disallowed claim is restored and no final distribution is directed.
metadata.Material record: CF&I and related entities sponsored two qualified pension plans. They failed to contribute approximately $12.4 million for the 1989 plan year by September 15, 1990 and filed Chapter 11 on November 7, 1990. The allowed claim under review is the approximately $1.24 million ten-percent section 4971(a) assessment. Plan qualification and basic assessment liability are undisputed. Other disallowed section 4971(a)/(b) claims are outside review. The lower courts found this assessment noncompensatory and subordinated it despite an express finding of no IRS inequitable conduct. Their reason was harm to innocent creditors, who would receive only a small fraction of their claims; PBGC was an unsecured creditor. The plan's Class 13 receives nothing, with alternative Class 12 general-unsecured placement receiving some funds if subordination or separate classification fails. Sections 1122(a), 1129(a)(7) and the claimed relevance of section 726(a)(4) were advanced as alternatives but not decided below as independent grounds.
metadata.Opinion topology: Souter writes Part I, priority, for the eight-Justice coalition just named, and Part II, equitable subordination and the remand required by that ground, for all nine. Thomas writes separately, concurring in Part II and dissenting from Part I. The majority's classification rests entirely on statutory text, established bankruptcy usage and operation; no distinct legislative-history rationale is adopted. Scalia consequently joins the complete majority priority explanation. There is no fractured controlling rule or Marks inference.
metadata.Participation and channel: Chief Justice Stone-Zsela and Justices Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer participate at argument and decision; no case-specific nonparticipation is established. Nine Justices supply a quorum and five a majority. Granted merits review permits these two separable issues; it supplies no constitutional punishment question or review of the disallowed claims.
metadata.Result: Vacated and remanded; denial of excise-tax priority preserved, 8-1; stated equitable subordination rejected, 9-0.
metadata.Stone fixed core and implementation: Only after receiving the frozen CF&I reconciliation did assembly read the CF&I block in `../runtime/OT_1995CHUNK9_STONE.md`. Stone's approved vote vacates and remands while preserving denial of excise-tax priority and setting aside categorical equitable subordination. The two holdings below reproduce those legal positions and limits, including inherited bankruptcy construction, separation from constitutional punishment, ordinary-unsecured fallback, preservation of lawful independent plan arguments and supported case-specific equity, and no unsupported dollar award. He joins both parts of the Court opinion. Both presented components and the remand are addressed expressly, so no standing fallback is needed.

metadata.Controlling explanation: The Court applies the existing demanding intermediate scrutiny, not strict scrutiny or a least-restrictive-means test. Craig v. Boren supplies the important-objective and substantial-relationship requirements; Mississippi University for Women v. Hogan places the burden on the State and requires justification for the discriminatory allocation itself. Hogan's exceedingly persuasive justification describes that burden. J.E.B. rejects sex as a conclusive proxy for individual capacity, while Kelley permits genuinely justified sex-conscious educational choices. Klinger requires comparison of the particular benefit and gives neither immunity nor automatic liability merely because whole institutions differ.
